Sports.title: Why McLaren thinks Norris is even better now than his F1 title-winning year
Sports.content:
Just over a month ago, it seemed pretty clear that McLaren was going to be unable to successfully defend the Formula 1 drivers’ title in 2026.

Coming into the Hungarian Grand Prix, Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli led the standings with 204 points to his name, while the papaya drivers combined couldn’t even match that tally – Lando Norris was on 103, Oscar Piastri on 92.

However, McLaren introduced a substantial upgrade package at the Hungaroring, focusing on front and rear corner bodywork as well as introducing a floor and rear wing.

The consequence was immediate: Norris won from pole and repeated the feat in Zandvoort, courtesy of a round-the-outside move on challenger Antonelli in Turn 1. He is now ‘just’ 83 points adrift of the championship lead.

The straightforward conclusion would be that McLaren’s updates simply delivered, but team principal Andrea Stella is adamant that Norris is consistently extracting the most from the MCL40 – even hinting at the Briton outperforming his machinery.

“Lando is driving and operating at a very high level, in absolute sense, in relation to a Formula 1 world champion,” Stella commented following the Dutch Grand Prix. “He's driving at the level of a world champion.

Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Mark Sutton / Formula 1 via Getty Images

“And like I always say for Lando, what I like the most of his journey in Formula 1 is that he keeps improving. And especially after the start of the 2025 season, something clicked, which is not only a single click, but is a way of working with Lando, for Lando, and that we are adopting also on Oscar's side now in particular. And this approach has led Lando to continuous improvements.

“So it's almost like I see Lando stronger and stronger race by race. Because this weekend was nowhere near a weekend in which we could fight for the victory for granted, especially after having seen the performance in the sprint.

“But we invested in trying to understand where was the opportunity from a tyre exploitation point of view, and car improvement. Actually, both drivers improved from this point of view, but unfortunately a question mark remains as to the behaviour of the second stint of Oscar.

“So there's overall a positive trajectory for both, but at the moment Lando is capable of maximising the performance in qualifying trim. If we think the start of 2025, this had become a bit of a concern that he overcame. And then, when you have conditions in which the car slides in the race, there's not much grip, he is the master in this kind of conditions.”

Qualifying performance indeed is a key point to look at.

Over the course of the 2025 season, the McLaren drivers were evenly matched on one lap, with their qualifying head-to-head (including sprint qualifying) a perfect 15-15 split.

As F1 switched to new machinery in 2026, Norris was down 3-1 going into the unexpected April break. But since then, the reigning champion has thrashed his team-mate 12-1, with Piastri quicker in Monaco only. The average gap between them is not huge – 0.128s – but it is consistently to Norris’ advantage, amid the Australian’s latest struggles.

Lando Norris' move on Kimi Antonelli Photo by: Michael Potts / LAT Images via Getty Images

Yet, Stella reckons what really has been making the difference is Norris’ enhanced state of mind, leading to perfected racecraft.

“If you want to look at Lando from another angle, I would say that definitely he is now expressing a higher level of assertiveness as he drives,” the Italian pointed out. “You know, the manoeuvre to pass Antonelli today is a really good demonstration of that. He's demonstrating more self-confidence.

“This is interesting, and I quite like it – the self-confidence sometimes is not demonstrated by being the most aggressive. Sometimes you are self-confident when you think like, ‘You know what? I'm not going to have a fight now because I may lose in this fight. It's a very long race. See you at the end of the race.’

“It's this confidence in your means, in your strength, that I quite like. Which means that sometimes you are actually the one backing off when the situation becomes too risky.

“We need to remember that in the last couple of races that he won, he didn't defend the pole position. He was actually second at the end of the first lap. But I did not hear or perceive any decay in his confidence, as to the fact that he was fast and he was just preparing his opportunity to then cash in on his competitiveness. So I think assertiveness and confidence are probably the two characteristics that he has improved the most from a non-technical, non-operational point of view.”

Additional reporting by Ronald Vording and Filip Cleeren

Sports.title: Norris extends McLaren contract until 2030 | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Reigning world champion Lando Norris has signed a new deal keeping him at McLaren until at least 2030.

The team made the announcement during McLaren’s annual factory open day for family and friends.

“McLaren is my home, and I’m very pleased to be signing a new contract to keep me with the team until at least 2030,” said Norris.

When I started this journey nine years ago, I was clear about the goals I wanted to achieve: to get McLaren back to the front and to win championships,” he continued. “We’ve achieved that goal, but we want more, we want to keep on winning, and we know as a team that we’re capable of achieving it.”

Norris made his Formula 1 debut with the team in 2019 and has raced for them ever since. He scored his first grand prix victory in 2024 and won the world championship with them last year. He already hold the record for the longest F1 career spent entirely at a single team, having started 163 grands prix for them so far, 13 of which he won.

McLaren also confirmed Norris will receive one of the MCL39 chassis he raced during his championship-winning 2025 season.

Following Oscar Piastri’s new deal with the team last year, both McLaren’s drivers are contracted to drive for the team until at least 2028.

McLaren Racing CEO Zak Brown said he was “incredibly pleased” with Norris’s new deal. “His journey with the team is a fantastic example of our commitment to identifying, developing and supporting world-class talent, and his achievements speak for themselves.

“Together with Andrea [Stella, team princpal], Oscar and the wider team, Lando has helped drive McLaren into a new papaya era of success, helping us go from the back of the grid, to double consecutive constructors’ titles in 2024 and 2025 and our first drivers’ championship in 17 years. We are extremely excited about what lies ahead and remain fully focused on continuing to compete for wins and championships.”

Sports.title: Featured Comment: Reintroducing refuelling would bring more negatives than positives | Brief
Sports.content:
Formula 1 team bosses are right to argue Mohammed Ben Sulayem’s plan to reintroduce refuelling would create more negatives than positives, says reader @Stefmeister:

I wasn’t a fan of refuelling in F1 the last time and I wouldn’t be in favour of it returning.

I just always felt that it was more detrimental to the racing and never really liked the impact it had on how the races played out or how it impacted strategies.

Refuelling was always more planned and easier to read and predict with less room to adapt and change what you were doing based on how your race was playing out or what those around you were doing. You came up with a strategy the day before, went into the first stint with say 20 laps of fuel and with little room to alter that stint length the rest of your race had to be based off that.

Before and after when it was just about tyres things are a lot more reactive, harder to plan, harder to predict and you have a lot more room to change things on the fly based off how your race and what those around you are doing.

Today you can start a race looking to stop on lap 20 but if your tyres are wearing less than expected then you have scope to go a lot longer which you don’t have with refueling because if you put 20 laps of fuel in then you can’t go much longer without doing massive fuel saving.

And drivers in general have less input with refueling because yes they can do things to save fuel but they are still limited by how much was put in the tank. With tyres they can do more to extend, They can have input on changing strategy and can ask to go long if they feel tyres are holding on et cetera…

Just overall for me refueling introduces far more negatives than positives and I’d hate to see it come back.

@Stefmeister

Sports.title: Alpine confirm Colapinto will remain alongside Gasly in 2027 line-up | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Alpine has confirmed Franco Colapinto will remain at the team next year for what will be his second full season in Formula 1.

The 23-year-old joined the team last season, replacing Jack Doohan from the seventh round of the season in Miami. He ended the season point-less as Alpine struggled throughout the year with an uncompetitive car.

He has enjoyed more success this year, his first full season as an F1 driver, taking his best result so far with sixth place in the Canadian Gerand Prix. Colapinto has scored 19 points so far, putting him 12 in the championship, two places behind team mate Pierre Gasly.

The pair will remain team mates next year. “For me, having consistency is very important,” said Alpine’s executive consultant Flavio Briatore. “We are now settled from a driver point of view and I have said many times that, while this is an important piece of the puzzle, the most significant we have to get right is designing and building a fast race car which absolutely remains our number one priority.

“We have seen Franco truly grow and mature into a great driver this year. His results in Miami and Montreal especially confirmed what I already knew: Franco belongs in Formula 1 and he belongs at this team.”

Colapinto said he is “very pleased” to renew his contract with Alpine. “I feel very happy and very settled here and it’s been even better that we have made significant progress this year compared to last.”

He made his F1 debut in 2024 at Williams, replacing Logan Sargeant after the Dutch Grand Prix. The Alpine driver is the only Argentinian to race in F1 over the last 20 years and the team arranged a show run for him in Buenos Aires in April.

Sports.title: Mercedes told Antonelli he would get F1 chance before Hamilton’s exit was announced | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli has revealed how quickly Mercedes reacted to Lewis Hamilton’s decision to leave the team at the beginning of 2024.

The world championship leader said he first learned Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff intended to promote him to the team before Hamilton’s decision to join Ferrari was announced.

Ferrari announced Hamilton would join them in February 2024. Antonelli said Mercedes told him of their decision shortly beforehand.

“It’s 2024, the year I’m turning 18, it’s February, I was in Silverstone,” he said in a recent interview for one of the team’s sponsors. “I was testing Formula 3 to learn the track, because I was going to race there with Formula 2.

“I remember at the end of the day, Toto called me over to his office. And already there, I was a bit confused, because I’m like, [this] doesn’t really happen.

“So I got into his office. Obviously, it’s Toto, there’s Rosa [Herrero Venegas, PR manager] and she’s the one helping me during race weekends.

“Toto, first of all, didn’t waste any time, went straight to the point and it was like this was even before Lewis was announced. To Ferrari. So he said, look, Lewis is going to Ferrari and we were thinking to put you in the car for next year. And I’m like, ‘whoa’.”

Antonelli had won the Formula Regional European Championship the year before. “My eyes were wide open and I was like, ‘are you kidding me?’ Because I hadn’t even started F2.

“So I had still so much to prove that I could earn that spot. And Toto was already talking about it.”

Wolff asked Antonelli if he would be ready for the opportunity. “I said, yeah, I’ve got to be ready,” Antonelli recalled.

Mercedes began a programme of F1 tests for Antonelli that year, culminating in his first appearance in an official practice session at Monza. Although Antonelli crashed five laps into the session, the following day Mercedes announced he would take Hamilton’s place in 2025.

However Antonelli had already learned of Mercedes’ decision long before that weekend.

“The official announcement came just at the start of summer break. It was, I think, just the start of August, probably, first day of August. I was at home with my family, and Toto organised this call, and where there were also all the big names from Mercedes.

“There was James Allison [technical director], Gwen Lagrue, who was the one who took me in the junior programme. There was Bradley [Lord], Rosa again, there was all of the big ones. Toto in the call went straight to the point and said he’s going to be our driver for next year. And it was an incredible moment.”

Sports.title: Why F1 team bosses believe refuelling “doesn’t add a lot to the spectacle” | Formula 1
Sports.content:
FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has suggested reintroducing refuelling to Formula 1 as a means of making the cars run at a lower weight.

However three bosses asked about the proposal are not convinced it would improve the racing.

Racing Bulls team principal Peter Bayer, who previously worked as the FIA’s secretary general, said the idea has been studied recently and found wanting.

“When I was still working with the FIA, we had a working group with Formula 1, with Ross Brawn [former F1 sporting director] back in the days, and his team, about how to improve the entertainment, the spectacle.

“One of the big ideas of some people was refuelling. We were digging very deep into historic footage, data that we had, and it showed that other than a couple of very spectacular and dangerous images, refuelling has not done really anything for the sport because most of the overtaking suddenly took place in the pit lane. So I wouldn’t be a big fan of that because it’s proven that it actually doesn’t add a lot to the spectacle.”

Refuelling also adds complexity for fans who are trying to follow the races, said Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu.

“I’m personally not a big fan of refuelling, really,” he said. “When I was watching from outside, refuelling, it’s just that the race was so difficult to understand as a spectator sitting on the stand.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“Also in terms of qualifying, et cetera. I’m fond of a qualifying car being the lightest, the driver going for everything. So in short, I’m not fond of refuelling – and also the weight and cost and everything – I’m not a big fan.”

Williams team principal James Vowles, who previously headed Mercedes’ strategy division, pointed out that refuelling would take a lot of the intrigue away from pit stops.

“We could fundamentally predict exactly where the car is going to stop. You’re always going to take the car right to the end of its fuel load because that’s when it’s its fastest, which now means you can predict what’s going to happen, whether someone’s on a two or three or one, it doesn’t matter.

“Nowadays, with the exposure to the outside world, everyone will start getting that information. It actually takes quite a bit of the intrigue out of it for me.”

However he said he is in favour of trying to reduce the weight of the cars. “I’m completely in support of that,” he said. “I think going back to refuelling is not the right solution for it, however.

Vowles also admitted to having a personal reason to oppose refuelling. “It’s quite warm wearing a race suit when you’re on the pit wall, so I’d prefer not to do that again!”

Sports.title: Chantelle Cameron Outworks Mikaela Mayer for Three Belts
Sports.content:
Cameron kept advancing, finding right hands at close range before increasing her body attack from the fifth round. That gave Mayer more to defend than the punches coming upstairs. Once Cameron got close, Mayer needed a way to interrupt her work and create room again. Trading there gave Cameron the kind of fight she wanted.

By the eighth, Mayer was bleeding from the nose. Cameron suffered a cut near her left eye in the ninth, but neither backed off. Both continued exchanging through the closing seconds of the tenth, with Cameron’s sustained inside work earning her the decision.

The fighters confirmed afterward that a rematch is planned, and Mayer has an adjustment to make beyond starting well behind her jab.

Lateral movement after punching and tying Cameron up before she can unload inside are possible answers. Mayer needs to make her opponent earn each approach, rather than allowing one successful entry to become a prolonged exchange.

Cameron wants their second meeting contested over three-minute rounds. Longer rounds would give her more time to sustain those attacks before the bell, but the benefit is not automatic. She would have to maintain that output, while Mayer would have more time to establish her jab and make Cameron miss.

Their first meeting rewarded Cameron’s ability to keep working at close quarters. Unless Mayer can shorten those exchanges, another fast start may leave her facing the same difficult second half.

Sports.title: Lester Martinez Looks To Make A Statement Against Luka Plantic
Sports.content:
When asked about who he thinks will win, Trainer Esau Dieguez believes Canelo will ultimately win the fight, and they hope it will earn Lester the world title fight. However, to do so, he must first get past undefeated challenger Plantic. He must not overlook or underestimate Luka, who could pose some technical challenges.

A fighter who had success in the amateurs, having defeated a young Mbilli. Esau knows he is a legitimate threat and has prepared for that: “We know he’s a strong fighter, and he’s coming into this fight fully prepared. Seeing who he trained with and prepared with [Joel Diaz] for this fight, we know the trainers he has are good, but we are confident we will win. We prepared extremely hard…extremely hard, and we expect to win. We didn’t come to see if we can but because we can.”

Martinez has an 80 percent knockout ratio but struggled to drop the gritty and tough veteran Immanuel Aleem in his last fight, going the distance. Lester appears focused and ready to demonstrate he is worthy of a world title, telling us at yesterday’s weigh-in what he expects from Plantic: “Look, I’ve fought with undefeated fighters; I’ve had those experiences. The boxer who we’re fighting tomorrow has a good record and has good power from what I can assess from his record. He’s a good fighter. I think this fight will lend itself to prove I’m adept to fight for the world title.”

Lester had his training camp in Colorado Springs, training in elevation, scaling the rigorous Manitou Incline multiple times during camp to build his stamina and conditioning. He even had a sparring session with former undisputed super middleweight champion Terence Crawford.

Luka may have amateur experience but is limited as a professional, having only fought in thirteen fights. Martinez will test him on the inside and may choose to box instead of exchange with him once he feels his power. This is Lester’s moment, with his countrymen coming out in full support to back the Guatemalan interim champion, he must now perform to expectations and give them a great show, anything less than a dominant performance may delay his championship aspirations. Plantic will seek to test Martinez’s technical abilities; Lester must effectively cut the ring and utilize his jab, which will be key in his victory.

Sports.title: Will Queensberry Risk Itauma Against Hrgovic Again?
Sports.content:
Itauma remained in distress afterward and was removed from the ring on a stretcher. Frank Warren later attributed that to a leg injury and exhaustion, but the closing sequence still showed a young heavyweight with nothing left when Hrgovic attacked.

Darshan Desai offered the sympathetic reading shared by many Itauma supporters:

“Moses Itauma will come again. He is 21 and he looked sensational at points in that fight. Just needs to work on his gas tank, and get more rounds and experience. I still think he’ll win a world title very soon.”

That may all prove true. Itauma’s career does not need to be buried after one loss at 21. Yet “coming again” should mean rebuilding, not returning to the heavyweight who left him helpless against the ropes. It could be more than a gas tank that Itauma needs for him to beat Hrgovic. Punch resistance has a lot to do with it, too. Itauma showed that he can dish it out, but he can’t take return fire nearly as well.

Queensberry Sent Him There Too Soon

Before facing Hrgovic, Itauma had completed only 31 professional rounds. He had never gone beyond the sixth and had boxed only five rounds against Jermaine Franklin in his previous contest.

Hrgovic brought more than 100 professional rounds and experience against Daniel Dubois and Zhilei Zhang. He had already fought while exhausted, hurt and under heavy pressure. None of those conditions had confronted Itauma before.

That difference took control once the fight moved beyond Itauma’s familiar territory. The early speed remained impressive, and he dropped Hrgovic in the second. Instead of treating the knockdown as part of a 12-round fight, Itauma continued pouring power into combinations against a man known for absorbing punishment.

Once Hrgovic survived, Itauma’s energy drained and no second method surfaced. There was no lower gear to conserve strength, no defensive adjustment and no way to discourage the Croatian once he began walking forward.

Itauma’s stamina problem was inseparable from his defensive collapse. He spent too much energy whenever Hrgovic was hurt, then remained in punching range with his hands low, leaving him vulnerable. Hrgovic was able to recover while landing heavy shots of his own. He showed tonight that he doesn’t have the gas tank to go for a finish against a heavyweight like Hrgovic. Itauma was throwing wildly, getting caught with right hands from Hrgovic. A second fight would invite the same problems.

The rush to make Itauma one of the youngest heavyweight champions helped create this situation. His knockout victories allowed Queensberry to promote every short night as evidence that he was ready. In truth, those quick finishes denied him the preparation he needed before meeting someone who would not disappear.

If Queensberry wants to throw Itauma back on the frontlines against Hrgovic, they could be risking his career. He looked battle-torn at the end, being stretchered out of the ring. After the way this fight ended, there’s no way of knowing how this will affect him. Given his age, he doesn’t need to fight Hrgovic again.

Pride Cannot Choose Itauma’s Next Fight

The difficulty will come if Itauma demands another chance. Queensberry spent months presenting him as the next heavyweight ruler and a fighter mature beyond his years. Losing after that buildup creates more than disappointment. The urge to erase the defeat may convince him that beating Hrgovic is the only way to recover what vanished against the ropes.

A second fight would give Hrgovic knowledge that cannot be erased. He knows he can absorb Itauma’s early attack, extend him beyond the rounds he prefers and overwhelm him once the speed and energy disappear.

Itauma’s endurance requires work, but so do his pacing, defensive discipline and ability to survive when a durable opponent refuses to fold. Those improvements come through fights and rounds, not through revisiting a frightening stoppage after one training camp.

Hrgovic has IBF mandatory Frank Sanchez waiting for him. Queensberry should allow that fight to proceed while Itauma recovers and learns how to operate after his early attack fails. If Itauma becomes the champion his handlers promised, Hrgovic may still be there later.

Sending him directly back would not prove confidence. It would show that Queensberry allowed a badly hurt 21-year-old to make a critical career decision while pride and shame were still driving him.

Sports.title: Filip Hrgovic Breaks Moses Itauma in Ninth
Sports.content:
Hrgovic Stops Itauma in Round Nine

IBF Intercontinental champion and 2016 Olympic bronze medalist Filip “El Animal” Hrgovic, 21-1 (16), stopped WBO Intercontinental champion Moses Itauma, 14-1 (12), at 2:27 of the ninth round. The bout was scheduled for 12 rounds.

Itauma dropped Hrgovic to one knee with a left hand during the second round. Referee Howard Foster administered an eight-count before allowing the action to continue.

The southpaw’s hand speed, sharp combinations and body punching carried the next several rounds. Itauma repeatedly beat Hrgovic to the punch and built a large lead while the Croatian absorbed heavy shots without breaking.

Everything changed once Itauma crossed into territory he had never experienced as a professional. His movement slowed, his punches lost force, and his defensive shape began to disappear.

Hrgovic attacked from the opening seconds of the ninth. A right hand hurt Itauma midway through the round, and the exhausted challenger struggled to remain upright. He eventually collapsed into the corner, prompting trainer Ben Davison to throw in the towel as Foster halted the contest.

Itauma had done most of the better boxing, but Hrgovic had prepared for the portion of the fight that the younger man had never seen. The early knockouts that built Itauma’s reputation offered no evidence of how his body would respond after six hard rounds against a full-sized heavyweight who refused to leave.

Hrgovic credited his Christian faith after the comeback.

“It was not me tonight. It was Jesus Christ in me. Holy Spirit.”

The new champion admitted Itauma had outboxed him and said he did not know where the energy for his ninth-round attack came from. He also thanked trainer Abel Sanchez, manager Keith Connolly and the rest of his team for producing the best training camp of his career.

Itauma required medical attention and was removed from the ring on a stretcher after the fight. Hrgovic became Croatia’s first heavyweight world champion.

Sam Noakes Decisions Denys Berinchyk

In the co-main event, former British and Commonwealth lightweight champion Sam Noakes, 19-1 (16), defeated former WBO champion and 2012 Olympic silver medalist Denys Berinchyk, 19-2 (9), by unanimous decision over 10 rounds. The vacant WBO International lightweight title was at stake.

Noakes outworked Berinchyk during the opening four rounds as the Ukrainian returned from an 18-month absence. A right hand stunned Berinchyk during the closing seconds of the fifth.

Berinchyk had a better eighth despite eating another right hand near the bell. Noakes regained control in the tenth and closed the fight strongly.

The judges scored it 100-90, 99-91 and 98-92. Bob Williams was the referee.

Constantin Ursu Retains After Vaughan Cut

British and Commonwealth welterweight champion Constantin “The Moldovan Monster” Ursu, 16-0 (7), knocked out Ben “The Bomber” Vaughan, 12-3 (4), at 0:03 of the eighth round.

Vaughan gave Ursu a competitive fight before an accidental clash of heads opened a cut over his right eyebrow in the fifth. The injury worsened as the bout continued, while Ursu began taking firmer control during the seventh.

The ringside doctor inspected Vaughan twice. With the eye closing and the cut no longer safe, the contest was stopped before meaningful action began in the eighth. Michael Alexander was the referee.

Nelson Hysa Stops Thomas Narmo

WBA Gold and WBO Global heavyweight champion Nelson “The Albanian Eagle” Hysa, 25-0 (23) knocked out Thomas “The Last Viking” Narmo, 14-1 (14), at 0:36 of the second round of a scheduled 10.

Hysa took the first round before closing the fight early in the second. A lead right landed against the side of Narmo’s head and sent him down. Narmo beat the count, but referee Howard Foster determined that he was in no condition to continue.

Aloys Youmbi Outpoints Sherif Musah

WBC Continental cruiserweight champion Aloys Youmbi, 12-1 (9), 205¼, of Penge, South London, defeated Sherif Musah, 4-2-1 (2), 202¼, of London, by decision.

Youmbi was returning after more than a year away and had prepared to face southpaw Mike Perez before Musah accepted the fight on short notice. The switch to an orthodox opponent contributed to an awkward opening.

Through the first three rounds, Youmbi held the edge by countering the aggressive Musah. A right uppercut rocked Musah during the final 15 seconds of the third, forcing him to hold.

Musah remained competitive during the closing rounds, but Youmbi landed the cleaner punches. Referee Lee Every scored the six-round bout 60-54.

Arbnor Jashari Defeats Numan Hussain

Lightweight Arbnor “Kid Dynamite” Jashari, 10-0 (3), defeated Numan Hussain, 8-2 (2) by a six-round points decision.

Jashari rocked Hussain with a right hand during the closing seconds of the second. Hussain answered before the bell, but Jashari’s quicker combinations carried the remaining rounds.

Referee Lee Every scored it 59-55.

Guido Vianello and Moses Jolly Draw

WBC Continental Americas heavyweight champion and Italian Olympian Guido “The Gladiator” Vianello, 14-3-2 (12), drew with late replacement Moses “The Native” Jolly, 12-0-1 (8), in an eight-round bout.

Vianello bloodied Jolly’s nose with a right hand in the second. Jolly turned the fight into a rougher contest and tossed Vianello to the canvas during the fourth, although it was not ruled a knockdown.

Blood from Vianello’s left ear required an examination by the ringside doctor. Both heavyweights had success during the seventh and eighth, leaving referee Amy Pu to score the fight 76-76.

The draw reflected eight untidy but competitive rounds. Vianello delivered the straighter punches, while Jolly’s pressure and physical strength kept him in the fight.

Tony Curtis Edges Imad Naseeb

Super flyweight Tony “Lightning” Curtis Jr., 14-1 (3), 112½, of Woolwich, London, defeated Imad Naseeb, 8-1 (2), 111½, of Warrington, over six rounds.

Naseeb switched between southpaw and orthodox while pressing forward through the first four rounds. Referee Lee Every warned him several times for punches behind the head.

During the fifth and sixth rounds, Naseeb trapped Curtis in a corner and knocked out his mouthpiece in each round. Curtis, trained by Roy Jones Jr., continued moving and countering well enough to take the decision.

Every scored it 58-56.

Frankie Wood Stops Callum Lee

Featherweight southpaw Frankie Wood, 5-0 (2) stopped Callum Lee, 8-1 (1), at 1:21 of the sixth and final round.

Lee’s left eye began swelling during the opening round, although much of Wood’s work was directed toward the body. Lee countered effectively and remained competitive through five.

Wood increased the pressure in the sixth and dropped Lee with a lead right hook to the chin. Lee rose, but referee Amy Pu waved off the contest after deciding he was unable to continue safely.

Sam King Outpoints Jack Swallow

Middleweight Sam King, 7-0-1 (1), defeated Jack “Mad Dog” Swallow, 4-13-1 (1), by points.

Returning after six months away, King pressed the action and kept Swallow on the defensive for most of the contest. King’s work rate and cleaner punches decided the rounds.

Referee Amy Pu scored it 40-36.

Zayn Ahmed Stops Liam Fitzmaurice

Super featherweight southpaw Zayn “The Hurricane” Ahmed, 3-0 (1), 130¼, of Slough, stopped Liam Fitzmaurice, 0-19, 132½, of Tyldesley, Lancashire, at 2:47 of the second round of a scheduled four.

During the final minute of the second, Ahmed landed a right to the body that dropped Fitzmaurice. Referee Amy Pu immediately stopped the bout.

Hassan Ishaq Decisions Enzo Munoz

Super bantamweight Hassan “Shooter” Ishaq, 4-0 (3), defeated Enzo “El Bulls” Bahiano Munoz, 4-17-4 (2), over four rounds.

Ishaq’s punches caused swelling around Munoz’s left eye during the opening round. Munoz switched to southpaw and remained durable, producing his best attack during the closing seconds of the fourth.

Munoz had been stopped only once and again lasted the distance. It was Ishaq’s first professional bout to reach the scorecard.

Referee Lee Every scored it 40-36.

Thomas Treiber served as ring announcer.

Sports.title: Hrgovic Stops an Exhausted Moses Itauma
Sports.content:
It was a classic case of conditioning issues and inexperience, alongside a protected resume, finally catching up with the young phenom. Itauma collapsed into the turnbuckle late from pure exhaustion, which forced the corner to throw in the towel. Hrgovic makes history as Croatia’s first heavyweight world champion.

The 21-year-old Brit opened fast, dropping Hrgovic during round two with precise punches. Itauma built an early lead across the middle rounds through crisp flurries plus dedicated body work. Hrgovic showed off his granite chin, soaking up heavy artillery while remaining dangerous inside the pocket.

Things flipped once the contest pushed past six rounds, taking Itauma into uncharted territory. His output plummeted, his technique unraveled, then his gas tank hit empty. Hrgovic maintained steady forward momentum. Itauma stumbled badly after missing a right hand, fell against the ropes, prompting his corner to end the bout. It delivered pure drama following their heated weigh-in scuffle, proving veteran toughness outlasts raw explosiveness over the long haul.

One could see it happening slowly after the five rounds, as Itauma had his mouth wide open, sucking air like a fish out of water, showing the classic signs of a fighter unequipped for fast-paced fights that move beyond 4 rounds. More than that. Itauma just wasn’t used to getting hit back due to the poor opposition his Queensberry promoters had matched him against. They did him no favors by matching him the way they did, and tonight was an example of what happens when promoters do this to their fighters.

Hrgovic Credits His Faith and Camp

Hrgovic admitted Itauma had outboxed him through much of the fight and credited the comeback to his Christian faith.

“It was not me tonight. It was Jesus Christ in me. Holy Spirit.”

He said he had been losing every round and did not know where the energy for his ninth-round attack came from. Hrgovic attributed the late surge to the Holy Spirit.

The new champion also thanked Abel Sanchez for getting him into the best condition of his career, manager Keith Connolly for changing his life and the rest of his team for building what he called a perfect training camp. Itauma had won the boxing match through eight rounds, but Hrgovic’s preparation and endurance kept him alive long enough to reverse it.

The win makes Hrgovic Croatia’s first heavyweight world champion.

Queensberry Promotions has a big decision to make about whether they put their young fighter, Itauma, back in with Hrgovic again for a rematch. It’s not a good sign that Itauma had to be taken out of the ring on a stretcher after the contest. They would be taking a big risk with Itauma if they put him back in with Hrgovic. If he loses again, his career would be irreparably damaged, and it would be hard to come back from it.

On the flip side, they can’t return him long-term to the type of opposition that they’d been matching him against for the last 3 years since he turned pro. Before tonight’s fight, Itauma had faced largely older fighters in their 40s and late 30s. Queensberry had done an admirable job of making him look invincible, but it had done nothing to develop him. We saw tonight that Itauma wasn’t remotely prepared for an opponent that could take him past six rounds and hit him back.

Sports.title: Moses Itauma vs Filip Hrgovic Live Results and Fight Updates
Sports.content:
Lightweight Sam Noakes (19-1, 16 KOs) collected the vacant WBO International lightweight title after securing a wide unanimous decision over Denys Berinchyk. The judges turned in matching wide cards of 100-90, 99-91, and 98-92.

The 29-year-old Noakes relied on steady volume, youth, and physical strength to break down the veteran former champion across ten full rounds. Noakes maintained complete control from the pocket, building an insurmountable lead without needing a knockdown to seal the result.

The bout served as Berinchyk’s return to action following his world title defeat against Keyshawn Davis in February 2025. For Noakes, the dominant performance offered an emphatic bounce-back victory after his close decision loss to Abdullah Mason for the WBO belt last November.

Guido Vianello and Moses Jolly Fight to Draw

Guido Vianello (14-3-2, 12 KOs) and Moses Jolly (12-0-1, 8 KOs) settled for an unpopular eight-round draw after referee Amy Pu turned in a 76-76 scorecard. Vianello seemed to control the action, dictating the tempo from the opening bell.

The Italian landed crisp, direct punches, relying on sharp boxing fundamentals. Jolly refused to fold, smothering the range to turn stretches of the bout into an ugly inside scrap.

Bleeding from Vianello’s left ear prompted a doctor’s check early in round seven, though the action was allowed to continue. It goes down as another frustrating verdict for Vianello, who boxed well enough to take the win, only to come away empty-handed on the official card.

Nelson Hysa Stops Thomas Narmo in Round Two

Heavyweight Nelson Hysa (25-0, 23 KOs) stopped Thomas Narmo (14-1) by second-round TKO. He spent the first round studying the 6-foot-7 Narmo. Once round two started, Hysa went straight on the attack. He landed a crushing right hand that sent Narmo tumbling into the corner. Narmo managed to stand, but he was clearly unsteady, forcing the referee to halt the bout.

It was a classic performance from Hysa. He took a quick look at his opponent, brought heavy pressure, and finished the job early. Live reports highlighted how quickly he charged forward to drop Narmo. Hysa took the opening round 10 to 9 on the official card before securing the stoppage.

Constantin Ursu Stops Ben Vaughan in Round Eight

Welterweight Constantin Ursu (16-0, 7 KOs) stopped Ben Vaughan (12-3, 4 KOs) by eighth-round TKO after a severe cut forced a halt to the action.

The contest remained competitive through the early rounds until an accidental head clash in the fifth opened a deep gash above the right eye of Vaughan. The corner worked hard between rounds, allowing Vaughan to stay in the pocket and test Ursu. The ringside physician examined the damage, gave the green light, but stepped in for a second look during round eight. With the laceration worsening, the doctor called an end to the bout.

It was an unfortunate technical stoppage rather than a brutal beatdown, closing out what had been an entertaining scrap. Ursu preserves his undefeated record and retains both of his titles.

Arbnor Jashari Outpoints Numan Hussain

Arbnor Jashari remained perfect with a clear points decision over Numan Hussain. The Swiss Albanian prospect was quicker to the punch and produced the sharper combinations, repeatedly beating the 38-year-old former Southern Area champion during the exchanges. Hussain used his experience and durability to remain in the contest, but lacked the speed and output needed to disrupt Jashari’s control.

Aloys Youmbi Decisions Sherif Musah

Aloys Youmbi returned from a year outside the ring with a 10-round decision over late replacement Sherif Musah. The cruiserweight initially struggled with the change in opponent after preparing for southpaw Mike Perez. Musah’s orthodox stance, forward pressure and clinching dragged Youmbi into an awkward inside fight, where several of his early right hands missed the target. Youmbi eventually corrected his footwork and found success with short hooks while leaving the clinches. Musah denied him the crowd-pleasing knockout, but Youmbi was never seriously troubled and controlled enough rounds to earn the decision.

Tony Curtis Defeats Imad Naseeb by Points

Tony Curtis controlled the six-rounder with his jab, hand speed and longer reach, keeping Imad Naseeb from settling into effective punching range. Naseeb tried to force his way inside but spent too much of the fight following Curtis without landing enough clean work. Curtis remained composed, dictated where the exchanges took place and collected the referee’s decision.

Frankie Wood Stops Callum Lee in Round Six

Frankie Wood broke through in the final round after Callum Lee had made him work for the victory. Lee remained competitive through much of the scheduled six-round bout, but Wood’s sustained pressure gradually wore him down. The stoppage gave Wood the most impressive result among the early undercard winners and ended Lee’s perfect record.

Sam King Outpoints Jack Swallow

Sam King used his size and steadier work rate to take a six-round points decision over Jack Swallow. The durable Swallow stayed with him and completed the distance, but King produced the cleaner boxing and controlled most of the rounds. It was a professional performance against an opponent accustomed to extending developing fighters.

Zayn Ahmed Stops Liam Fitzmaurice in Round Two

Zayn Ahmed made quick work of Liam Fitzmaurice, forcing the stoppage during the second round of their scheduled four-round bout. Ahmed took command early and did not allow Fitzmaurice’s greater professional experience to turn the contest into a prolonged affair. The result was the most predictable of the opening bouts, with Fitzmaurice losing.

Hassan Ishaq Decisions Enzo Bahiano Munoz

Hassan Ishaq had to settle for his first points victory after beginning his career with three stoppages. Enzo Bahiano Munoz absorbed Ishaq’s offense and remained in the fight through all four rounds, but offered too little in return to threaten an upset. Ishaq adjusted, boxed his way through the distance and earned a comfortable decision.

Sports.title: Ben Whittaker Gets Bivol Route Without Elite Win
Sports.content:
Calling Wallace Whittaker’s toughest test says more about Whittaker’s matchmaking than it does about the Australian-based fighter.

Wallace’s Ranking Does All The Work

His entire professional career has taken place in Australia, and BoxRec ranks him No. 16 among light heavyweights. His best win was a split decision over Jerome Pampellone in August 2024. Since then, he has beaten Asemahle Wellem, Dylan Colin and Walter Gabriel Sequeira.

Sequeira was 28-13-2 when Wallace stopped him in April. That victory helped preserve the glossy record Matchroom can now present as Whittaker’s arrival at world level.

In practical terms, Wallace is Richard Rivera or Benjamin Gavazi with a better sanctioning body number attached. If he had built this record on British cards, he would be described as a domestic-level fighter. The IBF position does not transform him into one of the world’s leading light heavyweights.

His style also flatters Whittaker. Wallace advances in upright lines and does not apply the rough inside pressure Liam Cameron used to disrupt him. He should provide room for Whittaker to move, showboat, and fire counters at a target coming directly toward him.

Cameron made Whittaker uncomfortable by crowding him and turning the fight physical. Wallace has not shown that same ability. Matchroom found a fighter carrying a large reward while presenting fewer of the difficulties Whittaker still needs to solve.

The Dangerous Opponents Remain Elsewhere

At 29, with an Olympic silver medal and four years as a professional, Whittaker should be past opposition designed to flatter him. Rivera and Gavazi already served that purpose. Wallace brings a much greater reward without a corresponding increase in danger.

Would it really have been asking too much for Eddie Hearn to pursue Joshua Buatsi, Imam Khataev, Willy Hutchinson, Radivoje Kalajdzic or Arlen Lopez?

Lopez was the obvious choice. He defeated Whittaker in the Olympic gold medal fight, giving Matchroom a revenge story that required no promotional invention. Whittaker could have settled the biggest loss of his amateur career while proving he belongs near Bivol.

Instead, we get Wallace. Not Buatsi. Not Khataev. Not Hutchinson. Not the Cuban who denied Whittaker Olympic gold. Wallace.

The IBF created this soft route through regional belts and a split decision over Pampellone. Matchroom was happy to take it. Whittaker can reach the front of the line without defeating a single proven world-level light heavyweight.

Beating Wallace will not prepare him for Bivol’s precise jab, footwork or ability to control distance for 12 rounds. It merely moves Whittaker from favorable matchmaking into a title fight against one of the most technically complete boxers in the sport. The missing stage is the one in which he proves himself against a contender who can punish his mistakes.

Whittaker will probably knock Wallace out and be praised for another destructive performance. The result may earn him a mandatory position, but it will not answer the question his matchmaking keeps avoiding.

How good is Ben Whittaker when the opponent was not selected to lose?

Sports.title: John L. Sullivan Wins Disputed Title From Dominick McCaffrey
Sports.content:
That distinction allowed the show to proceed. It did nothing to produce an orderly championship.

Sullivan Had 40 Pounds on McCaffrey

Sullivan was 26 and weighed approximately 208 pounds. The 21-year-old McCaffrey came in near 168, leaving the smaller Pittsburgh boxer to handle a massive physical disadvantage.

McCaffrey could not trade directly with Sullivan’s heavier rushes. He used footwork, slips, and clinches to interrupt the larger man before another full attack developed. After injuring his right hand, McCaffrey relied heavily on his left and defensive positioning, turning survival into a technical exercise rather than a test of strength.

Sullivan was the recognized American bare-knuckle champion, but his preparation left him tiring as the fight progressed. McCaffrey’s camp also believed Sullivan needed a knockout within the scheduled six rounds to win. Surviving accounts differ over what the signed agreement actually required.

Sullivan supplied the heavier blows. One shot to the side of McCaffrey’s head dropped him during the middle rounds. McCaffrey later claimed he broke his right hand against Sullivan’s head in the third and completed the fight using primarily his left.

The larger man began fading late. McCaffrey pressed him and remained ready to continue. A timekeeping mistake ended the sixth after approximately one minute, prompting referee William Tate to order another round to replace the missing fight time. That explains the peculiar result listed by BoxRec: Sullivan won on points in round seven of a six-round fight.

A Championship Born Under Protest

Tate awarded Sullivan the decision based on the greater number of clean blows. McCaffrey’s camp protested, maintaining that lasting six rounds entitled him to a draw. The absence of an athletic commission left no independent authority to settle the disagreement. The promoter controlled the money, the referee’s interpretation determined the result, and McCaffrey’s only remaining option was a lawsuit.

The crowd treated McCaffrey’s survival as a moral triumph. Sullivan still collected nearly $6,000, representing approximately 60 percent of the gate, while McCaffrey received far less.

Sullivan became recognized as boxing’s first gloved heavyweight champion, yet the sport had not suddenly become modern merely because the fighters wore gloves. The disputed terms, confused timekeeping and uncertain ruling showed that Queensberry rules had arrived before boxing possessed a reliable system for enforcing them.

Sullivan later retained his bare-knuckle claim by defeating Jake Kilrain over 75 rounds in 1889. James J. Corbett finally took the gloved championship from him in 1892. McCaffrey continued boxing larger opponents, later becoming an instructor and police officer while insisting for the rest of his life that Sullivan had never properly beaten him.

Chester Park in Cincinnati, photographed in 1911. John L. Sullivan fought Dominick McCaffrey at the venue in 1885. Photo: Columbus Metropolitan Library/DPLA, public domain.

Ghana News.title: Ghana High Commission to UK steps in as stranded musician Barosky considers returning home
Ghana News.content:
Ghanaian highlife musician Barosky has expressed his readiness to return to Ghana following an intervention by the Ghana High Commission in the United Kingdom to assess his welfare and explore ways of supporting him.

The development follows public concern over the musician’s condition after a distressing video of him circulated widely on social media, prompting an outpouring of concern from Ghanaians in Ghana and abroad.

The Ghanaian High Commissioner to the UK, Mrs Sabah Zita Benson, subsequently travelled to Manchester to meet Barosky and members of the Ghanaian community as part of efforts to determine how best to assist the veteran musician.

Mrs Benson said the mission was initiated after the High Commission received several messages drawing attention to the video.

“When the video came out, a lot of people forwarded it to us. So immediately, I instructed our consular office to reach out and see how we can resolve it,” she said.

According to the High Commissioner, the decision to personally meet Barosky was informed by his contribution to Ghanaian music and the need for the Ghanaian community to rally around him.

“Barosky has contributed immensely to Ghanaian music, and we all need to come together as a community to help him get back on his feet,” she said.

Mrs Benson said the High Commission was willing to facilitate his return to Ghana should that be his preference.

“So, I decided to make this move to hear from him and see how to help him settle, and, if he is willing to go home, we will assist him to do that,” Mrs Benson said.

She stressed that restoring the musician’s wellbeing would require collective effort from the Ghanaian community.

“Getting him back on his feet again means we must come together as a community and help him.” ‘Such a great talent’

The High Commissioner also paid tribute to Barosky’s musical talent, questioning why a musician of his calibre should be allowed to struggle without support.

“Your talent was what shocked people. You are such a great talent, and how are we allowing it to go to waste?” she said.

She explained that the Ghana High Commission continued to use the country’s creative and cultural industries to promote Ghana internationally.

“We at the High Commission are promoting Ghana through arts, culture, music and food,” she added.

The intervention has since offered Barosky an opportunity to consider returning home, with the musician indicating that he would be willing to return to Ghana if the necessary arrangements could be made.

Barosky expressed appreciation to Mrs Benson and members of the Ghanaian community for their concern and support.

The development has also renewed attention on the need to recognise and support veteran Ghanaian musicians whose contributions helped shape the country’s highlife tradition.

Ghana News.title: Norway’s new king remembers ‘my dear father’ in first speech
Ghana News.content:
King Haakon VIII of Norway has paid warm tribute to his late father, Harald V, in his first speech to the nation since taking the throne.

"Thank you for being such a good dad," he said in an at-times emotional televised address, seated at a desk in Norway's royal palace, beside a picture of the late king, two lit candles and a bowl of white roses.

Harald, 89, who was seen as a moderniser and "people's king" during his 35-year reign, died in hospital on Friday morning after being treated for a rare blood condition.

"Now it is my turn," his 53-year-old son said, adding that a "major task" awaited him and that he wished to be "present and attentive" going forward.

Haakon stressed national unity in the speech, saying the royal family believed in a "society built on law and justice, where everyone is of equal value".

He said Harald had been a good father to himself and his sister, Princess Märtha Louise, as well as a "warm and funny grandfather" to his six grandchildren and a "loving and caring husband" to his widow, Queen Sonja.

The new king appeared to choke back tears as he noted that Saturday would have been their 58th wedding anniversary.

Harald brought the family together "with a natural authority", of which he might not have been aware himself, his son recalled.

He had "always stayed true" to his "values and commitments", the new king stressed.

"He constantly reminded us in the family that each of us must do things in our own way. Find our own style. Be ourselves," Haakon said.

He also remarked on the "powerful and moving experience" of seeing thousands of Norwegians gather outside the royal palace in the capital Oslo with "flowers, tributes and candles".

"We are in mourning, yet at the same time it brings comfort and strength that so many are grieving together with us," he said.

Norwegians have been laying flowers outside the royal palace in Oslo since news broke that Harald had died on Friday. A national period of mourning has been declared, with no date yet given for his funeral.

Among them was Norway's Prime Minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, who laid flowers outside the palace and signed a book of condolences after greeting the new king, said the country was "united in grief and gratitude".

Haakon will swear an oath of allegiance in parliament on Tuesday and will later participate in a consecration service with his wife, Queen Mette-Marit - a stripped-down version of a coronation, which Norway no longer holds.

He assumes his new role at a difficult time, as the royal family has faced health challenges and scandals this year.

Mette-Marit came under scrutiny when it was revealed that she had had a three-year friendship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, for which she publicly apologised.

She later received a lung transplant, after suffering from pulmonary fibrosis since 2018. Doctors will not declare her stable until next year, meaning her husband must balance his new official duties with her care.

Her son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, was convicted in June of rape and other offences and sentenced to four years in prison. He is appealing.

Høiby is not a member of the royal family, but was raised with them since he was four years old, when Haakon married his mother.

Haakon's sister, Märtha Louise, has also courted controversy for remarrying an American self-styled shaman in 2024, their business activities ultimately leading her to step back from royal duties.

Without directly referencing these controversies, Haakon said during his speech: "Our family has experienced the importance of standing together in order to remain steadfast both within ourselves and for one another even during difficult times."

He said he, along with Mette-Marit and Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, would "always strive to understand the life situations of different people".

He added: "No one who lives in this country knows what we will face together, but what we do know is that we will stand by one another through both good days and difficult ones."

Although Harald remained popular until his death, a poll for newspaper Aftenposten earlier this year suggested that support for the monarchy had dropped from 72% in 2024 to 54%.

However, Norwegian royal experts told the BBC that the new king, while facing questions about the turbulence surrounding his family, was respected, hard-working and, they believed, able to move forward despite the challenges.

Ghana News.title: Guinea-Bissau chosen to pilot ECOWAS community health policy
Ghana News.content:
Guinea-Bissau is taking the lead in efforts to put a new ECOWAS regional community health policy into practice, with the West African Health Organisation (WAHO) beginning high-level talks with the country's authorities.

WAHO Director General Dr Melchior Athanase Joël C. Aïssi began the meetings in the capital, Bissau, on Tuesday, 18 August, as part of a mission to build support for the implementation of the Regional Community Health Policy.

The policy is intended to be implemented across ECOWAS member states, with Guinea-Bissau serving as the pilot country.

Dr Aïssi, accompanied by ECOWAS Resident Representative in Guinea-Bissau Ambassador Ngozi Ukaeje and a senior WAHO delegation, first met the country's Minister of Public Health, Commodore Dr Quinhin Nantote.

The meeting at the Ministry of Public Health focused on Guinea-Bissau's priorities in community health and what would be needed institutionally and technically to put the regional policy into effect.

The delegation then met the Minister of Agriculture and Rural Development, Amadu Uri Guissé, at the Government House/Ministry of Agriculture.

The discussions brought attention to the role of sectors beyond health in advancing community health.

A wider government role

WAHO says the mission is aimed at getting member states to take ownership of the regional policy and strengthening political commitment to its implementation.

In Guinea-Bissau, that means bringing relevant sectors of government into the process.

The organisation says the meetings are also intended to create the conditions needed for effective implementation of the policy.

The engagement with the agriculture ministry reflects the multisectoral approach being encouraged as Guinea-Bissau prepares to implement the policy as the pilot country.

The meetings with other authorities of the Transitional Government are expected to continue on 19 August.

Laboratory equipment to be handed over

The second day of the mission will also see WAHO officially hand over laboratory equipment it has procured for Guinea-Bissau's National Public Health Laboratory (LNSP).

The handover is part of a programme that will also include the opening of a workshop on Guinea-Bissau's commitment to implementing the new Regional Community Health Policy.

The workshop will take place in Bissau from 19 to 21 August.

WAHO says the ongoing engagements are intended to strengthen institutional dialogue and mobilise relevant sectors around the policy.

For Guinea-Bissau, the focus now shifts from adopting the regional policy to putting it into practice.

And as the pilot country, its experience is expected to form part of the effort to advance implementation of the ECOWAS Regional Community Health Policy across the region.

Ghana News.title: Health service support centres to give patients in 3 West African countries a stronger voice in healthcare
Ghana News.content:
Patients in Benin, The Gambia and Togo are set to have new spaces where they can raise complaints and concerns about the healthcare they receive.

The West African Health Organisation (WAHO) has launched projects to establish Health Service User Support Centres in the three countries as part of efforts to improve the quality and safety of healthcare in West Africa.

The centres are expected to give patients and other users of health services a structured place to report problems, seek guidance and get support when they encounter difficulties during their healthcare journey.

But WAHO says the centres are not intended to be simple complaints desks.

They will also provide opportunities for dialogue and mediation, while information gathered from patients will be used to identify recurring problems and help improve healthcare.

The projects were officially launched in Lomé, Togo, on 21 August 2026.

The ceremony brought together representatives of the ECOWAS Commission, WAHO and the Togolese government, as well as representatives and presidents of the Medical Councils of Benin, The Gambia and Togo.

‘A space of dignity’

WAHO Director General Dr Melchior Athanase J. C. Aïssi said patients' complaints and feedback should be treated as an important source of information for improving health systems.

He said the centres should go beyond recording complaints.

A Health Service User Support Centre, he said, is “a space of dignity where the complainant’s voice is received, documented and transformed into action for improvement”.

The centres are expected to help health authorities identify risks, learn from patients' experiences and provide appropriate responses.

The initiative is also being presented as a way of strengthening trust between patients and healthcare providers.

ECOWAS Resident Representative in Togo, H.E. Deweh Emily Gray, praised WAHO and the Medical Councils of the three countries for their commitment to the project.

She said the centres could help strengthen trust between communities and healthcare facilities.

She also called for strong coordination and the sharing of lessons between the three countries so that experiences from one country can benefit the others.

Vice-President of the ECOWAS Commission, H.E. Damtien Tchintchibidja, said the initiative fits into the wider vision of an ECOWAS that is increasingly focused on its people.

She said regional integration should result in tangible improvements in services provided to citizens, particularly healthcare.

She urged the Medical Councils to ensure that the centres become accessible and trusted places where patients' concerns can be dealt with promptly and respectfully.

The Togolese Minister of Health and Public Hygiene, Universal Health Coverage and Insurance, Jean-Marie Koffi Tessi, was represented at the ceremony by the Director General of Studies, Planning and Health Information, Dr Yawa Djatougbe Apetsianyi.

The minister said a health system should not be judged only by its ability to prevent disease and provide treatment.

It should also be able to listen to patients, respect their dignity and take their concerns into account.

The centres are therefore expected to play a role in both responding to individual complaints and identifying wider problems affecting health-service users.

First three countries

Benin, The Gambia and Togo are the first three countries to benefit from the initiative.

The projects are part of a regional effort led by ECOWAS, with technical support from WAHO.

The three countries began refining their respective approaches at a planning meeting in Abidjan in September 2025, where their Medical Councils presented their projects.

WAHO says supporting the three countries at the same time will also allow them to learn from one another.

Lessons from the first phase are expected to help develop approaches suited to each country's circumstances while contributing to a broader regional approach to patient support, mediation and protection of health-service users.

For WAHO, the broader goal is to make patients' experiences and concerns part of efforts to improve healthcare.

The organisation says the initiative is intended to support safer, more accountable and more responsive health systems, while strengthening trust between communities, health professionals and health institutions.

Ghana News.title: Akufo-Addo mourns late Ya-Naa Abukari II at Gbewaa Palace
Ghana News.content:
Former President Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo has visited the Gbewaa Palace in Yendi to mourn the late overlord of Dagbon, Ya-Naa Abukari II.

The former President called on the Regent of Dagbon, Kampakuya-Naa, to extend his condolences to the traditional authority and the people of Dagbon following the passing of the late overlord.

Member of Parliament for Karaga and former Finance Minister, Dr Mohammed Amin Adam, who accompanied Nana Akufo-Addo to the palace, described the visit as an honour and said it was deeply meaningful to witness the former President pay tribute to the late Ya-Naa.

In a Facebook post on Saturday, August 29, Dr Amin Adam said he was humbled to witness the tribute to the “enduring bond” between Nana Akufo-Addo and the late overlord.

He said Dagbon would continue to remember the former President’s role in the peaceful restoration of unity in the Kingdom, as the people honour the legacy and reign of Ya-Naa Abukari II.

The late Ya-Naa Abukari II had previously expressed gratitude to Nana Akufo-Addo for his contribution to peace and stability in Dagbon.

In 2020, the overlord praised the former President for his role in the peace process and described the prevailing peace in Dagbon as a source of pride for the Kingdom.

Ghana News.title: The Mother’s secret: How Eni Akonobea turned motherhood into a philosophy for flourishing
Ghana News.content:

There is a particular kind of wisdom that comes from learning to care for another human being.

It is the wisdom of noticing what has not yet been said. Of anticipating what may be needed. Of creating safety before it is requested.

Of knowing that nourishment is not always food, that protection is not always physical, and that sometimes the most important thing you can give another person is simply the conditions in which they can flourish.

For Eni Akonobea, that understanding began with motherhood.

The birth of her daughter became the unexpected inspiration behind what would eventually become Eni Asiri — a company and philosophy built around the intentional curation of the conditions in which people live, work, and flourish.

There is meaning in the name itself.

Eni means mother in Akuapem, while Asiri means secret in Hausa. Together, they form a deeply personal idea: The Mother's Secret.

But for Eni, this is not simply about biological motherhood. It speaks to the qualities embodied by a mother at her best: attentiveness, nourishment, protection, discernment, hospitality, presence, and the quiet stewardship of another person's well-being.

These are qualities that transcend motherhood itself. They can be embodied by anyone who understands that a flourishing life is not created by achievement alone, but by the conditions surrounding it.

It is from this idea that Eni’s understanding of wellness began to evolve.

Rather than viewing wellness as something an individual practises — a collection of routines, treatments or habits — she became interested in the wider ecosystem of a person’s life.

Who and what has access to their attention? What kind of environment surrounds them? Who helps carry what they carry?

What conversations are they having, and which ones have they avoided? Does their success actually create a life they have the capacity to enjoy? What protects their peace?

These questions eventually shaped Eni’s distinctive professional identity as a Wellness Curator.

She describes Wellness Curation as the stewardship of everything that quietly shapes the quality of an

intentional individual’s life; curating the people, places and practices that create greater comfort, clarity, ease and capacity for growth. It is a philosophy that sits at the centre of wellbeing, lifestyle, emotional intelligence, hospitality and intentional living. And at its heart is an idea that can be traced back to the beginning of Eni’s journey as a mother:

A flourishing life does not happen by accident. It is carefully held, thoughtfully nourished, and intentionally curated.

This philosophy has developed into what Eni calls Refined African Wellness. Refined African Wellness

It is neither a geographical label nor an attempt to make conventional wellness more aesthetically African. It is a worldview informed by the richness of African ways of living: hospitality, community, rhythm, nature, storytelling, craftsmanship, generosity and the understanding that wellbeing is deeply relational.

Eni is interested in what happens when these principles are thoughtfully brought into contemporary life.

What might leadership look like when emotional wealth is treated as seriously as financial wealth?

What might luxury mean when time, privacy, ease and meaningful connection become more valuable than accumulation?

What might wellness become when the environment around a person is considered as important as the practices they perform?

These questions sit at the centre of Eni Asiri. The Work Beneath the Philosophy

Much of Eni’s work is concerned with what exists beneath visible success.

Through Healing Dialogues, she creates space for intentional conversations around emotional wealth, the inner realities of living and the things that are often difficult to articulate.

Through The Margin, her private executive stewardship practice, she works behind the scenes to create greater ease, continuity and capacity for individuals whose lives carry significant responsibility.

The work is rooted in discretion and thoughtful stewardship, curating the practical and personal conditions that allow a person to give their attention to what matters most.

Her Keynote Addresses and executive wellness work bring these ideas into organisations, while her broader wellness curation practice extends the same philosophy across private clients, leaders, entrepreneurs and organisations.

At the heart of this work is Emotional Wealth: the inner resources that influence how individuals experience success, relationships, leadership and life itself. For Eni, external achievement without emotional wealth can create a life that looks successful while becoming increasingly difficult to inhabit.

Her work therefore asks a different set of questions. What allows a person to enjoy what they have worked so hard to build?

What protects the quality of their inner life as their responsibilities grow?

What emotional conditions enable a leader not simply to perform, but to lead well? And what does it mean to build a life that has room for both ambition and peace?

Across all of Eni Asiri’s expressions, the answer returns to the same philosophy: wellbeing is not only about what happens within a person. It is also shaped by what surrounds them.

The people they have around them. The environments they inhabit. The demands placed upon them. The quality of their support. The conversations they are able to have. The space they have to think, rest, and simply be.

For Eni, wellness is therefore not simply about adding more to life but rather becoming intentional about what deserves to remain in it.

And perhaps that is the deepest meaning behind the name Eni Asiri: that some of the most valuable things we need to flourish are not loudly advertised or easily measured. They are quietly learned, carefully held, and thoughtfully passed on.

Eni Asiri

Ghana News.title: JoySports Invitational 2026: Corporate Ghana wraps up a day of thrilling sporting action at Legon
Ghana News.content:
The University of Ghana Sports Stadium came alive on Saturday, August 29, 2026, as Corporate Ghana swapped office desks, suits and formal meetings for running shoes, football boots, swimming gear and enduring competitive spirit at the JoySports Invitational Tournament 2026.

The annual corporate sporting fiesta got underway as early as 6:00 am with a morning walk, setting the tone for a packed day of fitness, competition, entertainment and networking.

The event brought together companies, institutions, corporate executives, employees, CEOs and sports enthusiasts, all united by a common desire to compete, connect and have a good time.

The walk was followed by an energetic aerobics session before participants spread across the various venues to compete in a wide range of sporting and recreational activities.

From football and swimming to table tennis, scrabble, chess, tag of peace, board games and ludo, there was something for almost every kind of competitor.

The programme also featured the much-anticipated CEO penalty shootout for both male and female executives, alongside fun-filled challenges including lime and spoon, sack race and the 100-metre sprint.

Among the notable personalities at this year's event was Ayawaso West Wuogon MP John Dumelo, who joined the corporate community as a special guest of honour for the sporting celebration.

Football provided some of the day's biggest moments, with corporate teams battling not just for goals but for bragging rights.

With cheers from supporters ringing around the venue, the football matches showed that the corporate setting had done little to dampen the competitive instinct.

Once the whistle went, the suits were forgotten and the tackles, saves, goals and celebrations took centre stage.

Away from the football pitch and swimming pool, competitors went head-to-head in table tennis, Scrabble and chess, while board games and ludo provided plenty of opportunities for strategy, concentration and friendly rivalry.

The physical challenges brought a different kind of excitement. The lime and spoon and sack race tested balance and coordination, while the 100-metre sprint offered competitors the chance to show off their speed.

And then there was the CEO penalty shootout, where the executives stepped into the spotlight and showed that leadership skills are not the only thing they can bring to the table.

The male and female categories added another layer of fun to an already packed programme.

By the end of the day, the 2026 JoySports Invitational Tournament had delivered far more than a collection of sporting competitions.

It created a space where colleagues could compete as teammates, executives could become competitors, and companies could build connections away from the boardroom.

There were winners, narrow defeats, dramatic penalty shootouts, podium finishes, cheers from the sidelines, and plenty of moments of friendly rivalry.

From the 6:00 am morning walk to the final sporting challenges, the message was clear: corporate life may be serious, but Corporate Ghana knows how to play. And at the JoySports Invitational Tournament 2026, the competition was only part of the fun. The real victory was bringing everyone together.

In all, 34 companies participated in the event, including the sponsors.

The participating teams are McDan Group, Equity Health Insurance, Labadi Beach, 3D Wireless Plus, Best Education Services Limited, Royal Kingdom Estate, The Chosen Hospital & Fertility Centre, Adansi Travels, AlSale Services, Piwak Natural Health, Ghana Publishing Company Limited, Old Mutual, Fair Wages and Salaries Commission, La Community Bank, Premier Health Insurance, Valex Lease Equipment Limited, The Luckiest, Narh-Bita Hospital, Latex Foam, Volta Catch, SIC, Heritage Christian University, National Petroleum Authority, Minerals Commission, National Identification Authority, Axis Pension Trust, Ayuda Hub, Sapholda Ventures, Tema Oil Refinery, Toyota Ghana Limited, Virtual Security Africa, MoMo Fintech, Multimedia Group and GIMPA.

The 2026 tournament, powered by Luckiest, is supported by Toyota, Superior Quality, the Minerals Commission, Ayuda, Latex Foam, Vallex Lease-Equip Ltd and Virtual Security Africa.

Ghana News.title: Rotary Club of Accra-Airport, SCEF donate school supplies to over 200 street-connected children
Ghana News.content:
Rotary Club of Accra-Airport, in partnership with the Street Children Empowerment Foundation (SCEF), has donated back-to-school items to more than 200 street-connected children in the Accra Metropolitan Area as part of efforts to support their education and secure a better future.

The beneficiaries received the items at a back-to-school programme held at the Wesley Methodist Basic School in Accra on Saturday, August 29, 2026. The items include: Exercise Books, Note Books, Pens, Pencils, Erasers, Rulers and other educational materials.

The initiative, under the theme: “Quality Education: The Pathway to a Brighter Future,” brought together representatives of SCEF, Rotarians, beneficiaries and other stakeholders to encourage vulnerable children to remain committed to their education.

President of the Rotary Club of Accra-Airport, Rotarian David Kwatia Nyante, said education remained a powerful tool for transforming lives, restoring dignity and creating opportunities for children.

He said the Rotary Club's partnership with SCEF had over the years focused on supporting vulnerable children, particularly those connected to the streets, by helping to provide them with opportunities to pursue their education.

“Education is far more than lessons in a classroom, it’s a powerful force that transforms lives, restores dignity, opens doors, and creates lasting opportunities,” he said.

Mr. Nyante stressed that the provision of school supplies was aimed at ensuring that children did not miss out on learning because they lacked basic educational materials. He noted that the impact of the intervention could be seen in the stories of beneficiaries who had returned to school with renewed confidence and hope for the future.

“Education empowers, builds confidence, strengthens communities, and equips children with the knowledge and values to shape their own futures,” he added.

“To our dear beneficiaries, I urge you to take your education seriously. Your current circumstances do not define your future,” he said, urging them to remain disciplined and determined in pursuing their dreams.

The Rotary Club of Accra-Airport President further appealed to corporate organizations, community leaders, civil society organizations and individuals to support initiatives aimed at helping vulnerable children stay in school. He said, supporting through funding, school supplies, mentorship, and skills training and volunteering could help create more opportunities for children and ensure that no child was left behind because of hardship or a lack of opportunity.

Founder and Executive Director of SCEF, Paul Semeh, also addressed the gathering, highlighting the Foundation's work to support and empower street-connected children.

Mr. Semeh explained that the “Pathways to My Future” vision board activity was designed to help the children reflect on their dreams, understand the skills and education needed to achieve them, and identify practical steps they could begin taking now.

He said the exercise was not intended to tell children what to become but to create a safe and encouraging space for them to express and plan their aspirations. “Don’t tell children what to dream. Help them discover, express and plan their dreams,” he said.

The programme also featured representatives from Kempinski Hotel, supporting partners of the program.

David Dayina, a Sales Executive at Kempinski Hotel, spoke to the children about career development, purpose and the importance of remaining open to opportunities.

He encouraged them not to be discouraged if they had not yet figured out exactly what they wanted to become, but rather to continue exploring, learning, building relationships and gaining experience.

One of the beneficiaries of the intervention, Mary Lamptey, a student of the Accra Technical University, expressed gratitude to SCEF and its partners for the support, saying the assistance had given her an opportunity to pursue her education and work towards a better future.

“I am very grateful to SCEF, Rotary Club of Accra Airport, and everyone who has supported us throughout our journey. Their support has helped us to continue our education and believe that, regardless of where you come from, you can work hard and achieve your dreams,” she said.
