World.title: We Must Not Forget The Victims Of Liberia’s Civil War
World.content:
Liberia’s fourteen years of civil conflict ended long ago, but many of its victims are still suffering. Some live with bullets and fragments in their bodies, lost limbs, impaired vision, chronic pain and emotional trauma. Others remain in poverty because the war destroyed their homes, farms, businesses and families. Many feel abandoned and forgotten by the country for whose conflict they paid such a terrible price.

By Tiawan Saye Gongloe

At the end of the war, former fighters received disarmament and demobilization packages, including money, vocational training and other forms of assistance to help them return to civilian life. That support was necessary for peace. But it created a painful imbalance: those who carried the guns received organized assistance, while many of the people injured, widowed, displaced and impoverished by the war received little or nothing. Liberia must correct this historic injustice.

I therefore propose the creation of a National War Victims Relief Fund for an initial period of five years. Every unemployed adult Liberian who is able to contribute should pay L$100 per year. Every employed Liberian should contribute US$1 per year, and Liberians living abroad should also be encouraged to contribute at least US$1 annually. The Government should match these contributions at a ratio of US$5 for every US$1 contributed under the national scheme.

The fund should be used to provide medical treatment, medication, prosthetic devices and modest welfare support to severely disabled victims. It should also provide interest-free microloans to victims who can engage in farming, trading or small businesses. The goal should be to reduce suffering, restore independence and give victims renewed hope in a caring Liberia.

This fund must be completely separate from the establishment of the War and Economic Crimes Court. The court concerns accountability for crimes committed during the conflict. The relief fund concerns care and responsibility for people who are suffering today. A wounded victim who needs medicine should not have to wait for a prosecution, and a widow living in poverty should not have to wait for the creation of a court before receiving assistance. Liberia can pursue justice and care for victims at the same time.

The fund must also be transparent and protected from political interference. A credible national registry of qualified victims should be established, and the General Auditing Commission should audit the fund annually. Most importantly, administrative expenses should not be deducted from the victims’ money. Salaries, offices and other operating costs should come from a separate appropriation in the national budget.

Someone may ask, “Why now?” The answer is simple: it is better late than never. The passage of time does not erase the suffering of those who still carry the physical, emotional and economic scars of the war. Delay is not a reason for continued neglect; it is a reason to act now.

This is more than a financial proposal. It is a national statement that Liberia remembers its victims, cares about their suffering and accepts responsibility for helping them rebuild their lives.

Such collective care can help heal old wounds, restore hope and make victims feel that their country has not abandoned them.

The fighters were assisted because Liberia needed peace. The victims must now be assisted because justice, compassion and national responsibility demand it.

We must not and cannot forget the victims of Liberia’s civil conflict.

World.title: Liberia: Supreme Court Denies Koffa, Co-Defendants’ Prohibition Petition, Clears Way for Capitol Arson Trial
World.content:
High Court Upholds Judge Willie’s Authority to Disband Jury; Koffa Team’s Challenge Rejected

By:Willie N. Tokpah

Monrovia-The Supreme Court of Liberia has denied a petition for a Writ of Prohibition filed by former House Speaker J. Fonati Koffa and several co-defendants in the Capitol Building arson case, clearing the way for Criminal Court “A” to proceed with the prosecution.

The ruling represents a major victory for the prosecution and effectively rejects the defendants’ attempt to overturn Resident Judge Roosevelt Z. Willie’s decision to disband the jury previously empaneled to hear the case.

The petitioners, including Koffa, Dixon W. Seboe, Abu B. Kamara, K. Jacob C. B. Debee, Christian Kofa, John Nyanti, Eric Susay, Thomas Isaac Etheridge and Stephen Broh, had asked the Supreme Court to restrain Judge Willie from proceeding after he dissolved the jury following allegations of juror misconduct.

The Supreme Court, however, found no sufficient legal basis to issue the extraordinary writ, holding that Judge Willie acted within his lawful authority in making the decision concerning the jury.

The decision does not determine the guilt or innocence of Koffa and his co-defendants.

Rather, it resolves the immediate legal challenge over whether the trial judge acted unlawfully in disbanding the jury.

Why Judge Willie Disbanded The Jury

The controversy arose after prosecutors asked the trial court to dissolve the entire jury, alleging that the panel had become compromised and could no longer fairly and independently adjudicate the case.

The prosecution pointed to several incidents involving jurors during testimony, including questions raised concerning evidence presented by the State.

One of the disputed incidents occurred during the testimony of LNP Chief Superintendent Rafael A. Wilson.

A juror questioned Wilson after he testified concerning photographs and evidence gathered during the investigation of the Capitol Building fire.

According to the proceedings, the juror questioned how photographs had been obtained when Wilson had earlier indicated that there was no CCTV camera inside the Capitol Building.

The juror subsequently asked that a photograph be produced and, after it was exhibited, raised a question concerning whether a person appearing in the image resembled defendant Thomas Isaac Etheridge.

Prosecutors argued that the nature of the questioning suggested that the juror had already begun evaluating the evidence and forming an opinion about a defendant before the conclusion of the trial.

The State further alleged that some jurors had consulted among themselves before putting questions to witnesses, which prosecutors argued demonstrated a loss of impartiality and undermined their ability to fairly determine the case.

Defense Rejected Claims Of Juror Misconduct

Koffa and his co-defendants strongly challenged the prosecution’s allegations.

Their legal team argued that prosecutors had failed to identify specific jurors who had committed misconduct and had, in some instances, mischaracterized or misquoted the jurors’ remarks.

The defense maintained that jurors asking questions about evidence did not, by itself, constitute misconduct.

They further argued that even if misconduct had been committed by an individual juror, such conduct could not automatically be attributed to the entire panel.

According to the defense, there was no sufficient evidence that the jurors had received outside influence, improperly communicated with outsiders or reached conclusions concerning the defendants’ guilt before deliberations.

The defense therefore argued that there was no legal basis to dissolve the entire jury or declare a mistrial.

Political Affiliation Also Became An Issue

The jury controversy was further complicated by the removal of one juror after the court determined that she had failed to disclose during jury selection that she held a leadership position within the Congress for Democratic Change

The prosecution raised concerns about potential bias because some of the defendants have political associations with the CDC.

Another juror was challenged after prosecutors presented photographs they claimed showed her among supporters at an event associated with defendant Abu B. Kamara.

Judge Willie, however, rejected that challenge after finding that the photographs had not been sufficiently authenticated to establish that the person depicted was the juror.

The juror denied that she was the woman in the photograph and maintained that the person shown was her mother.

Supreme Court Says, Prohibition Cannot Lie

The defendants subsequently turned to the Supreme Court, arguing that Judge Willie’s decision to disband the jury was unlawful.

The High Court had previously intervened in the matter, including ordering a stay of proceedings while the prohibition petition was considered.

But after scrutinizing the arguments, the Supreme Court has now declined to grant the requested relief.

The Court essentially determined that the trial judge had acted within the authority vested in him to make the disputed ruling concerning the jury.

The petition for prohibition was therefore denied.

The case stems from the December 18, 2024 fire at Liberia’s Capitol Building, an incident that damaged portions of the country’s legislative complex and triggered a major criminal investigation.

The government subsequently charged Koffa and several others in connection with an alleged conspiracy surrounding the fire.

The defendants have pleaded not guilty to all charges and have consistently challenged the prosecution’s allegations and evidence.

The proceedings have involved contentious disputes over witness testimony, photographs, videos, audio recordings and other evidence the prosecution intends to use to establish its case.

The jury controversy became one of the most consequential procedural battles in the trial after prosecutors argued that questions raised by jurors demonstrated that the panel had become compromised.

Judge Willie ultimately sided with the prosecution and disbanded the jury.

Koffa and his co-defendants then sought Supreme Court intervention.

World.title: Liberia: Fundamental Weaknesses In State’s Evidence Against Murder Suspect Kaiser
World.content:
Supreme Court Overturns Lower Court’s Conviction, Orders His Release, After Years In Prison

‘State’s Evidence Failed to Corroborate’, As High Court Restores Rights of Man Convicted in Fatu Blasuah Murder

By Willie N. Tokpah

Monrovia- The murder conviction of Valington B. Kaiser, alias “Bishop,” has been overturned by the Supreme Court of Liberia, declaring that the evidence presented by the prosecution failed to sufficiently corroborate the case against him and ordering that his rights and dignity be restored.

Kaiser, who has spent more than three years behind bars at the Monrovia Central Prison, walked away from the country’s highest court a free man Friday, following the landmark decision.

The ruling brings a dramatic turn to a murder case that began with the brutal killing of 18-year-old Fatu Blasuah at the former LPRC compound in Monrovia in May 2022 and culminated in Kaiser’s conviction before Criminal Court “A” in March 2023.

The Supreme Court, in reviewing the lower court’s judgment, found fundamental weaknesses in the State’s evidentiary case, concluding that the pieces of evidence relied upon by the prosecution did not sufficiently corroborate one another to sustain Kaiser’s conviction.

With the conviction overturned, the Supreme Court has restored Kaiser’s legal standing and liberty, bringing an end, at least for now, to more than three years of incarceration stemming from a conviction the nation’s highest court has now rejected.

From Murder Scene To Prison Cell

The case dates back to May 16, 2022, when the body of Fatu Blasuah was discovered at the Old LPRC Compound in Monrovia.

Police reported that the 18-year-old had suffered multiple stab wounds.

Investigators reportedly recovered a silver knife with a green handle from the scene.

Kaiser, who was then about 20 years old, was subsequently arrested and accused of involvement in the killing.

Investigators also pointed to CCTV footage which they said placed Kaiser in or around the area where Fatu’s body was discovered.

The prosecution further alleged that Kaiser and Fatu had been involved in a romantic relationship before her death.

Those allegations formed part of the evidence presented against him at trial.

A Mother’s Testimony

During the trial, Fatu’s mother, Maima Sackie, testified about her daughter’s relationship with Kaiser and the events preceding her disappearance.

She told the court that Kaiser was known to the family and frequently visited Fatu.

According to her testimony, Fatu left home after telling her that Kaiser had contacted her concerning a phone he had left with her.

Fatu did not return home that evening.

The family later became alarmed and eventually learned that a body had been discovered around the LPRC area.

The prosecution relied on the testimony, along with the CCTV footage, the knife reportedly recovered from the scene and other evidence, to build its case against Kaiser.

Jury Found Kaiser Guilty

After approximately a month-long trial before Criminal Court “A,” a 12-member jury returned a guilty verdict against Kaiser on March 1, 2023.

Reports from the time indicated that 10 of the 12 jurors voted to convict him.

The verdict resulted in Kaiser’s continued detention at the Monrovia Central Prison, where he remained for years while pursuing legal remedies against his conviction.

But the case did not end with the jury’s verdict.

Kaiser challenged the judgment, eventually bringing the matter before the Supreme Court—the final judicial authority in Liberia.

Evidence Did Not Corroborate

In its review, the Supreme Court scrutinized the evidence upon which the conviction rested.

The High Court determined that the various pieces of evidence presented by the State failed to adequately corroborate one another, raising serious questions about whether the prosecution had met the legal threshold required to sustain a criminal conviction.

The significance of the ruling is profound.

A guilty verdict by a trial jury cannot stand simply because suspicion surrounds an accused person.

The prosecution must establish guilt through legally sufficient evidence.

In Kaiser’s case, the Supreme Court has now determined that the evidentiary pieces relied upon by the State were insufficiently corroborated to sustain the judgment against him.

From Convicted Murderer To Free Man

The decision dramatically changes Kaiser’s legal status.

For more than three years, he lived behind the walls of the Monrovia Central Prison after being convicted of one of the most serious crimes under Liberian law.

On Friday, August 28, that conviction was overturned by the Supreme Court.

The ruling restores his liberty and, with it, the presumption of innocence that stands at the heart of Liberia’s criminal justice system.

Kaiser is now a free man.

World.title: Liberia: Maryland County Senator Engages Liberian Embassy, Diaspora Leaders in France
World.content:
Amb. Teeko Tozay Yorlay, Sr. (left) and Senator James Biney of

Maryland County.

PARIS, France – A Maryland County Senator, who chairs the Liberian Senate Committee on Executive and serves as ranking member of the Committee on Foreign Affairs, has held separate engagements with officials at the Liberian Embassy in Paris and leaders of the Liberian community in France.

By Jaheim T. Tumu

According to a release, the Senator visited the Embassy of Liberia in Paris on Thursday, where he was received by Liberia’s Ambassador to France, Dr. Teeko Tozay Yorlay, Sr., and members of the diplomatic staff.

During the meeting, the Senator commended Ambassador Yorlay and the Embassy staff for their service to Liberia, particularly the sacrifices and challenges associated with representing the country abroad.

He praised the mission’s dedication, resilience and commitment to duty, noting that Liberia’s diplomatic representatives play an important role in advancing the country’s foreign-policy interests, providing services to Liberians abroad and strengthening relations with France and other countries of accreditation.

The Senator encouraged the Embassy staff to remain committed to their national responsibilities and continue upholding Liberia’s interests in their diplomatic engagements.

Senator Meets Liberian Community Leaders

Following his engagement at the Embassy, the Senator met with the leadership of the Federation of Liberian Associations in France as part of his outreach to Liberians living in France and across Europe.

The meeting provided an opportunity for the Federation’s leadership to present its vision, priorities and ongoing efforts to promote unity, cooperation and community development among Liberians in France.

The group also briefed the Senator on preparations for the upcoming Liberian Independence Day celebrations in Europe under the European Federation of Liberian Associations (EFLA).

The Federation described the annual gathering as an important platform for promoting Liberian culture, national identity, diaspora solidarity and stronger connections between Liberians abroad and their homeland.

Discussions also focused on the need for greater and sustained engagement between the Government of Liberia and diaspora organizations across Europe.

The Federation highlighted the potential contribution of the Liberian diaspora to national development through investment, knowledge and skills transfer, advocacy, tourism promotion and other forms of constructive engagement.

Call for Stronger Government-Diaspora Engagement

The Senator welcomed the concerns and recommendations presented by the Federation and acknowledged the significant contributions Liberians abroad continue to make to the country’s development.

He emphasized the importance of maintaining effective channels of communication between the Government of Liberia and organized diaspora communities, particularly those in Europe.

The Senator encouraged the Federation to continue working collaboratively to promote the interests and welfare of Liberians in France while contributing to Liberia’s broader national development agenda.

The engagements in Paris concluded with a shared commitment to strengthening Liberia’s diplomatic service, deepening Government-diaspora relations and ensuring that the concerns, aspirations and contributions of Liberians living in Europe remain an important part of national development discussions.

World.title: Liberia: Finance Unlocks Jobs, Hope”-Governor Saamoi Declares as CBL Launches Enhanced Collateral Registry Aimed at Boosting Secured Lending
World.content:
As CBL Launches Enhanced Collateral Registry Aimed at Boosting Secured Lending

Congo Town– The Central Bank of Liberia (CBL) has launched an Enhanced Collateral Registry System, a major financial sector reform aimed at expanding access to credit for businesses and individuals by allowing lenders and borrowers to more efficiently register and verify collateral through a modern digital platform.

By Jaheim T. [email protected]

The launch, attended by senior government officials, development partners, representatives of financial institutions, and members of the private sector, marked what CBL Executive Governor Henry F. Saamoi described as an important step toward strengthening secured lending, promoting responsible borrowing, and deepening financial inclusion across Liberia.

In his keynote address, Governor Saamoi said the new system is designed to help unlock financing opportunities for entrepreneurs, small businesses, farmers, and other productive sectors of the economy that often struggle to access formal credit despite owning valuable assets.

“We are not merely launching a technological platform. We are launching a powerful instrument for economic empowerment,” Saamoi said.

“We are launching a reform that will help unlock capital, expand opportunity, and strengthen the foundations of inclusive economic growth in Liberia.”

The Governor explained that many Liberian businesses possess assets such as equipment, contracts, vehicles, inventory, and land, but have historically faced challenges converting those assets into bankable collateral due to weaknesses in the country’s credit infrastructure.

According to him, the enhanced registry addresses that challenge by creating a more transparent, reliable, and accessible framework for secured transactions.

The modernized system allows both movable and immovable assets to be registered through a unified digital platform that can be accessed around the clock.

Financial institutions can electronically register, amend, assign, discharge, and search security interests more efficiently, reducing delays and uncertainty in lending transactions.

Saamoi said the initiative forms part of Liberia’s broader effort to build a modern financial system capable of supporting investment, job creation, and sustainable economic growth.

He noted that the reform is aligned with the government of Liberia’s ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development, which emphasizes inclusive economic growth and expanded access to financial services.

“We are not simply introducing new technology,” the Governor said. “The Enhanced Collateral Registry represents another important milestone in our collective efforts to modernize Liberia’s financial infrastructure and create a financial system that works for every Liberian.”

One of the key features of the upgraded platform is its ability to connect with other national databases and institutions.

The registry is linked with institutions such as the National Identification Registry, the Liberia Land Authority, the Liberia Business Registry, and vehicle registration systems.

This interoperability enables lenders to verify ownership information, identity records, and existing claims on assets with greater confidence.

According to the Saamoi, better access to reliable information will help reduce lending risks, strengthen transparency, and improve confidence within the financial system.

Experts say these improvements could encourage financial institutions to expand lending to sectors that have traditionally been underserved.

Saamoi emphasized that the reform could have a particularly strong impact on micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs), which remain the backbone of Liberia’s economy.

He said many entrepreneurs possess productive assets but are unable to access financing because traditional lending models often favor conventional forms of collateral.

“For too long, many small businesses, women-owned enterprises, young entrepreneurs, farmers, and rural producers have lacked access to traditional financing despite owning productive assets,” he said.

“A more inclusive financial system is not merely a banking objective. It is a national development imperative.”

Governor Saamoi said the true success of the registry would not be measured by the technology itself but by its impact on people’s lives and businesses.

“The real value of this platform will not be measured by the technology itself,” he said. “Its true value will be measured by the businesses it helps grow, the investments it supports, the jobs it creates, and the lives it transforms.”

The Governor summarized the broader vision behind the reform. “Today, we launch an enhanced system. Tomorrow, we unlock finance. Finance unlocks enterprise. Enterprise unlocks jobs. And jobs unlock hope.”

During his remarks, the Governor pointed to results achieved under the Liberia Investment, Finance and Trade (LIFT) Project as evidence that increased access to finance can produce positive economic outcomes.

He disclosed that a US$6 million line of credit established under the project had been fully deployed through seven participating financial institutions by the second quarter of 2026.

According to the Central Bank, the facility helped 358 MSMEs obtain affordable financing, with some businesses receiving loans of up to US$100,000.

The Governor further revealed that women-owned businesses accounted for 64 percent of all loan disbursements, while 130 beneficiary enterprises were located outside Montserrado County.

Reflecting on those achievements, Saamoi said the data demonstrates that Liberian entrepreneurs have the capacity to grow if given adequate support and access to financing.

“The truth is that Liberian entrepreneurs do not lack ambition. Liberian entrepreneurs do not lack innovation. Liberian entrepreneurs do not lack determination,” he said. “Too often, they simply lack access.”

Development partners also welcomed the launch and described it as an important milestone in Liberia’s economic development agenda.

World Bank Country Manager, Georgia Wallen said access to finance remains one of the biggest obstacles facing Liberian businesses.

She noted that many entrepreneurs possess productive assets but lack the traditional collateral required by lenders to secure financing.

“The Enhanced Collateral Registry System helps to bridge this gap,” Wallen said. “It will give lenders greater confidence to accept a wider range of assets, and it will help borrowers unlock the value of the assets that they possess.”

She recalled that Liberia’s first collateral registry, launched in 2014 with support from the International Finance Corporation (IFC), had produced encouraging results by facilitating more than US$237 million in financing within its first two years of operation.

According to Wallen, the enhanced version seeks to build upon those gains while addressing challenges identified over time.

Wallen stressed, however, that technology alone would not guarantee success. She said widespread adoption by banks, businesses, regulators, and other stakeholders would be necessary to ensure the registry achieves its intended objectives. She disclosed that training programs and public awareness campaigns are already being planned to support implementation.

The judiciary also expressed strong support for the reform. Commercial Court Judge Eva Mappy Morgan described the enhanced registry as a critical development that could improve transparency in lending transactions and strengthen the enforcement of financial agreements.

Morgan explained that disputes often arise when collateral cannot be properly identified or when multiple claims exist over the same asset.

She said the new system would help provide clarity regarding ownership and security interests, reducing legal uncertainties that have historically complicated the recovery of non-performing loans.

A more reliable collateral framework, she added, could increase confidence among lenders and investors while strengthening the overall business environment.

As Liberia continues its broader financial sector modernization agenda, the Central Bank says the Enhanced Collateral Registry will work alongside a modernized Credit Reference System currently being developed under the LIFT Project. Both systems are expected to improve credit information, support better lending decisions, and strengthen confidence throughout the financial sector.

World.title: Liberia: Supreme Court Recalls US$50,000 Fines Against Martin Kollie, Alex Williams
World.content:
MONROVIA — The Supreme Court of Liberia has recalled and corrected a portion of its ruling delivered Thursday, August 27, in a damages case involving former LISGIS Deputy Director General Wilmot Smith and Ecobank Liberia.

By: Willie N. Tokpah

Chief Justice Yamie Quiqui Gbeisay, as the Court resumed its ongoing ruling session on Friday, August 28, clarified that the inclusion of activist Martin K.N. Kollie and Alex Williams in a US$50,000 general damages award each was an inadvertent error in the Full Bench’s opinion.

According to the Court’s clarification, Kollie and Williams were not parties to the case before the lower court in the manner contemplated by the judgment and, therefore, could not properly be subjected to the damages award.

The Supreme Court consequently cancelled the US$50,000 award against Kollie and the separate US$50,000 award against Williams.

However, the Court’s US$250,000 special damages award against Ecobank Liberia remains in effect.

The clarification came just one day after Thursday’s ruling generated widespread public attention, particularly over the inclusion of Kollie and Williams in the damages portion of the judgment.

With Friday’s correction, Ecobank Liberia remains solely responsible for the US$250,000 award arising from the Supreme Court’s decision in the matter involving Smith.

Following Thursday’s ruling, Kollie and Williams separately took to Facebook to challenge the decision, saying they had never been cited or informed about any case involving them.

Both said the inclusion of their names in the judgment came as a surprise.

The Supreme Court’s clarification now removes the financial penalties against the two men, while leaving the US$250,000 special damages award against Ecobank Liberia intact.

More details are expected as the Supreme Court continues its ongoing ruling session.

Summary

Tuesday’s preliminary hearing in the cocaine trafficking case against former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor has been pushed to Wednesday, September 2, at 10:00 a.m., after the Ministry of Justice requested a last-minute continuance. The delay comes as questions grow around the state’s timeline linking her to an alleged cocaine network.

Court Grants Continuance Hours Before First Hearing Was Set to Open

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

MONROVIA — The preliminary hearing in the cocaine trafficking case against former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor will not go forward until next as Wednesday, September 2, 2026.

Early this morning, The Ministry of Justice’s Office of the City Solicitor asked the Monrovia City Court for a continuance just hours before the case was due to open, and Stipendiary Magistrate Cllr. L. Ben Barco granted it.

The hearing will now resume Wednesday, September 2, at 10:00 a.m.

In its request, the government said the Supreme Court’s closing of its March Term of Court had pulled several senior lawyers away to attend on their supervisors, leaving the prosecution short of the counsel it needed for the day.

It is a short delay, but it lands at a moment when the state’s own account of the case is drawing closer scrutiny. Howard-Taylor faces nine charges built around allegations that a businessman, Sheikh Bassirou Kante, introduced her to an alleged Croatian-Ukrainian cocaine network in “early 2022,” first at her Congo Town residence and later in Dubai.

What has quietly complicated that narrative is a matter of public U.S. court record: Kante was arrested in Maryland on April 20, 2022, on wire fraud and money laundering charges unrelated to narcotics.

The charge sheet gives no specific date for the Congo Town meeting or the Dubai trip, and no travel records placing Kante in Liberia or the Gulf ahead of his arrest have yet been made public. That gap has left room for a question the defense is expected to press hard on Wednesday: where, precisely, was everyone when this was supposed to have happened?

Howard-Taylor has denied all charges.

Her legal team has called the case baseless and politically motivated and says it will contest it vigorously when the hearing resumes.

FrontPageAfrica will continue to follow this story as it develops.

World.title: Liberia: National Flag Day Oration: “FROM HERITAGE TO HOPE: THE FLAG THAT UNITES US”
World.content:
By Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, Minister of Finance and Development Planning

Republic of Liberia On the Occasion of the 179th Anniversary of National Flag Day August 24, 2026

His Excellency the President of the Republic of Liberia;

Members of the Legislature present;

Former Officials of Government,

The Dean and Members of the Cabinet and other officials of Government;

The Doyen and Members of the Diplomatic and Consular Corps;

Traditional and Religious Leaders;

Members of our Armed Forces and National Security Institutions;

Our Teachers and Students;

Members of the Fourth Estate;

Distinguished Guests;

Fellow Liberians at home and throughout the Diaspora;

Ladies and Gentlemen:

I am deeply honored to stand before you on this historic occasion as we commemorate the 179th anniversary of Liberia’s National Flag Day under the inspiring theme:

“From Heritage to Hope: The Flag That Unites Us.”

Today, we gather not merely to celebrate a national symbol. We gather to reflect upon who we are, where we have come from, what binds us together, and—perhaps most importantly—where we intend to go as one people and one Republic.

Our flag is cloth, but it is more than cloth. It is color, but it is more than color. It is history, but it must also be hope. It is a reminder of yesterday, a symbol of our common identity today, and a solemn promise to the generations of tomorrow.

FROM HERITAGE

One hundred and seventy-nine years ago, our forebears gave this Republic a flag to represent the aspirations of a newly independent African nation.

Eleven alternating red and white stripes and a lone white star resting upon a field of blue became the emblem under which generations of Liberians would live, struggle, celebrate, mourn, disagree, reconcile, rebuild, and dream.

That flag has witnessed our finest hours. It has also witnessed our darkest days.

It has flown in times of peace and conflict. It has been raised at inaugurations and lowered in mourning. It has accompanied our men and women in uniform and flown above our schools, public buildings, diplomatic missions, and international gatherings.

Through political transitions; through a brutal civil war that destroyed infrastructure and took countless lives; through public-health emergencies such as Ebola and COVID; through economic downturns and the difficult work of national reconstruction, the Lone Star has continued to fly high over land and over sea.

Distinguished Ladies and Gentlemen:

As I mount this hallowed podium on this National Flag Day, my mind’s eye races back through time, capturing vivid scenes from my distant past.

I see myself on August 24, 1978, a first grader at Bolahun Public School in Wawoma Clan, Kolahun District, Lofa County, proudly dressed in my school uniform—a white shirt and green short trousers—marching alongside my fellow first graders behind the students in the higher classes. Hundreds of students from village schools across the Clan have also converged on Bolahun for the grand Flag Day parade.

The entire clan has practically descended upon the town. Parents, relatives, friends, and well-wishers throng the streets, or more precisely paths, to witness the beautiful spectacle of schoolchildren marching proudly toward the designated point to salute our red, white, and blue flag.

I can still hear the cheers.

As each drill commander approaches the designated line and gives the salute, the crowd erupts in applause and laughter.

Those moments brought the entire town alive.

For us as children, National Flag Day was never merely a day to salute the flag. It was a day of celebration and fun—a day when students felt especially proud to be in school and parents experienced the joy of watching their children march with excitement and confidence.

Nearly five decades later, those memories remain vivid.

That little first grader marching through Bolahun in 1978—the little boy who would later return to Monrovia and continue his schooling in Logan Town, Jamaica Road, Kakata, and other places—could not have imagined that one day he would stand before his country as National Flag Day Orator, called upon to reflect on the meaning of the very flag he once marched so proudly to salute.

But that possibility should never be unique to one person.

It should be part of the Liberian promise available to every child.

Every Liberian child should be able to look at the Lone Star and say:

My country sees me. The circumstances of my birth do not determine the boundaries of my possibilities.

My dreams matter.

That is the Liberia we must build.

THE FLAG THAT UNITES US

My fellow Liberians:

If the flag belongs to all of us, then loyalty to that flag requires us to seek the common good.

But unity does not mean uniformity.

Indeed, look at what we witnessed during today’s parade: students dressed in different uniforms, coming from different schools, marching in different formations—but all saluting one flag.

There is a lesson for Liberia in that image.

We too may wear different political uniforms. We may come from different counties. We may belong to different tribes, religions, professions, associations, and social groups. We may disagree passionately about policies, personalities, and the direction of our country.

But above all those uniforms flies one flag.

We can disagree and still be Liberians.

And as I said in 2010 at the induction of officers of the Federation of Lofa Associations in the Americas FLAA) :

“Our individual counties exist within a country called Liberia, and while we have our individual county flags that belong to some of us, we have a single national flag that belongs to all of us. So, our county-centricity must never conflict with or undermine our country-centricity.”

Today I would add:

Our party-centricity must never undermine our country-centricity.

There must always be something above everything else.

That something is Liberia.

LET US INDIVIDUATE

We must resist the temptation to stereotype one another negatively because of political, county, tribal, religious, or other associations.

There is nothing wrong with loving the group to which we belong. But while loving our own group, we must recognize that other Liberians have an equal right to love theirs.

Our membership in one group does not make everyone in our group good.

Membership in another group does not automatically make someone else bad.

Every county, tribe, religion, or political party has its good, its bad, its ugly.

Every government has its good, its bad, its ugly.

The media has its good, its bad, its ugly.

The same is true of civil society, religious institutions, the business community, and every other human institution.

Why?

Because institutions are populated by imperfect human beings.

So let us individuate.

Let us assess each Liberian primarily by who that person is, what that person does, the values that person demonstrates, and what that person contributes to the common good.

Being outside government does not automatically confer sainthood on anyone, except if we fall for that feeble argument that the environment outside government is a paradise populated only by angels and cherubim.

Conversely, being in government does not automatically make a person bad, except again if we surrender to the warped argument that government by nature is an evil construct populated only by demons.

There are Liberians outside government who protect the flag every day through their service to country. And there are legions of Liberians in government working diligently and patriotically for the forward march of our nation.

The location of a person matters less than the character and patriotism of the person.

PATRIOTISM MUST BECOME PRACTICE

Distinguished Ladies and Gentlemen:

In recent years, the celebration of our nation’s Independence Day has taken on a remarkable new momentum. Liberians at home and across the Diaspora are increasingly adorning themselves in our national colors and celebrating Liberia with a passion, pride, and enthusiasm perhaps greater than we have witnessed in generations.

It is as though Liberians are falling in love with their country all over again—renewing their marital vows to our beloved Liberia in symbolic ceremonies of national recommitment taking place across the world every Independence Day.

This growing spirit of patriotism is a beautiful and encouraging phenomenon. It must be nurtured and sustained. Whatever we have done—as a people and as a government—to inspire this renewed affection for Liberia, we must continue to do, and do even better.

But It is easy to dress in national colors.

It is easy to sing the national anthem.

It is easy to wave the flag.

The harder task is to live by what the flag demands of us.

The raising of the flag and the singing of the national anthem should not merely make us teary-eyed. They should extract from us a commitment to take practical actions in the interest of our country.

Patriotism is not only what we say about Liberia. Patriotism is what we do for Liberia.

A public official who protects public resources is raising the flag.

A teacher who enters the classroom prepared to educate the next generation is raising the flag.

A nurse or doctor who faithfully cares for patients is raising the flag.

A member of our joint security forces who resists the tempting overtures of drug cartels and enforces the law regardless of name, status, wealth, or connections is raising the flag.

A businessperson who pays legitimate taxes and treats workers fairly is raising the flag.

A journalist who pursues truth responsibly is raising the flag.

A citizen who refuses corruption even when nobody is watching is raising the flag.

A young Liberian who chooses education, hard work, creativity, entrepreneurship, and service over despair is raising the flag.

The flag, therefore, should inspire more than emotion.

It should inspire responsibility.

Because love of country without responsibility to country is incomplete.

THE FLAG IN THE OFFICE

This responsibility has particular meaning for those entrusted with public office.

When the President, Vice President and other public officials assume office, they take an oath solemnly pledging allegiance to the Republic and undertaking to uphold its Constitution and laws.

That is why the flag is hoisted on all public buildings. That is why the flag is in the offices of public officials.

It is not merely decoration.

The flag represents millions of Liberians at home and throughout the Diaspora. Its presence should remind every public official that a government office is not a private space for advancing personal interests at the expense of the common good.

In a sense, every day that flag in a public office speaks silently to the official seated beside it, saying:

Liberia and Liberians are right here with you.

Liberia is watching you. Liberia is counting on you.

So, think Liberia. Love Liberia. Build Liberia.

THE LIBERIAN ENTERPRISE AND THE RESPONSIBILITY OF LEADERSHIP

Distinguished Ladies and Gentlemen:

Our country is like a common enterprise in which every citizen is a shareholder.

Those privileged to occupy public office do not possess a greater ownership share in Liberia. On election day, the President in the Executive Mansion or a fisherman in West Point, is entitled to one ballot—not two, not three—one.

Public office therefore does not increase one’s ownership of Liberia. It increases one’s responsibility to Liberia.

And leadership itself extends far beyond public office. Responsibility for country rests on the shoulders of every Liberian, especially those who can rightly be called Liberian leaders. And I use the phrase “Liberian leaders” broadly.

A Liberian leader is anyone whose position or influence can shape the thinking, behavior, and direction of other Liberians—for better or for worse.

Pastors and imams are Liberian leaders because congregations look to them for moral direction.

Principals and teachers are Liberian leaders because they shape impressionable minds.

Political party leaders are Liberian leaders because thousands take cues from their words and actions.

Talk-show hosts, panelists, editors, reporters, bloggers, and influencers are Liberian leaders because they influence what citizens believe to be true or false.

Business leaders, market association leaders, motorcyclist union leaders, trade union leaders, health professionals, sports leaders, community leaders—all exercise influence.

And influence creates responsibility.

A microphone creates responsibility.

A pulpit creates responsibility.

A classroom creates responsibility.

A political platform creates responsibility.

A social-media following creates responsibility.

Wherever influence exists, responsibility follows.

THE TRAGEDY OF THE COMMONS

There is, however, a danger that comes with common ownership.

Sometimes, because Liberia belongs to all of us, we behave as though Liberia belongs to none of us.

Economists describe a related phenomenon as the “tragedy of the commons”—when individuals pursue narrow private interests in ways that ultimately undermine the collective interest.

We say we want clean cities, yet some of us throw garbage from a moving vehicle.

We say Liberia needs a bigger national budget, yet some of us deliberately evade legitimate taxes.

We say we want a crime-free society, but when a friend or relative is lawfully apprehended, some of us demand that the police abandon the law.

We demand accountability from public officials, but excuse wrongdoing when the wrongdoer belongs to our party, county, tribe, church, family, or circle of friends.

That is how the common good is weakened.

Protecting the flag means understanding that what belongs to all of us must be protected by each of us.

FROM HERITAGE TO HOPE

My fellow Liberians:

The theme of today’s celebration does not stop at heritage.

It calls us from heritage to hope.

Heritage tells us where we came from.

Hope tells us where we can go.

But hope cannot simply be a wish.

National hope must be constructed.

It must be planned.

It must be financed.

It must be protected by strong institutions.

It must be powered by discipline, sacrifice, hard work, innovation, and what I call our thinking equity.

Our national development agenda—the ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development—is therefore an instrument of hope.

Not empty hope.

Not wishful hope.

But hope translated into plans; plans translated into projects; and projects translated into measurable improvements in the lives of our people.

DEVELOPMENT AS A NATIONAL UNITER

Distinguished Ladies and Gentlemen:

The Government of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai inherited enormous challenges. But we are not content merely to curse the darkness.

We are lighting candles. We are lifting the flag.

And based on what we are doing, I can now confidently say that this generation of Liberians will in few years be able to drive on paved roads from Monrovia to Harper and from Gbarnga through Zorzor, Voinjama, Kolahun, and Foya toward Mendikorma on the Sierra Leone border, things that previous generations of Liberians since the nation’s founding could only dream of.

We are working to expand reliable electricity, improve schools and healthcare, strengthen institutions, create jobs and opportunities, and connect communities that for too long have remained isolated from the full promise of national development.

Why?

Because one of the most effective ways to unite a country is to develop the country.

The roads we are paving do not ask the political party of the persons travelling on them.

The electricity we are expanding in Monrovia, in Buchanan, in Voinjama and across the country does not ask the tribe of the child studying beneath its light.

The hospitals we are improving or the ones we are building will not ask the county of the patient seeking treatment.

The schools we are equipping, rehabilitating or constructing, including the more than 100 schools for foundational learning that we are about to rehabilitate or construct, will not ask whether a child’s parents voted for the government or the opposition.

Development, when it is inclusive, is one of the most powerful expressions of national unity.

A road connecting two counties connects more than geography—it connects people, markets, opportunities, and hopes.

Electricity reaching a community does more than illuminate houses—it expands possibilities.

A functioning school does more than educate a child—it strengthens the future of the Republic.

This is how we move from heritage to hope.

Under the leadership of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, our government is working with urgency to expand the fiscal space necessary to finance the ever-growing ambitions of our people.

When some critics and cynics considered a billion-dollar national budget a distant and unrealistic aspiration, we chose to pursue the difficult work of expanding domestic revenue and strengthening fiscal capacity. And sometime in September this, we shall hit the historic billion-dollar mark, the first time since the founding of our country.

But a bigger budget is not an end in itself.

Its meaning lies in what it makes possible:

More roads.

More electricity.

Better schools.

Stronger healthcare.

More jobs and opportunities.

Stronger institutions.

And measurable improvements in the lives of our people.

That is the standard by which development must ultimately be judged.

COMPETITION WITHOUT HATRED

But development alone cannot unite a nation if our politics continually tears it apart.

We can compete politically without hating one another.

We can disagree without becoming enemies.

We can seek victory without requiring another Liberian’s destruction.

There is a dangerous form of politics that treats national life as a zero-sum game: for me to live, you must die; for me to rise, you must fall; for me to succeed, you must fail.

We must reject that mindset.

Some may consider such a position naïve or non- Machiavellian.

But we should never become comfortable acquiring our joy through the pain of others or celebrating our advancement through the destruction of others.

We can be competitive without being cruel.

We can succeed without destroying.

We can win without hatred.

A person’s political opponent is not a person’s political enemy. After all, the position or office in contention is not the personal property of political contenders. It is for the Liberian people.

When hatred becomes the organizing principle of politics, eventually everybody loses.

OUR SHARED PATRIOTIC COVENANT

Perhaps one of the challenges of our national life is that we have become very clear about what separates us but insufficiently clear about the minimum values that must unite us.

Liberia needs a minimum Patriotic Covenant—a set of irreducible national values to which government and opposition, Christian and Muslim, young and old, rich and poor can subscribe.

Let that covenant affirm:

That Liberia comes first.

That political power must be pursued peacefully.

That public resources belong to the people.

That corruption is wrong regardless of who commits it.

That truth matters.

That our differences must never justify hatred.

That the Constitution and the rule of law must prevail over personalities.

That no political victory is worth destroying Liberia.

And that every generation, in the spirit of intergenerational equity, has a duty to leave the Republic stronger than it inherited it.

These should not be government values or opposition values.

They should be Liberian values.

PEACE MUST NEVER BE TAKEN FOR GRANTED

Distinguished Ladies and Gentlemen:

Our history has taught us a costly lesson:

Division can destroy in a few years what generations labor to build.

Peace, therefore, must never be taken for granted.

We must guard it.

We must nurture our democracy.

We must strengthen the rule of law.

And we must ensure that our words—whether spoken from political platforms, radio stations, pulpits, community meetings, or posted online—do not reopen wounds that our nation has struggled so hard to heal.

Words matter.

A microphone can educate or inflame.

A radio program can inform or divide.

A political platform can inspire or incite.

A social-media post can build bridges or deepen fractures.

Our children deserve to inherit our progress.

Not our divisions.

Not our hatred.

Not our anger.

WHAT SHOULD THE FLAG SEE?

We often ask what do we see when we look at the flag.

Today, let us reverse the question.

If the flag could look back at us, what would it see?

Would it see citizens committed to building their country?

Would it see leaders placing national interest above personal interest?

Would it see young people equipped with knowledge, skills, and opportunity?

Would it see political opponents who disagree without hatred?

Would it see communities living peacefully despite their differences?

Would it see public resources being transformed into roads, schools, hospitals, electricity, jobs, and opportunity?

Would it see integrity becoming stronger day by day?

Would it see hope becoming stronger than despair?

Those questions cannot be answered by this speech.

They will be answered by our actions.

CONCLUSION: THE FLAG WE MUST LIVE

My fellow Liberians:

The flag we celebrate today came to us from history.

The Liberia beneath which it will fly tomorrow is ours to build.

That is the journey from heritage to hope.

And wherever the Lone Star flies, let every Liberian remember:

This is our heritage.

This is our hope.

This is our home.

This is our Liberia.

But let us also remember:

The flag cannot raise itself.

We raise the flag when we raise our standards.

We raise the flag when we raise our integrity.

We raise the flag when we raise our children with knowledge, discipline, and hope.

We raise the flag when we raise one another.

And we raise the flag highest when we put country above self.

So let us leave this celebration determined not merely to wave the flag, but to live the flag.

Not merely to salute Liberia, but to serve Liberia.

Not merely to hope for a better Liberia, but to build one.

May the Lone Star forever unite us.

May peace remain within our borders.

May hope rise in every Liberian heart.

And may Almighty God continue to bless the Republic of Liberia and save the State.

Happy 179th National Flag Day!

Long live the Lone Star!

Long live the Republic of Liberia!

I thank you.

World.title: Zesco Girls fall in COSAFA final
World.content:
‎ZESCO Ndola Girls missed out on the CAF Women’s Champions League COSAFA Qualifier 2026 title on Saturday evening after a 2-1 defeat to South Africa’s Mamelodi Sundowns in the final.

‎

‎It was a case of déjà vu for the Zambian champions, who were also losing finalists in last year’s COSAFA Qualifier.

‎

‎Sundowns made a perfect start when Refilwe Tholakele opened the scoring in the 2nd minute.

‎

‎ZESCO responded and fought back, equalizing deep in first-half stoppage time through Charity Mubanga to send the teams into the break locked at 1-1.

‎

‎The second half turned on two key moments. The Ndola Girls suffered a huge blow when star midfielder Eneless Phiri was injured and replaced by Fridah Kabwe.

‎

‎Then in the 64th minute, the referee awarded Sundowns a penalty after a VAR review confirmed a foul inside the ZESCO penalty area.

‎

‎Tholakele stepped up and converted to score her second of the match and restore Sundowns’ lead.

‎

‎ZESCO pushed for another equalizer but could not break down the South African defense.

‎

‎ZESCO reached the final after edging Silver Strikers of Malawi 2-1 on Thursday.

‎

‎Earlier in the tournament, the Ndola Girls topped Group A with 9 points from 3 wins.

‎

‎The COSAFA Qualifier serves as the regional pathway for Southern African clubs to reach Africa’s premier women’s club competition — the CAF Women’s Champions League. With the win, Mamelodi Sundowns will represent the COSAFA region at the continental finals.

‎

‎It was a heartbreaking end for ZESCO, who conceded a controversial late penalty to lose the regional crown for the second year running.

World.title: Kazungula woman dies in suspected suicide
World.content:
A 26-year-old female suspect was found hanging in the female cells at Kazungula Police Station.

The deceased identified as Milimo Mpongo of Makalanguzu village in Chief Sekute’s area in Kazungula district was detailed alone in the cells in connection with four theft complaints.

Southern Province Commanding Officer, Moono Namalongo revealed in a statement availed to the media that the deceased was discovered hanging in the female cells using a chitenge material she was wearing, which had been tied to a window burglar bar on August 28, 2026 between 07:00 hours and 08:00 hours.

Mr Namalongo explained that on August 27, 2026 between 14:00 hours and 16:00 hours Ms Mpongo allegedly visited four different Airtel money businesses in Kazungula district and requested transactions ranging from K1, 000 to K3, 400 to be deposited into her mobile money number.

“It is alleged that after the transactions, she would open a small black laptop bag she was carrying and claim that she had forgotten the money at home before disappearing from the respective places,” Mr Namalongo explained.

He said following the complaints, the deceased was apprehended and placed in police custody where the suspected incident of suicide happened.

Mr Namalongo further said officers on duty spoke to her the same day, August 28, 2026 around 07:00 hours, and was later discovered hanging in the female cells using a chitenge material she was wearing.

He added that Police informed the deceased’s relatives about the incident stating that the body was untied in the presence of a relative and taken to Kazungula District Hospital where she was certified dead.

“The body was later taken and deposited at Livingstone Hospital Mortuary awaiting postmortem examination. The investigations into the matter are ongoing,” said Mr Namalongo.

World.title: Govt. praised on timely payment of farmers
World.content:
Newly elected Lumwana Member of Parliament, Mathews Mashimamgo has applauded the government for the timely payment of farmers selling maize to the Food Reserve Agency (FRA), saying the new payment system allows farmers to receive their money within three days.

Speaking during a spot check at the Mutanda FRA Depot in Kalumbila District, Mr Mashimamgo said the prompt payments would enable farmers to invest their earnings in other businesses as they prepare for the next farming season.

Mr Mashimamgo also assured farmers that the challenge of constructing a concrete slab at the Mutanda FRA Depot would be addressed.

He said a contractor would be engaged next year with support from the community to improve the depot and provide farmers with a better environment in which to sell their maize.

Mr Mashimamgo further appealed to the government to consider opening more FRA depots in the constituency to improve access for farmers travelling from distant areas.

“As we get to Parliament, we will appeal to the President through the Ministry of Agriculture to open more FRA depots to ease access for farmers coming from far distances such as Kamiba, Mushingashi, Kayonge and Kananga,” he said.

Mr Mashimamgo said opening additional depots would help address the challenges faced by farmers who currently have to travel long distances to sell their produce.

He added that his office would continue visiting FRA depots across the constituency to obtain first-hand information on the challenges farmers are facing.

“We are going round to all depots in our constituency to have first-hand information and see what is happening on the ground,” he said.

Meanwhile, a farmer, Anna Shakopo thanked the government for purchasing maize from farmers and implementing the Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP).

Ms Shakopo said the new payment system had made it easier for farmers to access their money through banks and mobile phones.

“We thank the government for the new payment system. We can now receive our money through the bank and mobile phone,” she said.

She said previously, farmers had to spend long hours and sometimes sleep at banks while waiting to access payments from the FRA.

Ms Shakopo added that the improved payment system together with timely FISP-related payments and FRA funds had reduced the need for farmers to travel long distances to collect their money.

Another farmer, Friday Matebo, thanked the government for the initiatives being implemented to support farmers and called for an increase in the FISP allocation.

World.title: Chipata’s Kagunda community set to receive electricity
World.content:
More than 2,000 people in Kagunda Community of Chipata Central Constituency are set to access electricity for the first time following the implementation of an electricity connection project by the Chipata City Council.

The project, which will be implemented at a total of K907,524.32, by the Chipata Council through the Constituency Development Fund (CDF), has reached 90 percent completion.

Chipata City Council Assistant Public Relations Officer, Grace Lungu, says the project would connect households and community institutions to the national electricity grid and improve access to reliable power.

The provision of electricity would also create opportunities for socio-economic development in Kagunda Community.

She explained that access to electricity was expected to stimulate economic activities by supporting small and medium-sized businesses, improving productivity and creating an enabling environment for new enterprises to thrive.

Ms.Lungu said the Council remained committed to implementing infrastructure projects that respond to the needs of local communities and contribute to improved livelihoods.

She expressed confidence that completion of the project would help transform Kagunda into a more vibrant, connected and economically empowered community.

World.title: Paramount Chief Chitimukulu graces Kulamba ceremony
World.content:
Paramount Chief Gawa Undi has reiterated the use of traditional ceremonies as platforms to unite and promote peace among citizens.

The traditional leader says cultural ceremonies such as Kulamba play an important role in strengthening relationships among people beyond national borders.

The Paramount Chief was speaking at Mkaika in Katete during the 2026 Kulamba traditional ceremony of the Chewa people of Zambia, Malawi and Mozambique in a speech was read on his behalf by Chairperson of Fundraising Committee for Kulamba Ceremony, Reuben Kamanga.

“Our culture should protect peace and unity, not tribalism and nationalism among ourselves,” he said.

The Paramount Chief said the Kulamba ceremony will continue to serve as an important platform for bringing people together and promoting cultural ties among the Chewa-speaking people of Zambia, Malawi and Mozambique.

The ceremony attracted people from different walks of life, representing Zambia, Malawi, Zimbabwe and countries beyond the borders of the three countries

And the Paramount Chief said the continued participation of people from world over, demonstrates the growing importance of traditional ceremonies in promoting cultural unity beyond borders.

The traditional leader urged young people to embrace education while remaining connected to their cultural heritage.

Meanwhile, Paramount Chief Chitimukulu of the Bemba people graced this year’s Kulamba Traditional Ceremony which was held under the theme “Unity beyond Borders.”

Mwine Lubemba who also spoke through his Secretary, Richard Mukuka reiterated his counterpart’s message of embracing culture as a means of protecting peace and unity.

He said traditional ceremonies such as Kulamba demonstrate how traditional institutions can bring people together despite differences in nationality and community.

He has also called on Government to continue working with traditional leaders in preserving culture and strengthening the traditional leadership framework.

The annual ceremony provides a platform for subordinate chiefs from Zambia, Malawi and Mozambique to pay homage to Paramount Chief Kalonga Gawa Undi.

The ceremony saw different dignitaries and representatives of government from all the three countries in attendance.

World.title: Govt. reaffirms continued support small scale farmers
World.content:
Government has reaffirmed its commitment to supporting small scale farmers through the provision of agricultural inputs creating market opportunities.

Muchinga Province Deputy Permanent Secretary, Brian Sichande, says government recognizes agriculture as the backbone of the country’s economic transformation.

Mr Sichande was speaking during the commemoration of the Mutomolo Traditional Ceremony of the Namwanga people held at Chieftainess Waitwika’s palace in Nakonde today.

He commended the people of Waitwika Chiefdom for their hard work which has resulted in an anticipated bumper harvest in the 2025/2026 farming season.

Mr Sichande urged farmers to sell their produce to the Food Reserve Agency (FRA) to get fair and reliable prices.

“I urge farmers not to sell their market produce to suitcase buyers who often exploit them through unfair pricing. Government encourages farmers to sell their produce to the Food Reserve Agency (FRA) which offers fair and reliable prices and remains committed to protecting the interests of our farming communities,” he said.

He further stated that government has created Mwenzo Constituency on the western side of Nakonde and has increased Constituency Development Fund (CDF) allocation to K40 million which demonstrates the government’s efforts to empower local communities.

“Through CDF, local communities are able to actively participate in decision making processes and determine development priorities for their communities and the district as a whole,” he said.

Mr Sichande further described traditional ceremonies as channels for passing values from one generation to the next.

He added that culture remains one of Zambia’s greatest assets and contributes to social and economic development.

Mr Sichande stated that government remains committed to working with traditional leaders to transform the economy.

He also disclosed that the construction of Chieftainess Waitwika’s palace has reached an advanced stage.

“I am pleased to note that the construction of Chieftainess Waitwika’s palace is in progress and the superstructure has been completed pending other finishing works to complete the palace,” he said.

The Deputy Permanent Secretary also highlighted the tourism potential of Nakonde, citing the Zwangendaba Grave Site, Mwenzo Mission, and Old Fife as sites that can attract visitors if marketed.

Mr Sichande further commended the chiefdom for efforts in addressing early marriages and teenage pregnancies.

Speaking at the same event, Chieftainess Waitwika who spoke through her representative, Davis Simwanza urged households to keep enough food to enhance food security.

The traditional leader also appealed to government to supply farming inputs early to take advantage of Nakonde’s good climate.

“Nakonde has a very good and favourable climate for farming and as such I would request the government to provide farming inputs in time and adequately for our people to produce more. This will help in ensuring sustainable national food security is enhanced, a key factor to national development,” she said.

World.title: Chief Muyombe lauds Muyombe-Isoka road project
World.content:
Chief Muyombe of the Tumbuka people in Mafinga District, Muchinga Province, has commended government for the developmental activities being undertaken in his Chiefdom and the district at large.

Speaking during the Vinkhakanimba Traditional Ceremony, the traditional Leader who spoke through his representative, Frank Muwowo, highlighted several projects currently being implemented in the education and health sector as well as the Muyombe-Isoka road project.

Chief Muyombe further appreciated government for creating Mafinga South Constituency, saying the new constituency will bring services closer to the people.

“As we appreciate the progress made, our endless developmental needs remain significant, therefore I appeal for continued investment in the education and health sector,” he stated.

The Chief also appealed for increased provision of clean and safe drinking water, rural electrification, and support to agriculture in order to improve livelihoods of the people in the area.

He further hailed government for the ongoing construction of the Muyombe-Isoka road, which will improve road connectivity, facilitate the movement of agricultural produce, and improve access to essential services.

The Traditional Leader added that the road once completed will support trade, create opportunities for investment, and drive economic growth in the district.

“We therefore urge the Government to remain committed and see to it that this important road project for the people is completed,” he said.

Chief Muyombe emphasized that development is anchored on peace, unity and strong partnership between government and traditional leadership.

“I therefore reaffirm our commitment to working with the Government and all stakeholders for the development of our Chiefdom,” he said.

Meanwhile, Muchinga Province Permanent Secretary, Tuesday Bwalya, who was represented by Mafinga District Commissioner Boyd Kaonga, said government will continue to support cultural preservation and infrastructure development in Mafinga.

Dr Bwalya said culture remains one of Zambia’s greatest assets and has become a significant driver of social and economic development.

“Traditional ceremonies are a filament and it is indeed encouraging to see people gathered here to celebrate and appreciate the rich cultural heritage of the Tumbuka-speaking people of Muyombe in Mafinga District,” Dr Bwalya said.

He reaffirmed Government’s commitment to working closely with traditional leaders in transforming the economy.

Dr Bwalya announced that government has reserved funds for the construction of an arena for the traditional ceremony.

He said the facility will also include other sports infrastructure such as volleyball, football and netball pitches to support youth talent and community activities.

On education, the Permanent Secretary noted that the sector has remained focused on increased access to quality education for the majority of Zambians, as evidenced by the introduction of free education from Grade 1 to 12.

He said the policy has led to an influx of pupils in classes, creating a shortage of classroom spaces and desks and government has since procured 750 desks for Mafinga South Constituency at a cost of K1.3 million.

Dr Bwalya said he was pleased to note that the Rural Electrification Authority has electrified 245 housing units around the Chief’s Palace in Mafinga District.

He further highlighted the construction of the Isoka-Muyombe road as a major milestone for the district that Government is working on.

The Permanent Secretary also said with the creation of the new constituency and the allocation of K40 million under the Constituency Development Fund, will address some outstanding challenges in the area.

He added that the Skills Development Bursary from nursery to youth level, is another milestone, as government continues to offer opportunities for vulnerable youths to access skills training centers and secondary schools.

Dr Bwalya further urged the traditional leader and his subjects to continue championing that noble cause while also promoting and preserving cultural values that define the country’s identity as a people.

World.title: Lungu maintains scoring form at Pirates
World.content:
Zambian international striker Gamphani Lungu on Saturday scored a goal when his South African club Orlando Pirates secured their spot in the final of the MTN8 with a 3-0 victory in the semifinal showdown against Sekhukhune United at Orlando Amstel Arena.

‎

‎Lungu scored Pirates’ second goal after beating his compatriot Toaster Nsabata in the Sekhukhune goal in the 39th minute.

‎

‎The ex-Power Dynamos forward fired in the second for Pirates when Yanela

‎Mbuthuma collected a pass from Appollis before calmly setting up Lungu.

‎

‎”That was an incredible way to reach the MTN 8 finals! I’m really humbled to have scored again. We’ll keep working diligently and are excited for the next match,” Lungu reacted after the match.

‎

‎He played 82 minutes before being replaced by Mpho Padime.

‎

‎Lungu is one of the players widely expected to be called by Zambia coach George Lwandamina for next month’s Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers against Algeria and Togo.

‎

‎He has been enjoying good scoring form after his big move from Siwelele FC to Pirates last June.

‎

‎Meanwhile, Lungu and the Buccaneers made history by becoming the first-ever club to reach the final of the competition on five consecutive occasions.

‎

‎They did so by completing a 4-0 aggregate win over Babina Noko, after the 1-0 triumph in the opening leg gave them a slight advantage.

‎

‎Pirates now await the winner of the tie between Mamelodi Sundowns and Lamontville Golden Arrows, with the second of the two remaining berths set to be decided on Sunday afternoon.
