World.title: Ousted Ukrainian defense chief Fedorov takes advisory role with Italy
World.content:
Fedorov, who called for wartime elections after being pushed out of government in President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s latest reshuffle, also stressed that he is not decamping to Rome. “My main focus remains unchanged,” he wrote, adding he will continue working in Ukraine on projects to strengthen the country’s defense and attract international resources.

Crosetto first offered the position in July, saying he called Fedorov the day after his dismissal and asked: “When would you like to come to Rome to work with me as an adviser?” He praised Fedorov as an innovator who had “completely changed the rules of the game on the battlefield.”

The former minister was dismissed in mid-July after roughly six months at the helm of Ukraine's defense department amid tensions with the country’s military leadership and policy disputes. His removal triggered rare wartime protests.

He has since sharpened his criticism of President Zelenskyy, calling for elections earlier this month despite Russia’s ongoing invasion and warning that Ukrainians “cannot endlessly live” without understanding how major decisions are made.

Zelenskyy has rejected the idea, warning that wartime elections could “destroy” the country.

World.title: Climate and AI to loom large in von der Leyen’s State of the Union
World.content:
During Friday's discussion with the cabinet chiefs, Seibert linked the expected focus on climate to the damage caused by floods and wildfires over the summer, according to the two officials, who were briefed on the gathering. They were granted anonymity to discuss the closed-door talks.

The climate focus comes as von der Leyen’s Commission tries to defend its 2040 emissions-cutting target while responding to mounting pressure from industry and national capitals to limit the economic cost of the green transition.

The discussion also touched on how to present AI’s impact on jobs. Von der Leyen’s team has asked the Commission’s relevant policy units, in particular DG Connect, to provide fresh statistics for the speech on the number of jobs likely to be lost and created as AI adoption spreads, according to one of the officials.

Seibert also raised migration as a likely topic in the address, referring to the crisis in the Spanish autonomous city of Ceuta, according to one of the officials. The Commission is expected to revamp the mandate and operations of EU border agency Frontex, a third official said.

The Commission president's speech is expected to include references to social policy around the 10th anniversary of the European Pillar of Social Rights next year, alongside Ukraine and enlargement, according to one of the officials. But the topics have yet to be finalized.

The meeting was the second major opportunity for commissioners to get their priorities name-checked, with their cabinets having already submitted two- to three-page pitches to Seibert. The Commission's policy units, known as the directorates-general, also submitted documents outlining the topics they want von der Leyen to cover.

World.title: What it’s like to live through Kyiv’s constant air raids
World.content:
Kyiv has survived more than 20 air raid alerts since Thursday night. Some were an hour long, while others lasted for up to 10 minutes.

Indeed, every alert, as Russia continues its persistent destruction of millions of books, food warehouses and liquor factories, also means everything has to stop until we hear the words: “Air raid alert is over.” Dozens of trains are delayed, and businesses shut down and wait, losing customers and money.

But “survivors must still go to work,” as we like to joke bitterly. People are still expected to commute, even though Kyiv’s subway has stopped running between the left and right banks of the River Dnipro. Sleep-deprived civilians need to walk for hours, squeeze themselves into buses, or get stuck in traffic on bridges, just to get to work and back home. Transport chaos overground means even more danger for people stuck in large groups all around the city.

But our wartime economy, on which we need to rely more and more due to the slowing of foreign aid, cannot afford to stop.

“The country’s defense spending is constantly growing, and this requires maximum mobilization of domestic resources,” said Hlib Vyshlinsky, the executive director of the Center for Economic Strategy think tank based in Kyiv. “The policy of zero tolerance for the risk to the life and health of civilians under constant missile and drone strikes becomes irrelevant, because the state is still not able to protect them at 100 percent.”

As a Kyivan, I can tell you that this terror sends your mental stability into a spiral.

World.title: Iceland's EU referendum: polling stations close as Europe awaits results
World.content:
The partial results show a neck-to-neck race with the 'Yes' at 51.2% and the 'No' at 48.8%, with over 87,000 votes scrutinised.

 

In line with the opinion polls, the 'No' is heading toward 60% in more rural regions, whereas initial results from the capital Reykjavík point to around 58% for the 'Yes'.

The first nearly 10,000 votes scrutinised for the Southern Constituency give 'No' a significant advantage with 59.8% of the votes, against 40.2% for 'Yes'. The Southwest Constituency was equally split with 9,900 votes for 'Yes', and 9,900 for 'No'.

Similarly, with a little less than 6,000 votes counted, the initial results from the Northwest Constituency see the Eurosceptic camp at 60.8%, and the 'Yes' camp at 39.2%, whilst the Northeast Constituency with nearly 10,000 votes has the 'No' at 56% and the 'Yes' at 44%.

By contrast, the initial results for Reykjavík's south constituency with over 20,000 votes scrutinised have the 'Yes' at 55.9% and 'No' at 44.1%. The capital's north constituency has nearly 21,000 votes scrutinised, with the 'Yes' at 59.4% and the 'No' at 40.6%.

The partial results are consistent with expectations, as rural areas are expected to be more Eurosceptic due to concerns related to fisheries and farming, whilst the capital Reykjavík is expected to be more pro-EU.

Polling stations closed at 10:00 pm local time on Saturday for Iceland's high-stakes EU referendum.

On Saturday, Icelanders were called to vote on whether to resume accession negotiations with the European Union or abandon any prospect of joining the bloc for the foreseeable future. Around 272,000 individuals were eligible to vote.

According to preliminary figures, voter turnout was higher than, or at least comparable to, the 2024 parliamentary elections, when it reached 80%, according to local media.

Until a few days before the vote, polls suggested a neck-and-neck race, with the pro-European camp's advantage steadily eroding.

"Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?" was the question on the ballot.

Iceland applied for EU membership following the 2009 financial crisis, but froze the talks after the election of a Eurosceptic government in 2013.

Further results are expected through the night as counting continues.

This is a developing story.

World.title: Bardella, Faure, Lecornu, Hollande, Philippe: Political season begins in France
World.content:
Before France knows who its next president will be, it must first adopt a budget for the year 2027.

 

That is the main task facing the French Prime Minister, Sébastien Lecornu, he told French daily Le Parisien in an interview.

With less than eight months to go before the first round of the presidential election and no majority in the National Assembly, Lecornu said he hopes to avoid a political stalemate by promising a budget"with measures that, for the most part, can be reversed by the new majority that emerges from the ballot box."

Lecornu is not planning to raise taxes, but is instead preparing an agricultural "rescue plan" and a reform of sick leave.

As for 2027, he repeats:"I don't know in what language I have to say it, I am not a candidate in the presidential election. I am not getting involved in the presidential campaign."

The Prime Minister was in Sens this Saturday for the summer school of the Laboratoire de la République, the movement set up by former education minister Jean-Michel Blanquer.

Olivier Faure calls for 'ecological socialism'

For his part, the First Secretary of the Socialist Party (PS), Olivier Faure, warned: "If the document that comes out of these debates is the one put forward by Messrs. Attal and Philippe with the support of the far right, then I am telling you we will vote to censure it!"

In his speech at the PS summer meetings, he also urged the left to "build a barrier"against the alliance between"the far right" and "big money". "The hour of ecological socialism has struck", he added, while continuing to keep everyone guessing about his intentions ahead of the left-wing primary.

Jordan Bardella believes the RN can 'win this election'

Visiting the Châlons-en-Champagne fair in the Marne, the president of the Rassemblement national (RN), Jordan Bardella, insisted that his party had "worked hard this summer on a programme to get the country back on its feet" and on the "presidential campaign".

For a time tipped as the far-right party's candidate, Jordan Bardella ultimately had to fall in behind Marine Le Pen.

A debate between Édouard Philippe and François Hollande

Another presidential contender, Édouard Philippe (Horizons), took part on Saturday in a debate with former Socialist president François Hollande, whose ambitions for 2027 appear to be growing.

At the Laboratoire de la République summer school, the two men agreed on what they see as the need to beware of the RN and La France insoumise (LFI)."In a country that is so divided, where discord has taken hold, where there is a form of radicalism, of populism, where people are set against one another, we must unite (…) against all those who divide,"François Hollande said.

Édouard Philippe, who hopes to bring together the right and the centre, also urged caution with regard to the two parties,"not because they are illegitimate in the public debate, but because they divide."

While they both sound the alarm over the state of the French economy, the former head of state and the ex-prime minister are not prescribing the same remedies: François Hollande is calling for an _"_increase in taxation", whereas Édouard Philippe advocates "keeping a lid on"social spending.

World.title: Solidarity Armada sails to Ceuta with 50 boats in support amid migration crisis
World.content:
A flotilla of around 50 vessels from the Costa del Sol and other Spanish ports set sail on Saturday for Ceuta to show their support for the city after the migratory crisis that has been unfolding since the end of July, according to local media.

 

The initiative, dubbed the Fleet of Solidarity with Ceuta, brings together around 120 participants under the slogan "We are all Ceuta, Spain responds as one". The organisers have arranged up to 60 free berths in the city's harbour for the participating boats.

The vessels have not departed as a single convoy, with each skipper leaving from their home port to cross the Strait of Gibraltar independently bound for Ceuta, where the participants have various activities planned over the weekend.

The call went out after the mass arrival of migrants in Ceuta on 30 and 31 July, when tens of thousands of people crossed irregularly from Morocco into the autonomous city, in one of the episodes of greatest migratory pressure seen on the border in recent years.

Once in Ceuta, the participants will take a guided tour of the city and attend a dinner at the Yacht Club. On Sunday the vessels are expected to undertake a trip through the waters surrounding the autonomous city.

Later, the boats from mainland Spain and those based in Ceuta will gather in the southern bay to send a message of unity "between Spaniards on both sides of the Strait", according to the programme for the initiative.

A weekend with no demonstrations expected

Ceuta faces a weekend with no new demonstrations planned, after several days of protests over the presence of thousands of migrants who entered the city on 30 July.

The latest rally on Friday brought together hundreds of residents on Trampolín beach, where they demanded the return of the migrants to Morocco and the clearance of the camp set up next to the Temporary Stay Centre for Immigrants (CETI), which remains overcrowded. The protests have been organised mainly through groups on social media.

For now, there are no new calls for protests this weekend, although local sources warn that they could take place at any time. On 2 September a demonstration is scheduled, organised jointly by the Provincial Federation of Neighbours' Associations (FPAV) and the association Foro Ceuta Siglo XXI.

World.title: Iceland's EU referendum sees high preliminary voter turnout in expected close race
World.content:
Iceland's capital Reykjavík recorded a higher voter turnout in the high-stakes EU referendum by noon than at the same time during the country's parliamentary elections in 2024, preliminary figures showed on Saturday.

 

In the hours after voters began casting their ballots in the referendum that will determine whether to reopen EU accession talks, 13.7% had voted by noon in the Reykjavík North constituency, compared to just over 10% in the 2024 election.

In Reykjavík South, just over 14% had voted by noon, compared to just over 11% for the parliamentary election.

More than 20% of voters cast early ballots in advance of election day, Iceland’s national broadcaster RÚV said.

A close race is expected, with a final poll on Friday indicating 50.4% of voters plan to vote yes and 49.6% no.

Icelandic Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir casts her ballot at Álftamýrarskóli polling station in Reykjavik, Iceland, Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. AP Photo/Marco Di Marco

Backers of EU membership say it’s best for Iceland to get closer to its European neighbours to combat issues that don't respect borders, such as climate change. They also say the euro would bring more stability than Iceland's volatile króna currency.

Opponents say the current setup is just right and that Iceland already enjoys all the benefits of European integration without the sovereignty compromises that inevitably come with full membership. They cite trade deals, such as one with China, that are more favourable.

"I think that we should be a part of a bigger unity. I think it's worth looking into it," Unnur Jokulsdottir, a 71-year-old retiree, said after casting her ballot in Reykjavík's City Hall.

In contrast, Olafur Thorsson, a 53-year-old fish trader, said he was sceptical.

"I used to like the European Union back when it was a good thing. But today it's become a sort of big economic prison," he said.

The country of just under 400,000 people applied to join the EU in the wake of a 2009 financial crisis that devastated its economy.

Membership talks were then suspended in 2013 when a eurosceptic government came to power.

A voter places a ballot into a ballot box at Reykjavik City Hall in Reykjavik, Iceland, Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. AP Photo/Marco Di Marco

A yes vote would trigger renewed negotiations with the European Commission covering 35 areas, from the economy to human rights.

The issue of fisheries — a pillar of Iceland's economy and over which Reykjavík wants to retain exclusive control — would have to be hammered out with Brussels, which this time around appears more willing to compromise.

On the global stage, the return of war in Europe with Russia's invasion of Ukraine has shaken established security doctrines.

Trump's unpredictability and his threats to take over neighbouring Greenland — which he has mixed up with Iceland on several occasions — have added to Icelanders' concerns.

Their island is strategically located in the sub-Arctic, has no military and depends on NATO and a 1951 bilateral agreement with the United States for its defence.

The result of the vote will be followed closely by the EU, which has not welcomed a wealthy, net contributor to its budget since 1995.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s government steps down as newly elected Kurultai holds first session
World.content:
Kazakhstan has entered a new political season with a reshaped political system after the country’s newly established unicameral parliament, with its lawmakers gathered for its first session on Friday in Astana.

 

It comes Kazakhstan’s pro-government Adilet party won more than 71 percent of the vote in last Sunday’s parliamentary election, that was triggered by a new constitution adopted earlier this year.

The session attended by all 145 members opened with an address by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, who formally declared the first session of the first convocation of the Kurultai open and described it as the beginning of an important new stage in the country’s development.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev at the first session of the Kurultai in Astana. Copyright: Aqorda Press Service

“From this day, the process of renewing the country’s political system begins. … The Kurultai will fundamentally modernise the system of government and give a powerful impetus to the work of the entire state apparatus.

By improving the quality of national legislation, the Kurultai will provide a strong foundation for the country’s legal system,” Tokayev said.

A new political system

Under the Constitution, the government is required to step down before a newly elected Kurultai. Kazakhstan’s government therefore relinquished its powers as the new parliament convened.

However, the country will not be left without a functioning government during the transition period. President Tokayev signed a decree instructing the cabinet to continue performing its duties until a new government is formed.

Under Kazakhstan’s new Constitution, which came into force on 1 July 2026, the previous bicameral parliament, consisting of the Mazhilis and the Senate, was replaced by a unicameral parliament called the Kurultai.

The term “kurultai” dates back centuries and historically referred to an assembly or council among the peoples of the Great Steppe.

The new Constitution was adopted in a nationwide referendum held on 15 March 2026.

“By coming together, our people accomplished a great deal in a very short period of time. Thanks to the nationwide referendum, the country successfully implemented a sweeping constitutional reform,” Tokayev said.

The Kurultai consists of 145 lawmakers elected for five-year terms and representing five political parties. The Adilet party, which absorbed Amanat, the successor to the long-dominant Nur Otan party, holds a commanding majority with 110 seats.

It is followed by the Auyl party with 10 seats, Respublica with nine, the Nationwide Social Democratic Party (OSDP) with eight and Ak Zhol with eight.

New speaker of the Kurultai

During the session, President Tokayev nominated Aibek Dadebai for the position of chairman of the Kurultai. Dadebai has headed the Adilet party since 7 May 2026 and has held several senior government and diplomatic posts, including serving as head of the Presidential Administration from February 2024 to May 2026.

Aibek Dadebai, Chairman of the Adilet party. Copyright: Aqorda Press Service

Tokayev said Dadebai had extensive experience in public administration and described him as an educated, patriotic and responsible citizen. “I consider him worthy of this position and ask the members of the Kurultai to support his candidacy,” Tokayev said.

Later in the day, lawmakers backed the nomination and elected Dadebai chairman of the Kurultai in a secret ballot.

Lawmakers also elected three deputy speakers: former senator Nurlan Beknazarov, former Mazhilis deputy speaker Dania Espaeva and Children’s Rights Commissioner Dinara Zakiyeva.

The Kurultai will have eight standing committees, seven of which will be chaired by representatives of the ruling Adilet party, while the remaining committee will be headed by a member of the Auyl party.

What happens next?

Kazakhstan’s new political structure will continue to take shape in the coming weeks. Once the Kurultai is fully organised, President Tokayev will put forward candidates for vice-president and prime minister, before appointing the new government following consultations with lawmakers. A deputy chairman of the Security Council will also be appointed to a newly created post.

Tokayev said he would deliver his annual address to the nation once the new parliament and government are fully formed.

The institutional changes will continue into September, with the Kazakhstan People’s Council expected to be established in the second half of the month. The new constitutional body will represent the country’s ethnic, regional, social and political diversity and will have the right to initiate legislation.

According to Tokayev, the process will renew “almost all key institutions of power” within a relatively short period.

World.title: Germany news: Merkel tells voters to 'stand up' for democracy
World.content:
Skip next section Merkel calls on Germans to 'fight for this democracy'

08/30/2026 August 30, 2026 Merkel calls on Germans to 'fight for this democracy'

Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel has called on her compatriots to "stand up" for democracy ahead of next weekend's state election in Saxony-Anhalt.

The far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) is leading polls raising questions about what kind of government will be formed.

Despite this, the majority of Germans are not AfD voters, Merkel said at a political event in Berlin on Saturday night.

"I believe that now, once again — something we haven't had to do for many decades — we must really fight for this democracy, simply stand up for it, be a little brave, stand by our word and say that this is a wonderful way to live," she said.

Merkel said the AfD had, to some extent, managed to "dominate all our discussions from morning to night" about politics in Saxony-Anhalt. This meant that many voters no longer knew the policies of the other parties, she said.

But while the AfD has long polled strongest in the eastern states, Merkel — who herself hails from the former East Germany — said the rise of the AfD was not limited to those areas.

"It has become a pan-German phenomenon," she said.

World.title: Norway’s new King Haakon remembers ‘dear father’ Harald in first speech as sovereign
World.content:
New monarch Haakon VIII paid an emotional tribute to his late father, Harald V, in his first address to the nation. Vowing to follow his own path, Haakon pledged to uphold Norway’s democracy, unity and inclusive values.

King Haakon VIII of Norway paid tribute to his late father, King Harald V, calling him "such a wonderful papa" in his first address to the nation as monarch.

"Above all, you were a person who remained committed to your values and dedicated to your duties," Haakon said Saturday in a televised speech. "We greatly mourn his loss. At the same time, it gives us consolation and strength to know that there are so many who are grieving with us."

Norway's King Harald died at 89, after more than three decades on the throne, during which time he became known as a reformer and a popular monarch. In a televised speech from the palace, Haakon praised his father as a "warm and devoted family man."

Haakon became emotional while speaking about his widowed mother, Queen Sonja. He noted that his parents would have celebrated their 58th wedding anniversary on Saturday.

Norway's King Harald V dies at 89 To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Earlier on Saturday, Haakon met at the palace with leaders of the Church of Norway, parliament and the Supreme Court. He also received Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, who viewed the late king’s casket after it was brought to the palace from Oslo University Hospital on Friday evening.

Flags flew at half-mast Saturday as mourners continued to gather at the palace, laying flowers alongside tributes left the previous day by more than 20,000 people.

Haakon stresses he will do things 'his own way'

Haakon said he would follow his own path, as his father did before him, while reaffirming the principles of Norway’s constitutional monarchy. He is due to swear an oath in parliament on Tuesday to uphold the country’s constitution and laws.

"We believe in our system of self-governance — and in democracy. We believe in a society built on the rule of law, where every individual has equal worth," he said.

Haakon automatically became king following his father’s death. Norway does not hold coronations, which were abolished by parliament in 1908.

But, like his father and grandfather before him, Haakon could opt for a consecration ceremony at Trondheim Cathedral, where Norwegian monarchs were crowned between 1814 and 1906.

The Norwegian prime minister told Reuters news agency that Haakon shared many of his father’s qualities, particularly his "ability to create an atmosphere of togetherness."

Crown Princess Sonja and Crown Prince Harald, future King and Queen of Norway, with newly born Crown Prince Haakon in Oslo, Norway. [FILE: July 26, 1973] Image: TT/IMAGO

Mourning and challenges for the royal family

A national period of mourning has been declared, with no date yet set for Harald’s funeral. Churches across Norway will hold memorial services Sunday, including one in Asker, south of Oslo, which the royal family was scheduled to attend.

Harald was widely regarded as a symbol of an open and tolerant Norway and praised for leading a modern, modest monarchy.

The king had been hospitalized in Oslo since August 17 with hemolytic anemia, a condition that causes the rapid destruction of red blood cells and can lead to fatigue and shortness of breath. His health had deteriorated in recent years, forcing him to reduce his official duties.

Haakon's wife, Mette-Marit, is under scrutiny for her ties to the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. [FILE: 17 June, 2026] Image: PPE/IMAGO

The royal family has also faced a series of challenges. Haakon’s wife, Queen Mette-Marit, has come under scrutiny over her ties to the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

In June, her son from a previous relationship was sentenced to four years in prison for two rapes, a sentence he is appealing.

Mette-Marit, 53, who has a serious lung disease, underwent a lung transplant in July.

World.title: Turkish, Somali forces free vessel seized by pirates in Somalia
World.content:
Turkish and Somali forces have freed the MV LUTUF after pirates hijacked the vessel off the coast of Somalia. The 10-day operation killed 14 alleged pirates and destroyed four boats used by the attackers.

Turkey’s navy and Somali armed forces have freed a hijacked vessel in Somali waters and killed 14 alleged pirates following a battle that lasted several days, Somalia’s government said on Saturday.

"During the 10-day operation, four boats used by the pirates were destroyed and 14 pirates were killed," said a Somali Defense Ministry statement. "The sustained military pressure finally forced the remaining pirates to abandon the ship."

The MV LUTUF, a Cameroon-flagged vessel, was hijacked on August 17 off the coast of the Nugaal region of Puntland state. The joint Turkey-Somalia operation was carried out as part of a defense cooperation agreement between the two countries.

The ministry did not provide details about any casualties or the well-being of the crew aboard the vessel but said, "The forces subsequently secured the MV LATUF, which has now safely resumed its journey."

According to AFP news agency sources, at least eight members of the crew were on board, including one Turkish national.

Resurgence of piracy along Somalia’s coast

The Horn of Africa has seen a resurgence in piracy since April, according to figures from the International Maritime Organization, with at least 15 attacks off the coast of Somalia this year.

At least five cargo ships were held hostage, the most recent of which was seized on August 20 off Yemen.

Maritime police patrol to ward off piracy off the coast in Puntland, Somalia [FILE: January 29, 2024] Image: Abuukar Mohamed Muhidin/Anadolu/picture alliance

These attacks are the highest since 2013. Piracy was rampant off the coast of Somaliain the 2000s. It peaked in 2011 before being curbed by international naval deployments and new protection measures for commercial shipping.

The resurgence of piracy in the Horn of Africa is adding to mounting challenges for international shipping in the Middle East, where vessels are already navigating around the contested Strait of Hormuz and seeking to avoid Houthi attacks in the Red Sea.

In recent years, pirate attacks have also increased along the West African coast, adding another layer of risk for commercial shipping.

World.title: Israeli settlers attack Palestinian homes in West Bank
World.content:
Masked Israeli settlers launched their first major attack since initiating a siege in the village of Qusra earlier this month. Saturday's attacks were met with rare criticism from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians in the occupied West Bank on Saturday, pelting them with rocks and trapping residents in their homes.

The incident was the first major attack by Israeli settlers since they began a siege in the villages of Qusra and neighboring Jalud earlier this month.

On Saturday, settlers descended on Qusra and began pelting Palestinians with rocks. When dozens of residents sought to barricade themselves in a home, settlers followed them in, according to the Israel Defense Forces (IDF).

"The security forces who arrived at the scene initially operated to remove the rioters from the home and separate the groups, in order to protect the residents inside the house," said an IDF statement.

Palestinian group watches for Israeli settlers in West Bank To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Who is the IDF protecting in such situations?

Although the IDF said settler vehicles had been impounded and authorities were gathering evidence, Palestinian media said the IDF protected the settlers during the melee.

A number of Palestinians said they were injured after being pepper sprayed by settlers, and reported that other Israeli settlers had tried to burn nearby fields owned by Palestinians.

One Palestinian said the IDF had fired tear gas into the home that he was in and held several people inside while at the same time letting Israeli settlers go free.

Other Palestinians said IDF officers had handcuffed, blindfolded and beaten residents trapped inside before letting them go.

Local Palestinians told international news teams that they had been trapped in their homes for hours waiting for help from the IDF.

The IDF did not comment on the use of tear gas nor accusations of handcuffs and beatings.

Saturday attacks elicit rare criticism from Netanyahu

Saturday's attacks took place just yards away from three other Qusra homes that radical Jewish settlers targeted in a siege that began three weeks ago.

Despite a massive Israeli military presence that local Palestinians say has kept them imprisoned in their houses, residents report near-daily settler encroachments.

Rights groups say settler aggression is part of an — illegal — effort to seize land from residents in the occupied West Bank, where Palestinians hope to one day found their own independent state. The Israeli government has rejected accusations of illegality. Various Israeli political figures have justified the settlements for security reasons or argued there are biblical grounds for the creation of the settlements.

The IDF has said it will continue "to operate in the areas of Qusra and Jalud to prevent further disturbances and restore order in the area."

Although settlers have been emboldened by the stance of Israel's far-right government — which has encouraged settlement building despite broad international opposition — the Saturday attack managed to elicit rare criticism from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

On Saturday, Netanyahu released a statement on X saying, "I strongly condemn the criminal acts of violence committed in the villages of Qusra and Jalud by a handful of rioters who are violating the law, causing a grave injustice to the law-abiding Jewish community, interfering with the IDF in carrying out its missions, and harming Israel's standing in the world."

Increasing Israeli settler violence has even garnered criticism from US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, who recently denounced radical settlers in the West Bank as "Israeli terrorists," adding that those behind the siege of Qusra could face US sanctions.

World.title: Zimbabwe crash involving church minibus kills 27
World.content:
Dozens of people were killed when a minibus carrying churchgoers collided head-on with a truck in central Zimbabwe. The crash near the town of Chivhu is the latest deadly road accident in the African country.

At least 27 people were killed in a minibus crash in central Zimbabwe after the vehicle carrying churchgoers collided head-on with a truck, police said Saturday. Seven people were injured.

Police spokesperson Paul Nyathi said members of a popular Indigenous African Christian denomination, known for wearing white robes, were traveling to a conference on Friday when their minibus collided with a truck on a major highway near the town of Chivhu, about 140 kilometers (87 miles) south of the capital, Harare.

The foreign-registered haulage truck was overtaking another vehicle when it collided with the minibus. Both vehicles were carrying an "unspecified" number of passengers, Nyathi said in a statement.

Footage shared on social media by public broadcaster ZBC showed the mangled minibus charred to a shell.

Zimbabwe faces road safety crisis

Authorities say 94% of road accidents occur due to human error. Many Zimbabweans rely on privately operated minibus taxis, known locally as kombis, for everyday transportation. The vehicles are often criticized for carrying more passengers than allowed.

Zimbabwe’s roads are also riddled with potholes after years of underfunding and neglect, while driving standards can be poor.

In April, at least 18 people were killed when a minibus burst into flames on a highway in southern Zimbabwe. Earlier that month, a woman and her five children were killed when their vehicle collided with a haulage truck on another highway linking Zimbabwe and South Africa.

Rescue personnel work at the site of a bus accident on a major highway near Harare [FILE: January 18, 2015] Image: Xinhua/imago images



Road crashes kill about 300,000 people across Africa each year, accounting for roughly a quarter of the global road death toll, according to the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa. The continent has the world’s highest road fatality rate, the commission says.

This is despite Africa’s 1.5 billion people accounting for only about 3% of the world’s vehicle fleet.
