World.title: It ain’t pretty: botched Botox on the rise in country’s youth
World.content:
Just as the new school year gets underway, the Dutch Health and Youth Care Inspectorate (IGJ) has warned about a five-fold increase in complaints resulting from failed cosmetic treatments involving Botox and other dermal fillers.

The IGC received 175 reports of failed treatments, up from some 35 per year in the preceding years. The skyrocketing numbers, they say, are largely due to increased demand for the procedures among youth looking for fuller lips and less wrinkles and a surge in places providing them.

Young people, IGJ inspector Rosemarie Jansen told broadcaster NOS, were especially vulnerable to cutthroat rates among providers who often lack the mandatory qualifications to provide them. That “lowers the threshold for young people, precisely because they do not have much to spend,” she said.

Some 67% of the complaints involved a practitioner who was not legally qualified or lacked the necessary medical competence.

In the Netherlands, a doctor is required to be present when a patient receives such cosmetic treatments, something which is lacking in the proliferation of places offering them.

The botched procedures have led to swelling and drooping eyelids, lip inflammation and allergic reactions. The ICJ says the number of complaints is likely unreported due to the shame many young people feel about getting cosmetic work.

Fillercheck.nl

To help combat the problem, the IGC, along with Tilburg University and the consumer platform wiemooiwilzijn, have created fillercheck.nl, a website where those seeking cosmetic treatments can go down a four-part checklist that gets them thinking about the treatment, lets them find out if their provider is qualified and, says the IGC, help them recognize red flags.

The Inspectorate is taking their message via pop-up clinics disguised as cosmetic treatment centres to students in Amsterdam, Nijmegen, Zwolle and Breda this week and next – just in time for university introduction weeks.

World.title: Poland is terrible at promoting itself – but has never had better press
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Daniel Tilles Two incidents this month have highlighted how state-led efforts to promote Poland abroad often disappoint. Yet, at the same time, the country has never had better international press. Politicians should let Poland’s successes speak for themselves, and support those already telling its story. Poles care a lot about what the world thinks of their country. Major Polish media outlets regularly devote entire articles to what Western journalists, commentators and influencers are saying about Poland. “A German showed what he saw on the streets of Poland,” read one typical recent headline by Onet, Poland’s biggest news website, which devoted an entire report to one video by a German-speaking TikToker with around 7,000 followers. One rarely sees such reports in more self-confident Western countries. Given Poland’s history, such sensitivity regarding the country’s status is not surprising. Poland was, up until the 18th century, a major European country. But, for most of the last 250 years, it has been under foreign subjugation. Only since 1989 has it been able to develop independently, and Poles are understandably keen for the world to take note of their return to the top table. Poland has emerged as Europe’s undisputed growth champion over the past 35 years. In the first part of a new series of articles and podcasts, @AlicjaPtak4 explores the reasons behind Poland's rapid economic development, and the dangers that may lie ahead https://t.co/bW3bnV7Ozn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2025 Polish politicians are also inevitably eager to capitalise on such sentiment by showing voters that they are making an effort to promote Poland abroad. The problem is that such efforts are often poorly conceived and executed – as two examples this month have shown. In mid-August, the sport and tourism ministry launched a new advertising campaign intended to attract visitors from western Europe and the United States. However, the first advert – featuring Polish football star Robert Lewandowski, supermodel Anja Rubik, Hollywood filmmaker Jesse Eisenberg, and actor Nikodem Rozbicki playing Fryderyk Chopin – was widely panned in Poland. Res Futura, an organisation that monitors social media sentiment, found that 85% of comments about the advert were negative. The campaign’s slogan – “Poland. More than you expected” – is negative and lacking confidence. The Polish Tourism Organisation says it is based on research showing that visitors to Poland are often positively surprised by how nice it is. Yet, while that is undoubtedly true, it does not mean it is a good idea to try to attract potential tourists by focusing on their low expectations. Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to attract tourists from Europe and the US. The first video, under the slogan "Poland. More than you expected", features footballer Robert Lewandowski, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg and supermodel Anja Rubik https://t.co/3jtqyUWQyy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 19, 2026 The video also has no narrative, with the creators seeming to think that showing famous faces will be enough. Rubik does not speak a single word, while Eisenberg says only “Poland” and Lewandowski “More than you expected”. The film itself does nothing to show that Poland is more than anyone expects. In fact, its depressingly colourless palette and focus on Warsaw’s Stalinist Palace of Science and Culture actually reinforce (false) stereotypes of Poland as grey, dull and post-communist. The country has so many interesting and colourful places that could have been showcased instead. The advert is also a wasted opportunity to tell a story about the film’s stars, especially Eisenberg, who has reconnected with his family’s Polish roots, produced a critically acclaimed movie set in Poland, and last year obtained citizenship. Instead, Chopin dominates the film, but his dialogue is incoherent. When he says, “Warsaw is where my heart is”, almost no potential visitors would understand that this is a reference to the real Chopin’s heart being transported from Paris, where he died, to Warsaw, where it is now entombed in a church. Not long after that advert launched, another controversy emerged around a state official, Barbara Mróz-Gorgoń, who had been appointed only weeks earlier by the government to lead the promotion of Poland. It quickly transpired that a report she had authored last year on creating a national brand – and which appeared to have played a big part in her getting the new job – contained significant errors, questionable methodology, and bizarre language. Many parts showed signs of being AI-generated. Mróz-Gorgoń, who has now resigned, insists that the report was the genuine product of work by her and her team at Marka Polska (Brand Poland), a think tank she leads. However, that is not particularly reassuring given the report’s content. Many parts are simply obvious: at the end of the 26-page text, the three recommendations for the government are to “develop a coherent, long-term national branding strategy”, “invest in promotional campaigns in key markets”, and “coordinate between ministries and other entities”. Other sections are very strange, such as noting that “Germany does not build its brand on the Holocaust”. But perhaps the most telling aspect is that, although the introduction claims it is “a comprehensive report on building…a coherent, long-term branding strategy in the international arena”, the document focuses entirely on how Poles themselves view their own country (its title is even A Self-Portrait of the Poles). It includes no research into what foreigners know or think about Poland and what could interest or attract them. While any national branding exercise should of course take account of the views of the native population, it is clearly incomplete without research into the target of such a campaign, the outside world. Yet that is sadly typical of many state-led efforts to promote Poland, which focus more on pleasing a domestic audience – the voters that politicians want to keep happy – than on being truly outward looking. A government official appointed last month to promote Poland's brand abroad has been hit by a wave of criticism after it emerged that she authored a report containing major errors, bizarre language, and signs of being generated by AI https://t.co/9fpfzFCFuI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 21, 2026 It should be noted that such failings are nothing new. Successive governments have been responsible for botched efforts to promote Poland. The uninspiring slogan “Poland. More than you expected” has been used since 2021. A previous one, “Polska. Spring Into”, launched in 2014, was simply bizarre and quickly disappeared. In 2016, the former Law and Justice (PiS) government established the Polish National Foundation (PFN), which was pumped full of money from state-owned companies and tasked with promoting Poland abroad. Instead, it focused much of its efforts on domestic activity, often intended to support PiS’s political agenda. The work it did do internationally was often of questionable efficacy, such as spending millions on buying a yacht, naming it “I Love Poland”, then attempting to sail it around the world (before it ended up breaking down and getting stuck in port). A senior official under the former PiS government has been charged over alleged misspending of funds. The case relates to a campaign in 2017 that used money meant for promoting Poland abroad to instead advertise PiS's judicial reforms domestically https://t.co/tH64Bekhec — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 15, 2026 Yet, despite woeful state-led efforts to promote Poland abroad, the country has in recent times been enjoying a soaring international reputation. Western media have been full of articles about the country’s economic success; about how not only are Polish emigrants returning from the UK, but many Brits are moving to Poland too; about how Poles are becoming major buyers of property in Spain; about how companies with roots in Poland, such as InPost and ElevenLabs, are pioneering their industries. Social media feeds are full of influencers extoling Polish cities, with their safe, clean streets; the beauty of Polish nature, with its mountains, lakes and beaches; and the sense of dynamic development that you can feel as soon as you set foot in the country. Last weekend,@thetimes reported on how Brits are moving to Poland. This weekend, on how Poles are replacing Brits as property owners in Spain. pic.twitter.com/IDDdDlluTE — Daniel Tilles (@danieltilles1) June 21, 2026 This positive publicity is largely organic – it is the product of Poland’s own actual successes, not of artificial efforts to create an image of success. It is generated from the bottom up, not from the top down. While the state can play a role – for example, by arranging visits for foreign journalists and influencers and supporting media and institutions that are already telling Poland’s story – it would be better for politicians to focus on creating the conditions for those successes, rather than concocting cockeyed schemes to promote them. World.title: Polish government sets out draft 2027 budget with deficit remaining at 7.1% of GDP
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s government has approved a draft budget for 2027 that keeps defence, healthcare and the energy transition among its spending priorities, while projecting another year of heavy borrowing. The deficit is forecast at 7.1% of GDP, unchanged from 2026 but well above the level of 3.7% the government had committed to reach by 2027 after Poland was placed under the European Union’s excessive deficit procedure in 2024. Rada Ministrów przyjęła projekt ustawy budżetowej na 2027 rok. Projekt odpowiedzialnie łączy finansowanie bieżących potrzeb państwa i przedsięwzięć wzmacniających jego bezpieczeństwo oraz potencjał rozwojowy.#BudżetPolaków 🔗 https://t.co/SjWyBUwi8U pic.twitter.com/X9ue6cw5ns — Ministerstwo Finansów (@MF_GOV_PL) August 28, 2026 The budget – which must still be consulted with business and trade union representatives before being approved by parliament and then signed by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki – sets total expenditure at 977.6 billion zloty (€225.4 billion), 58 billion zloty more than this year. Revenues are projected to rise by 68.4 billion zloty to 695 billion zloty, leaving a nominal budget deficit of 282.6 billion zloty, the highest on record and 10 billion zloty more than this year. Defence spending will remain high, at 198.1 billion zloty, equivalent to 4.5% of GDP, one of the highest levels in NATO. The healthcare budget will reach 274.1 billion zloty, up 26.3 billion zloty from 2026. Spending on energy security and transformation will rise 8.3% year-on-year to reach 19.7 billion zloty. The government expects GDP growth to remain strong, at 3% in 2027, while average inflation is forecast at 2.8%, within the central bank’s target of 2.5%, plus or minus one percentage point. Average wages are expected to rise by 5.9% next year in nominal terms, slightly slower than the 6.4% forecast for this year. The government expects that unemployment, measured according to the national methodology, will stand at 6% at the end of 2027, broadly unchanged from its current level. Poland’s gross borrowing needs are projected at 565 billion zloty in 2027, below the 688 billion zloty budgeted for this year. Debt-servicing costs, however, are expected to rise to 107 billion zloty, up 17 billion zloty from this year. Finance minister Andrzej Domański said that the rise in debt-servicing costs is driven by an increase in the overall volume of debt and the need to refinance bonds issued in 2020 and 2021 at very low interest rates. Poland's debt has been growing at the second-fastest rate in the EU this year, and is set to continue rising. What is behind this trend – and should we be worried – asks Alicja Ptak in the latest of her series of articles and podcasts on Poland’s economy https://t.co/1pvnb2ZxoY — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 30, 2025 The projected deficit leaves Poland under continued pressure to bring its public finances into line with EU fiscal rules. In 2024, the country was placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure after its deficit exceeded the bloc’s limit of 3%. Warsaw pledged at the time to bring the deficit below 3% by 2028. However, last year the deficit actually rose, from 6.4% of GDP in 2024 to 7.3% in 2025, which was the second-highest level among all EU member states. This year, Poland’s public debt passed the EU’s limit of 60% of GDP for the first time on record. “The 2027 budget represents a continuation of expansionary fiscal policy, and Poland is making no progress in correcting its excessive deficit and is taking no action to bring it below 3% of GDP,” wrote analysts at ING Bank Śląski today. “The result is a further increase in public debt.” Poland’s public debt has passed 60% of GDP for the first time, thereby exceeding the limit enshrined in EU law. The country is already under the EU's excessive deficit procedure, requiring it to take steps to bring public finances under greater control https://t.co/LNJ0YrP2Ge — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 12, 2026 Efforts to reduce the deficit have also been complicated by political stalemate between the government and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, who has vetoed several fiscal measures, including tax increases. Nawrocki did, however, approve a new levy on banks that came into force this year. The situation has led two of the big three rating agencies, Fitch and Moody’s, to shift Poland’s credit outlook to negative. This year, Fitch warned that the political gridlock between Nawrocki and the government was making tackling the deficit and debt more difficult. However, speaking today, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that the 2027 budget reflects Poland’s position at a time when war is being waged across its eastern border and other conflicts are weighing on the country’s finances. Meanwhile, 2027 will also see pivotal parliamentary elections, at which Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, will seek a second term while the right-wing opposition, supported by Nawrocki, will attempt to win power. Ratings agency Fitch has again warned that the "political gridlock" between Poland's government president – such as the current clash over EU defence loans – is hindering efforts to tackle "large fiscal deficits and rapidly rising debt" https://t.co/JSqwwayTdm — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 18, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish “vampire” burial sheds light on 17th-century efforts to keep the dead in their graves
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Researchers investigating an unusual 17th-century burial in northern Poland, in which the remains of a teenage girl were found with a padlock fastened to her toe and a sickle placed across her neck, believe the measures may have been intended to stop her returning from the dead. The burial, discovered in 2022 at an unmarked cemetery in the village of Pień, is an example of what archaeologists describe as “anti-vampiric” or “anti-demonic” burial, in which precautions were taken to protect the living from a deceased person believed to pose a danger. In a newly published academic paper, a team of researchers led by Dariusz Poliński, an archaeologist at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, say that the girl, whom they have named “Zosia”, may have been blamed by her contemporaries for misfortunes such as disease and famine. The unusual combination of objects that Zosia was buried with – a triangular padlock attached to her left big toe and an iron sickle laid across her throat, with the blade facing towards her neck – immediately attracted archaeologists’ attention when they were discovered. Poliński and his colleagues have used radiocarbon dating, DNA sequencing, isotope analysis and X-ray and microscopic imaging to investigate the burial. Their findings have now been published in the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports. The researchers have established that Zosia, who was aged between 17 and 19, died around the mid-17th century, most likely between 1620 and 1674. Her grave appears to have been secured in two stages, with analysis of soil layers showing that it was reopened after the initial burial and the sickle added later. “It was unusual that there were two precautions, two methods of showing that this skeleton should be kept in the grave – so the fear of the body coming back to life was greater,” Poliński told CNN. The researchers say the padlock had several possible meanings in funerary symbolism. It could mark the end of earthly life and the transition to the world of the dead, prevent contact between the living and the dead, break a run of bad luck, or protect the community from the deceased returning. “In some interpretations, it was also believed to help halt the spread of epidemics,” Poliński told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The sickle had a more direct purpose: if the deceased tried to rise from the grave, it was positioned to sever the head or slit the throat, preventing her from returning to the world of the living. However, the latest findings suggest there may have been a third protective element. Researchers found “a distinct green discolouration” in the oral cavity, suggesting that an object containing a high proportion of copper had been placed in the girl’s mouth. Given the extent of the discolouration, they have largely ruled out the possibility that it was simply a coin. “The protective measures taken at the time of the original burial and subsequently after the grave was opened clearly demonstrate the immense fear of Zosia,” said Poliński, quoted by news website Wirtualna Polska. The grave of a "vampire child" – who was turned face down and secured with a padlock to ensure he could not rise from the grave – has been discovered in Poland Researchers believe the site was a cemetery for those excluded or feared by the local community https://t.co/Ez2QgvMnuX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2023 Poliński believes that the woman may have been ill or had a physical or mental disability, leading her neighbours to treat her badly while she was alive and fear that she would haunt them after her death. However, the researchers found no skeletal evidence of trauma, violence or disease that might explain her treatment, and her cause of death remains unknown. The Pień cemetery, which has not been marked on maps, contains several other unusual burials, including a child buried face down with a padlock beneath the foot and skeletons weighed down with rocks. This has led researchers to suggest that the cemetery may have been located on unconsecrated ground, away from a church or chapel, and used for people who were poor, disgraced, feared, or otherwise excluded from the community. Zosia’s burial, however, appears to have been unusual in another respect. Analysis suggests she was of relatively high social status. Traces of silk and gold-and-silver thread near her skull suggest she wore an expensive cap, a luxury item generally associated with nobility or wealth. Two years ago, sculptor and artist Oscar D. Nilsson unveiled a 3D facial reconstruction of Zosia, based on measurements of her skull and skeletal clues about her age, weight and health. The reconstruction shows a young woman with blue eyes, light brown hair and a broad nose. “It’s really ironic, in a way,” Nilsson told Reuters at the time. “These people burying her, they did everything they could in order to prevent her from coming back from the dead…We have done everything we can in order to bring her back to life.” A team of scientists has reconstructed the face of a 400-year-old woman, once believed by her neighbors to be a vampire, revealing the human story buried by supernatural beliefs https://t.co/Q6sipo7h4O pic.twitter.com/0gLVIEfaZi — Reuters (@Reuters) October 30, 2024 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. A dispute has emerged between Poland’s government and the office of opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki over whether Poland would be willing to host allied nuclear weapons. Deputy defence minister Paweł Zalewski announced on Thursday that Poland wants to participate in the US-led NATO nuclear sharing programme, but without actually hosting warheads. That prompted criticism from Nawrocki’s senior foreign policy aide, Marcin Przydacz, who says Poland should host such weapons. Jedno zdanie wiceszefa MON wystarczyło, by wywołać polityczną burzę wokół kwestii broni jądrowej w Polsce. Paweł Zalewski stwierdził w Kwaterze Głównej NATO w Brukseli, że Polska nie chce głowic nuklearnych na swoim terytorium. Kilka godzin później zareagował szef MON Władysław… pic.twitter.com/EqjTPKqidg — OficjalneZero (@OficjalneZero) August 28, 2026 Zalewski met on Thursday with Elbridge Colby, US under secretary of defence for policy, at NATO’s headquarters in Brussels. Afterwards, he was asked by reporters if an expanded future US military presence in Poland might include nuclear weapons. “No. I would like to say this very clearly and openly: Poland does not want nuclear warheads on its territory,” replied Zalewski, quoted by broadcaster TVN. The minister added that Poland still wants to be part of NATO’s nuclear deterrence programme. However, he said that this could be achieved without hosting the weapons themselves. Those remarks triggered criticism from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s main opposition party. Former PiS defence minister Mariusz Błaszczak said that refusing to host warheads “in practice means renouncing participation in nuclear sharing”. “Poland should strive for full participation in nuclear sharing,” added Błaszczak. “This is not a matter of Poland possessing its own nuclear weapons, but of strengthening NATO’s nuclear deterrence on the eastern flank.” Criticism also came from other sources, including retired Brigadier General Stanisław Koziej, who served as head of the National Security Bureau (BBN) of former President Bronisław Komorowski, who is an ally of the current government. Koziej called Zalewski’s announcement “an incomprehensible strategic mistake in the field of deterrence”. He said that, to deter Russia, Vladimir Putin must know that there is the possibility Poland could host nuclear weapons. Chęci nie odstraszają. Odstraszają realne zdolności – własne i sojusznicze. A przede wszystkim takie, o jakich użyciu sami decydujemy. To elementarz, który warto przypomnieć https://t.co/Nc3xXnA7bU — Paweł Zalewski (@ZalewskiPawel) August 27, 2026 Late on Thursday, Zalewski commented on the controversy. He rejected Błaszczak’s claim that refusing to host warheads would effectively exclude Poland from nuclear sharing. “We want to participate in NATO’s nuclear deterrence programme without wanting the stationing of nuclear weapons in Poland,” he wrote. “Thanks to our efforts, NATO has opened up precisely such a possibility.” In response to Koziej, Zalewski argued that “intentions do not deter, real capabilities do…above all, those whose use we ourselves decide upon”. Meanwhile, defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz also weighed in, declaring that “Poland remains strongly interested in participating in the NATO nuclear sharing programme” and is also “conducting talks regarding the proposal for participation in a European nuclear protective umbrella”. Kosiniak-Kamysz did not, however, comment on the issue of Poland potentially hosting warheads. Rozwiewając wszelkie wątpliwości: Polska jest niezmiennie zainteresowana udziałem w programie NATO Nuclear Sharing. Prowadzimy także rozmowy na temat propozycji uczestnictwa w europejskim nuklearnym parasolu ochronnym. Stanowisko naszego rządu jest w tych kwestiach… — Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) August 27, 2026 On Friday morning, Przydacz, who is the head of President Nawrocki’s International Policy Bureau (BPM), joined the criticism of Zalewski, calling his comments “bizarre, absurd and completely inconsistent with what Poland has been saying so far and what the policy of the Polish state is”. “Both the presidential palace and the executive branch of the government have so far supported Poland joining the nuclear sharing programme as part of its deterrence policy,” he continued. Przydacz added that “it is not true” the country wants to participate without actually hosting warheads. “Poland also wants to have warheads on its territory,” he said. Nawrocki, who is a close ally of President Donald Trump, has made clear his support for Poland seeking a nuclear sharing arrangement with the United States. But it remains unclear exactly what the government’s plans are. Earlier this year, Poland entered discussions with France over the extension of the French “nuclear umbrella” over Europe. Later, however, Prime Minister Donald Tusk indicated that Poland would not want to actually host French nuclear-armed aircraft. Both last year and this year, Tusk has also hinted that Poland could seek to develop its own independent nuclear deterrent. However, Colby made clear that the US would “strenuously oppose” European countries such as Poland, Germany or the Scandinavian states seeking to develop their own nuclear weapons. Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has regularly clashed with the government, including vetoing a record number of laws. However, the two sides have sought to present a more united front on issues of national security. The United States would “strenuously oppose” Poland, Germany or the Scandinavian countries seeking to develop their own nuclear weapons, says a senior Pentagon official. His comments come amid discussions in Poland and Europe over nuclear deterrence https://t.co/e9J8tNxcc9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 5, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Kraków withdraws fireworks ban after negative court ruling
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! A ban on the use of fireworks that was introduced last year by Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has been withdrawn after the local authorities decided not to appeal against a court decision revoking it. Kraków had argued that the ban would boost the safety and health of both humans and animals. However, opponents of the measures, including the provincial governor, who launched the legal challenge against it, argued that it was excessive and undermined constitutional freedoms. Kraków bez zakazu fajerwerków. Miasto nie zaskarży wyroku WSAhttps://t.co/rPEYNhEMAQ — Fakty RMF FM (@RMF24pl) August 25, 2026 In November 2025, Kraków’s city council adopted a resolution banning fireworks, firecrackers, sparklers and other pyrotechnic materials being set off “for entertainment purposes”. The ban, which carried an exemption for last year’s New Year’s celebrations, applied in public spaces as well as private properties where the use of fireworks was deemed to impact public places. The city said the ban aimed to “protect the life, health and peace of residents” and “ensure public safety”, adding that the discharge of pyrotechnics created noise and air pollution and could pose a threat to the health and life of humans and animals. Some councillors also argued that a ban would benefit residents suffering from trauma, including World War Two veterans and Ukrainian refugees. The city’s then mayor, Aleksander Miszalski, cited a city poll finding that 67.5% of respondents supported a year-round ban on fireworks and 31.2% opposed it. However, the measures were criticised by the head of the Association of Pyrotechnic Importers and Distributors, Marta Smolińska, who told news service Puls Krakowa that the ban was an “extreme solution” that would hurt local businesses. She called instead for “promoting the responsible use of pyrotechnics”. In December, Krzysztof Klęczar, the government-appointed governor of the Małopolska province, of which Kraków is the capital, announced that he would challenge the ban in the Provincial Administrative Court. Klęczar argued that the measures may “violate the principle of proportionality of limiting constitutional freedoms and rights as well as the freedom…to conduct business activity”. National parks in Poland have appealed to revellers to refrain from using fireworks this New Year’s Eve to avoid awakening wild animals from their winter slumber. A number of cities have also called on residents to abandon the tradition to protect petshttps://t.co/T6RQHdsF9P — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 29, 2022 His arguments were endorsed by the court, which, in a ruling in late June, deemed the resolution introducing the ban “invalid” and ordered that the city of Kraków pay legal costs. The court said the ban “went beyond the competence of the city council” and “violated the principle of proportionality of the protection of constitutional freedoms and rights”. It added that it “was not necessary to protect health, life or public order”. While Kraków could have appealed against the ruling at the Supreme Administrative Court, it has decided not to take that step. An appeal “would probably have little chance of upholding the resolution,” spokeswoman Dominika Jaźwiecka-Bujalska told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Poland's largest opposition group has proposed a law banning fireworks, arguing that they cause distress, and even death, among domestic pets and wild animals https://t.co/UVzFMv3IEn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 23, 2021 At the national level, in 2021, Civic Coalition (KO) – which was then the largest opposition party and is now Poland’s main ruling party – proposed a law that would have banned the use of most fireworks and firecrackers to protect domestic and wild animals. While that legislation did not proceed beyond a parliamentary commission, two further bills seeking to limit the use of fireworks to protect animals are currently proceeding in parliament, reports local news service Portal Samorządowy. Several Polish cities have introduced their own restrictions, which in some cases have also faced legal challenges. Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city, also introduced a ban in January, which was likewise revoked in an administrative court after facing opposition from the provincial governor, reports PAP. Year-round bans remain in place in the Baltic resort town of Sopot, where there is an exemption for 31 December and 1 January, and the southern mountain resort town of Zakopane, a popular destination for New Year’s revellers, where the New Year period is included. World.title: Polish Olympic Committee chief detained over links to collapsed crypto firm

The president of the Polish Olympic Committee (PKOl), Radosław Piesiewicz, has been detained as part of a criminal investigation into Zondacrypto, a cryptocurrency firm that collapsed earlier this year and was a major sponsor of Poland’s Olympic team. The development comes a day after Waldemar Żurek, Poland’s justice minister and prosecutor general, revealed that prosecutors are investigating possible crimes relating to Zondacrypto’s financing of various individuals and organisations, including PKOl, Piesiewicz, and figures from Poland’s right-wing opposition. Dziś w ramach śledztwa w sprawie ZondaCrypto zatrzymany został Radosław P. Prokuratura będzie przekazywała dalsze informacje po zakończeniu czynności z jego udziałem, prowadzonych w Śląskim Wydziale PZ PK. — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) August 27, 2026 On Thursday afternoon, Żurek announced that Piesiewicz had been detained and would be charged. He said he was unable to reveal what the charges would be, but confirmed that prosecutors are investigating a €40,000 watch reportedly given to Piesiewicz by the former head of Zondacrypto, Przemysław Kral. Under Piesiewicz’s leadership, PKOl signed an agreement in 2025 with Zondacrypto that made the crypto firm the main sponsor of the Polish team at this year’s Winter Olympics in Italy. However, in April, Zondacrypto began to come under scrutiny after customers began reporting being unable to access their funds. The firm subsequently collapsed and Kral went into hiding abroad. Prosecutors estimate losses to its clients of at least 350 million zloty (€81.4 million). At a press conference today, Żurek confirmed that Piesiewicz had been detained in connection with the investigation into Zondacrypto, which concerns suspected large-scale fraud and other criminal activity. The development comes days after two leading media outlets, Wirtualna Polska and TVN, published a joint investigation in which they alleged that Piesiewicz received a watch worth €40,000 and other gifts from Kral. The gifts were allegedly given in exchange for Piesiewicz intervening on behalf of Zondacrypto with Poland’s consumer protection authority, UOKiK. Piesiewicz denies the allegations and says he bought the watch with his own money, with Kral simply helping facilitate the purchase. 🔴Szef Zondacrypto, prezes PKOl i złoty zegarek za 40 tysięcy euro Prezes Polskiego Komitetu Olimpijskiego Radosław Piesiewicz dostał od szefa Zondacrypto Przemysława Krala zegarek Patek Philippe wart 40 tysięcy euro oraz inne prezenty – wynika z ustaleń wspólnego śledztwa… — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) August 24, 2026 Piesiewicz, who became head of PKOl in 2023 under Poland’s former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, has long been a controversial figure. In 2024, after PiS had lost power, he publicly clashed with Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s new government following Poland’s poor performance at the Paris Olympics, where the Polish team finished with its lowest medal haul since 1956. This year, as Zondocrypto fell into crisis, it emerged that the company had failed to provide promised bonuses to Polish athletes following the Winter Olympics. In May, 82 of the 106 members of the Polish Olympic Committee supported a motion calling for an extraordinary meeting at which the sole item on the agenda was the dismissal of Piesiewicz from his position. He has so far refused to convene the meeting. Poland has finished @Paris2024 with just one gold and 10 medals in total – its worst result since 1956. The prime minister has suggested there are failings in how Polish sport is managed. But the head of the Olympic committee has blamed the government https://t.co/iS9OqF1RuB — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2024 On Wednesday, Piesiewicz and PKOl were among a list of individuals and organisations Żurek announced were being investigated by prosecutors over potential crimes relating to financing they had received from Zondacrypo. Most of them are linked to Poland’s right-wing opposition. They included the foundations of Zbigniew Ziobro, a deputy leader of PiS, and Przemysław Wipler, a former PiS politician now associated with the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja); conservative broadcaster Republika and its head, Tomasz Sakiewicz; and the Polish version of the American CPAC conference. Earlier this year, Tusk claimed that Zondacrypto’s financial success was “rooted not only in Russian money linked to…one of Russia’s most powerful mafia groups, but also to the Russian security services”. His ruling coalition has three times passed a bill to introduce tougher regulation of the crypto market. However, each time, it has been vetoed by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, who argues that the measures are too restrictive. Prosecutors are investigating possible criminal offences relating to financing by Zondacrypto, a collapsed crypto firm, of organisations and individuals linked to the right-wing opposition, including the Polish version of US conservative conference CPAC https://t.co/swceV864nA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 26, 2026 On Wednesday, Tusk wrote on social media that “we now know why Nawrocki and PiS have blocked the cryptocurrency bill like maniacs”. “Cash for watches worth €40,000 euros, [financing] for media, election parties, foundations of right-wing politicians,” he continued. “And the ‘Zonda’ show is just getting started.” PiS figures have, however, denied any wrongdoing in relation to Zondacrypto. “I’m outraged by the suggestion that PiS was involved in anything illegal,” one of the party’s MPs, Piotr Kaleta, told news website Interia. He noted that no evidence had been presented and no indictments made against PiS politicians. “Instead, we have ministers threatening to hold others accountable, and nothing has happened. This is simply meant to cover up the incompetence of the current government.” Teraz już wiemy, dlaczego z uporem maniaka @NawrockiKn i PiS blokowali ustawę o kryptowalutach. Kasa na zegarki za 40 tysięcy euro, na media, wyborcze imprezy, fundacje prawicowych polityków. A przecież serial „Zonda” dopiero się rozkręca… — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) August 26, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Poland has formally requested that the European Commission fine Meta, the owner of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, €250 million (1.1 billion zloty) for failing to tackle fraudulent advertising on its platforms. Its decision follows a high-profile campaign by Rafał Brzoska, the billionaire owner of Polish delivery giant InPost, over scam adverts on Facebook that exploit fake images of him and other prominent Polish public figures, including President Karol Nawrocki. Platformy cyfrowe muszą ponosić pełną odpowiedzialność za swoje działania i dlatego zawnioskowałem o nałożenie na Metę kary w wysokości miliarda złotych. Po analizie materiałów, w tym tych otrzymanych od Meta, a także kolejnych doniesień medialnych o braku kontroli nad… pic.twitter.com/1zSZg8MGf4 — Krzysztof Gawkowski (@KGawkowski) August 27, 2026 On Thursday morning, digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski announced that he had sent a request to the European Commission to take action against Meta, including fining it €250 million. “Inaction and ineffectiveness in combating harmful s and fraudulent content targeting Poles will not be tolerated,” wrote Gawkowski. “I expect the European Commission to conduct the proceedings swiftly and impose the fine. There is more than enough evidence.” The minister also called on Meta itself to “immediately introduce effective tools to eliminate scams, fake s, and the promotion of illegal applications. This Wild West on the platform must come to an end”. Gawkowski shared an image of the first page of a letter he had sent to Henna Virkkunen, the European commissioner for technological sovereignty, security and democracy, in which he argued that Meta’s failure to combat fraud may violate the EU’s Digital Services Act. He pointed to a study by CERT Polska, a Polish state IT security body, which found that, of 122 adverts reported to Meta as being fraudulent, in 106 cases the company rejected requests to remove them. Gawkowski noted that the European Consumer Organisation has reported similar concerns to the EU. On Wednesday, Gawkowski also shared copies of correspondence he had exchanged with Meta earlier this month. In response to the minister’s concerns, the tech firm had argued that it “does not seek to profit from” fraudulent advertising and outlined steps it was taking to address the problem. Meta disclosed that, between July 2025 and June 2026, it had, in Poland alone, removed 380,000 examples of content and 137,000 adverts for violating its policies on fraudulent practices. It noted that the vast majority were removed before users even reported them. Meta przesłała odpowiedź o działaniach związanych ze zwalczaniem scamów i wskazuje, że niektóre dane przekazuje z zachowaniem ścisłej poufności. W państwie szanującym obywatela takie dane muszą być jawne i dlatego podjąłem decyzję o ujawnieniu treści pisma. W piśmie Meta… — Krzysztof Gawkowski (@KGawkowski) August 26, 2026 Gawkowski’s intervention follows a high-profile campaign by Brzoska, one of Poland’s richest people and who, along with his wife, former TV presenter and businesswoman Omenaa Mensah, is a prominent public figure. Brzoska and Mensah have long complained about the unauthorised use of their likenesses in fraudulent social-media advertising, especially on Facebook. In 2024, Poland’s data protection authority ordered Meta to stop displaying adverts that featured false reports of Mensah’s death to promote scams. Earlier this month, Brzoska renewed his campaign, highlighting an example of a scam on Facebook that used a fake image of him being handcuffed by police in his home. Tak działa koncern @Meta w Polsce-nieustająco tolerując fake newsy na mój i wiele innych publicznych osób temat… Może innym to nie przeszkadza, ale jeśli moje małoletnie dzieciaki wysyłają mi te screeny pytając "o co chodzi Tato?", to jak się polskiemu zarządowi tej gównianej… pic.twitter.com/rp4CUscah1 — Rafał Brzoska (@RBrzoska) August 14, 2026 Brzoska – who also pointed to examples of Facebook running fake adverts featuring other prominent Polish figures, including President Nawrocki – launched a petition calling for platforms that run scam adverts to be fined 150% of the revenue they received from them. The petition – which, at the time of writing, has been signed by almost 91,000 people – cited leaked data, reported by Reuters last year, indicating that Meta estimated 10% of its sales in 2024, around €16 billion, came from advertising scams or illegal products and services. In comments to Reuters, Meta said at the time that the estimate was “rough and overly inclusive” and that the actual figure was lower. But it declined to provide an updated figure. Nowy dzień i nowy scam serwowany bez żadnych oporów przez @Meta z Prezydentem @NawrockiKn w roli głównej. Ale to managerowie Meta (Robert Bednarski, Jakub Turowski,Tomasz Parfjanowicz i Ewa Tumanow) mówią,że nic nie mogą w tej sprawie. Jeśli chcemy temu powiedzieć stanowcze… pic.twitter.com/ZVZl04yYY1 — Rafał Brzoska (@RBrzoska) August 24, 2026 This week, Brzoska welcomed Gawkowski’s moves against Meta. He also noted that, while the minister’s letter to Meta had been addressed to Jakub Turowski, Meta’s director of public policy for Central and Eastern Europe, the firm’s response to him was unsigned. “First-class cowardice,” declared Brzoska, who has repeatedly published the names of four of Meta’s senior Polish managers, including Turowski. The United States has donated $2.1 million worth of equipment for border protection, including drones and thermal imaging cameras, to Poland under an agreement signed on Tuesday. The Polish border guard says that the package is part of a wider US programme, worth an estimated €12 million, to support Poland and the Baltic states in response to the migration crisis engineered by Russia’s ally Belarus on their borders. Stronger border security strengthens our shared security. Today in Warsaw, the United States and Poland marked the donation of more than $2 million in U.S.-funded equipment to the Polish Border Guard @Straz_Graniczna . The donation, funded by the State Department’s @StateINL and… pic.twitter.com/8Mh1eHLo0t — US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) August 25, 2026 “Stronger border security strengthens our shared security,” declared the US embassy in Warsaw, announcing the donation of equipment, which includes 45 drones and nine advanced thermal imaging cameras. “This is just the next step in our security partnership,” they added. “Additional equipment, training, and expertise will follow.” The Polish border guard also confirmed that the support includes training packages and bilateral study visits, as well as the delivery of 15 snowmobiles to Poland next year. On Tuesday, it also hosted a delegation of senior figures from the US Border Patrol and US Customs and Border Protection for talks on “exchanging experiences, strengthening cooperation, and implementing advanced technologies in response to migratory pressures”. Since 2021, Belarus has been encouraging and assisting migrants – mainly from Africa and Asia – to attempt to irregularly cross into the European Union over its borders with Poland, Lithuania and Latvia. Tens of thousands of attempted crossings have been reported each year. In response, Poland has strengthened physical and electronic barriers along the border with Belarus. It has also eased rules on the use of firearms by uniformed officers to protect the border, and has temporarily banned asylum applications by people who irregularly cross from Belarus. As a result of such efforts, attempted illegal crossings are down 98% so far this year, while Poland also claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who do manage to cross. The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98% Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026 After meeting with American officials on Tuesday, the Polish border guard said that the head of the US delegation, Jason E. Schneider, acting chief patrol agent for the US Border Patrol’s Rio Grande Valley sector, had praised Poland as a “model and benchmark” for dealing with migratory pressures. World.title: Foreign Pupils on the Rise in Czech Schools — Nearly One in Five in Prague
World.content:
Of the nearly one million pupils attending Czech primary schools last academic year, almost 8% were foreign nationals, most commonly from Ukraine.

According to the Czech Statistical Office (CSO), Prague recorded the highest proportion, with foreign pupils making up 18% of all children in its primary schools.

Compulsory education is mandatory for Czech citizens as well as citizens of other European Union member states who reside in the Czech Republic for more than 90 days. The requirement also applies to foreign nationals with long-term residence permits.

Their children therefore have the same rights as Czech children, including access to free education, school meals and extracurricular activities.



The number of foreign pupils increased significantly after Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, nearly doubling that year. Their numbers have continued to rise ever since. Today, children from Ukraine account for 5% of all pupils in the Czech Republic.

The trend is similar in secondary schools, where the proportion of foreign pupils reached its highest level in the past 10 years, at almost 5% of the total.

Although the number of children in primary schools has remained relatively stable at just over one million in recent years, a sharp decline is expected in the coming years due to the falling birth rate, according to Vendula Kašparová of the CSO’s Social Development Statistics Department. The office said the birth rate has been falling continuously for the fifth consecutive year.

The decline is already visible at the kindergarten level. The number of children enrolled in kindergartens fell below 350,000 in the 2025/2026 academic year, the first time this has happened since 2013. Over the past three years, enrolment has dropped by more than 21,000 children, or around 5.8%.

Fewer Children Receiving Deferrals From Starting School

Kašparová identifies another clear trend: fewer children are being granted deferrals from starting compulsory school. Since the 2021/2022 academic year, the proportion of six-year-olds whose school entry was deferred has fallen from 24.1% in September 2021 to 17.7% in September 2025, representing just under 21,000 pupils.

Furthermore, an amendment to the Education Act is expected to reduce the number of deferrals even further. Under the new rules, deferrals will only be granted when justified by a medical condition that prevents a child from attending school.

This could include a serious medical condition following surgery, cancer treatment or a moderate intellectual disability.

World.title: Czechia, the Land of Burgers. More Fast Food Chains Enter the Market
World.content:
The Czech fast food market is expanding beyond its established players, with new international brands entering the country and existing chains opening restaurants in smaller cities.

McDonald’s and KFC continue to build their networks, while brands from Germany, the United States and Poland are looking for opportunities in the Czech Republic.

The expansion is increasingly moving beyond Prague and other major cities, with retail parks becoming an important location for new restaurants.



Burgermeister prepares Czech debut

One of the newest international brands preparing to enter the Czech market is Germany’s Burgermeister. The Berlin-based burger chain plans to open its first restaurant on Wenceslas Square at the beginning of next year.

The company already sees its Prague location as more than a single restaurant. It is also considering further locations across the country.

Popeyes and Burger King continue expanding

Burger King entered the Czech market 18 years ago and now operates around 70 restaurants. Popeyes arrived much later but has expanded quickly, opening 19 locations during its first three years in the country.

The companies are building a network that stretches from smaller regional towns to central Prague. In Králův Dvůr, a town of around 11,000 people, both Burger King and Popeyes operate at the Litavka Retail Park.

Popeyes is preparing additional restaurants at the Eden shopping centre and in the Budějovická area of Prague. The chain is also expanding into regional cities, with planned locations in Klatovy and Písek.

Five Guys adds another international brand

The Czech burger market gained another major international name last December when U.S. chain Five Guys opened its first Prague restaurant.

The restaurant is located in the former Máj department store on Národní Street. Five Guys is known for burgers prepared to order and a wide range of toppings, allowing customers to customise their meals.

Its prices, however, are generally higher than those of traditional fast food chains.

Another U.S. brand, Dave’s Hot Chicken, is also expected to enter the Czech market this year, according to consulting firm Cushman & Wakefield.

The chain specialises in spicy fried chicken and will therefore compete directly with established players such as KFC and Popeyes.

Czech chains are looking beyond their home cities

The expansion is not limited to international companies.

Czech burger chain Mama’s Burger is also developing its network. Originally based in Ostrava, the company has expanded into several larger Czech cities and operates a restaurant at Prague’s Arkády Pankrác shopping centre.

The company is also seeking franchise partners as it looks to increase the number of locations.

World.title: Slavia Prague to Face Bayern Munich, Arsenal and Porto in Champions League
World.content:
Slavia Prague have learned their eight opponents for the 2026/27 UEFA Champions League league phase following Thursday’s draw in Monaco.

Slavia will play four matches at home at Eden Arena and four away.

At home, Slavia will welcome Arsenal, Aston Villa, Villarreal and Lens. Their away fixtures will take them to Bayern Munich, Porto, Fenerbahçe and Sabah Baku in Azerbaijan.



The most high-profile home fixture will be against Arsenal, the reigning Premier League champions. Slavia also faced the London club in last season’s Champions League campaign, making the return meeting at Eden Arena particularly notable.

The toughest away assignment is likely to come in Munich, where Slavia will face six-time European champions Bayern at the Allianz Arena. The team will also travel to Portugal to meet Porto and to Istanbul for a match against Fenerbahçe.

The longest trip of the league phase will be to Baku to face Azerbaijani champions Sabah, who are making their debut in the Champions League league phase.

How the Champions League league phase works

The 2026/27 competition is being played under UEFA’s new league-phase format for the third consecutive season. Instead of a traditional group stage, all 36 teams are placed in one league table.

Each club plays eight matches against eight different opponents, with two opponents drawn from each of the four seeding pots. Every team has four home and four away games.

The top eight teams in the final standings will advance directly to the round of 16. Teams finishing ninth to 24th will enter a knockout playoff for the remaining eight places, while clubs finishing from 25th to 36th will be eliminated.

The league phase begins on September 8–10, with six rounds taking place before the end of 2026. The final two matchdays will be played in January, with the league phase concluding on January 27. UEFA will announce the exact dates and kick-off times for each individual match later.

World.title: MINT Market Returns to Prague’s Náplavka with More Than 130 Local Brands
World.content:
MINT Market returns to Prague’s Rašín Embankment on Sunday, September 6, bringing more than 130 independent brands and makers to the Vltava riverbank.

From 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., visitors can browse a wide selection of independent fashion, jewellery, ceramics, natural cosmetics, illustrations and original accessories, with many of the products made by small Czech and Prague-based businesses.



The popular design market is also known for its relaxed atmosphere, food stalls and chill-out area. Admission is free, and the riverside venue is fully accessible. The event is suitable for visitors of all ages.

MINT Market has been supporting independent and local creators since 2010.

Over the past 16 years, the project has grown from a small market into a nationwide platform, hosting more than 450 events in over 20 Czech cities and bringing together a community of more than 1,500 designers and makers.

For visitors, the September event offers a chance to discover products that are often made locally and in small quantities, while meeting the people behind the brands directly.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by The best design markets in CZ (@mintmarket.cz)

“Supporting small and local brands has been one of the core ideas of our project from the very beginning,” says MINT Market organizer Lenka Šašková.

“We provide creators with a place where they can showcase their products and meet their customers, because nothing can replace a personal meeting.”

The full list of vendors and further information about the September market can be found on the MINT Market website. Updates are also available through the Facebook event and Instagram.

World.title: Historic Invalidovna Building in Prague Begins Major Reconstruction
World.content:
The long-awaited reconstruction of Prague’s Invalidovna has officially begun.

The Baroque complex in Karlín will undergo a major renovation costing CZK 2.15 billion, with work scheduled for completion in 2030.

The project is the largest investment in the history of the National Heritage Institute (NPÚ). Alongside the restoration of the historic building, two new extensions will be constructed on the southern side of the complex.



One will provide facilities for the Prague Philharmonic Choir, while the other will house technical infrastructure needed to operate the site.

Much of Invalidovna will remain open to the public

Once the reconstruction is complete, the NPÚ will use part of the complex for restoration workshops, laboratories, archives and study rooms.

An underground garage with space for 50 vehicles is also planned.

Around 80 percent of the complex is expected to remain accessible to the public. The restored site will include exhibition and conference spaces, visitor routes through the Baroque interiors, a café and facilities for children’s groups operated by Prague 8.

A new multi-purpose hall in one of the extensions will be suitable for concerts, conferences and other events. The modern section will also contain technical facilities that cannot be accommodated inside the protected historic building.

The courtyard and gardens will be opened through the original entrances.

A Baroque complex with a long military history

Invalidovna was built between 1731 and 1737 based on plans by Kilián Ignác Dientzenhofer, one of the leading architects of the Czech Baroque. The institution provided accommodation and care for war veterans and their families until 1935.

The original complex was designed at a time when European armies were beginning to develop more systematic forms of care for soldiers who had been wounded or disabled in war.

Military campaigns were often accompanied by outbreaks of diseases such as cholera and typhus, which could kill even soldiers whose battlefield injuries were not life-threatening. Separate psychiatric institutions were later established for veterans suffering severe mental trauma after their military service.

World.title: PIZZA! PIZZA! POP-UP Returns to Holešovice Market on September 3
World.content:
Prague’s Holešovice Market will turn into a one-day celebration of Italian food next Thursday, September 3, with the fourth edition of PIZZA! PIZZA! POP-UP.

The event will run from 11 a.m. to 10 p.m., with more than two dozen food and drink businesses serving pizza, pinsa, pasta, arancini, Italian desserts, coffee and drinks. Admission is free.



Among the returning participants will be Pizza Metro, Mate’s PIZZA TRUCK, PIZZA Therapy, Pinsa Al Forno, HOLY PASTA, La Mia Spitzeria, Spojka Karlín, ŝam.ŝam.Piaggio, PIZZAKOLEM, Picoška, Vege Stará Placka, Naše maso and Cukrárna U Moučků.

This year will also bring a new style of pizza to the event. Third Coast Pizza will serve Detroit-style pizza, alongside the wide selection of Neapolitan pizza available from other vendors.

Visitors looking for something beyond pizza can try fresh pasta, pinsa, arancini and Italian sweets.

Drinks will include prosecco, beer, cocktails and coffee, with Gin Twist, Aperol Ape, Milujemě Prosecco, Pivovar Chroust and Garage 22 running various bars and stands. Garage 22 will also operate a negroni bar.

Bovelii Caffé will arrive in its red Piaggio, serving coffee roasted in Parma, Italy.

The programme will include music and Italian lessons from Lingua Nostra. Beads & Lemons will also be at the market with jewellery inspired by life by the sea.

PIZZA! PIZZA! POP-UP has been held at Holešovice Market for four years, bringing together restaurants, food producers and other businesses focused on Italian cuisine. This year’s edition will feature more participants than last year, including both returning vendors and newcomers.

World.title: Manifesto Market’s Craft Beer Returns for Its Third Edition
World.content:
Prague’s beer lovers can look forward to one of the city’s biggest beer events of the year as Manifesto Market brings back its annual beer festival for a third edition.

The two-day event will bring together some of the Czech Republic’s best-known craft breweries, alongside a guest brewery from Berlin, with more than 40 beers available to taste throughout the weekend.

Zichovec, Sibeeria, Chroust, MadCat, Fracek, Pivovar VIK and Berlin-based BRLO will each have their own pop-up tent, giving visitors the chance to explore a wide range of beer styles directly from the breweries.



More breweries are expected to be announced ahead of the event.

One of the highlights will be the festival’s limited-edition glass. It serves as the ticket for accessing the festival specials and can also be taken home as a souvenir.

The beer will be accompanied by food from more than 10 international kitchens at Manifesto. Visitors can expect everything from juicy burgers and tacos to spicy ramen and authentic Chinese roast duck, making it possible to turn the beer tasting into a full weekend meal.

World.title: More Czechs Are Living Paycheck to Paycheck, New Survey Finds
World.content:
The number of Czechs who have nothing left from their paycheck at the end of the month is rising.

This year, 13 percent say they have no money left after covering their expenses, up from 9 percent last year. Meanwhile, 84 percent have at least a small amount left over, five percentage points less than in 2025.

The findings come from a May survey conducted by loan provider Provident Financial among 1,000 respondents.



According to the survey, Czechs’ ability to save is declining. Only 43 percent of respondents have at least 20 percent of their monthly income left after covering their expenses, down nine percentage points from last year. Almost half of Czechs nevertheless regularly set aside part of their paycheck each month.

At the same time, their overall financial resilience appears to be improving. More than a quarter of respondents have enough savings to cover their expenses for more than a year, compared with just 15 percent last year. The share of people with no financial reserve at all has also fallen, from 18 percent in 2025 to 13 percent this year.

The gap between men and women in the amount of money left at the end of the month has also narrowed. This year, 45 percent of men have at least 20 percent of their paycheck left after expenses, compared with 59 percent last year. Among women, the figure has fallen from 45 percent to 39 percent.

The share of Czechs with enough savings to cover 12 months without their main source of income has increased sharply this year, rising by 11 percentage points compared with 2025. At the same time, the proportion of respondents whose savings would last less than three months fell to 12 percent, down from 17 percent a year earlier.

Men are considerably more likely than women to report having enough savings to cover at least six months of expenses. The figure is 63 percent among men, compared with 39 percent among women.

Education also appears to play an important role in financial preparedness. Seven in ten respondents with a university degree say they have enough savings to cover at least six months, compared with 43 percent among people with lower levels of education.

World.title: Terrifying: Bungee jumping goes wrong as rope gets wrapped around jumper’s neck
World.content:
A young festival-goer was taken to hospital after a bungee jumping accident at the Szeged Youth Days (SZIN) festival in southern Hungary on Friday night.

Almost fatal accident at Hungarian festival

The incident happened at the festival’s bungee jumping attraction at around 11 PM, with witnesses reporting that the participant encountered difficulties after being pulled back upwards by the elastic rope.

According to reports by RTL Híradó and local media, the rope became tangled around the young man’s neck during the jump. This particular detail has not been officially confirmed by authorities, however.

Bungee jumping rope reportedly wrapped around jumper’s neck

The participant had the bungee cord attached to his legs before being lifted in a basket by a crane to the jumping platform. He then jumped from the elevated basket.

The elastic rope stretched during the initial fall before pulling the jumper back upwards. According to witness accounts, the rope then became entangled around his body and neck, repeatedly pulling him up and down.

The incident prompted the festival’s on-site medical team to intervene immediately. Additional ambulance units were subsequently called to the scene, and the young man was taken to hospital in a stable condition.

Festival organisers say no serious injuries were found

SZIN organisers said the participant had been involved in an “unfortunate jump” and suffered an accident. The organisers remained in contact with his friends throughout the night.

At around 2 AM, they were informed that the hospital examinations had produced negative results and that the young man had been discharged. The incident occurred at the festival’s Partfürdő venue, where emergency services were also seen arriving at the scene.

Police launch investigation

Hungarian police have launched proceedings over suspected negligent endangerment in connection with an occupational activity. The investigation is expected to examine the circumstances of the accident and whether safety procedures surrounding the bungee jumping attraction were properly followed.

Despite the potentially serious nature of the incident, the participant was able to leave hospital without serious injuries, according to the information provided by the festival organisers.

World.title: Tisza supporter organised protest a day after the appointment of the new head of national asset recovery office
World.content:
A small demonstration was held in front of Hungary’s Parliament on Saturday over the Tisza government appointment of Anna Unger as head of the National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office (NVVH).

A protest was organised over the new leader of the asset recovery office

The protest, organised by Tisza supporter André Nyerges, was announced just one day after Parliament elected Unger to lead the newly established authority. The demonstration was billed as being “for the National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office, Miklós Ligeti and the political transition”.

Nyerges argued that the appointment of Unger represented a serious threat to Hungary’s political transition, claiming that the selection resulted from behind-the-scenes agreements. He said politicians needed to be held accountable, referring to previous remarks by Tisza leader Péter Magyar about the role of the party’s supporters in scrutinising politicians.

Unger elected with 137 votes

Parliament elected Unger, a political scientist by training, as head of the NVVH on Friday with 137 votes in favour, seven against and one abstention. Her nomination had previously been approved by Parliament’s Justice Committee following hearings of the candidates. Within the Tisza delegation, Márton Melléthei-Barna was the only member of the committee to vote against Unger’s nomination.

Melléthei-Barna later explained that he had wanted a legally qualified person to head the office. Prosecutor Katalin Tasnády was appointed as deputy head responsible for investigations. The decision caused controversy among some Tisza supporters, many of whom had backed Miklós Ligeti, legal director of Transparency International Hungary, for the position.

Protest attracts limited turnout

As HVG.hu reported, the demonstration was scheduled to last around 30 minutes. Fewer than 500 people had indicated their intention to attend on Facebook shortly before it began.

Nyerges later said on the event’s Facebook page that another, unnamed demonstration had allegedly been organised at the same time, making it difficult to determine which event some participants had intended to attend. He expressed disappointment at the turnout and argued that the political system had been able to avoid visible consequences despite the controversy.

Stay up-to-date: What’s the public’s problem with Unger? PM Magyar responded strongly to critics of Hungary’s new asset recovery chief

Government defends appointment process

The appointment also prompted criticism from some Tisza and Fidesz supporters. Prime Minister Viktor Orbán responded in a video message, arguing that the head of an important government institution should not be selected through a popularity contest or “reality show”, but through a professional concept and a strictly regulated selection process.

Following her appointment, Unger sought to address concerns about the new office in an interview, saying its focus would be on locating and securing assets while operating within the framework of the rule of law. The dispute over her appointment has nevertheless exposed divisions among Tisza supporters, with some questioning the decision to overlook Ligeti and others defending the parliamentary selection process.

World.title: Relief for drivers as Budapest traffic becomes easier with important flyover now finished
World.content:
Road traffic could resume on the renovated northern flyover at Flórián Square towards Szentendrei Road in the early hours of Sunday, 30 August, the Budapest Transport Centre (BKK) has announced. This marks the completion of the full-scale renovation of the two flyovers connecting Szentendrei Road with Árpád Bridge.

Budapest can finally have traffic eased a bit

In the coming period, only minor repairs and the restoration of the surface junction at Flórián Square will remain, meaning the bulk of the work — the two bridges themselves — will be completed in time for the start of the school year.

According to Budapest Transport Centre, the renovation of the more than 40-year-old flyovers was made necessary by the significant deterioration that had occurred over the approximately 20 years since their previous reconstruction.

Moisture and dirt had damaged the reinforced concrete structures in several places, while water ingress around the pillars had caused the reinforcement steel to rust and the concrete surfaces to deteriorate. The two flyovers play a key role in transport in the capital and its surrounding metropolitan area, carrying tens of thousands of vehicles every day.

Both flyovers have been renovated

The renovation, carried out as a BKK investment with KM Építő Kft. as the general contractor, involved a comprehensive structural and condition-improvement reconstruction of the northern and southern flyovers at Flórián Square, including their bridge fittings. The most important works included:

Reconstruction of the road deck: the condition and geometry of the deck slabs were improved, new full-surface waterproofing was installed on both bridges, and new asphalt surfacing was laid on the bridges and connecting ramps;

Repairs to the reinforced concrete structures: damaged concrete surfaces were removed, corrosion of the reinforcement steel was halted, missing reinforcement was replaced, new reinforced concrete surfaces were created, and the concrete surfaces were given renewed protection against salt corrosion;

Reconstruction of the abutments and bridge ends: new bearings and expansion joints were installed at the abutments, expansion joints above the pillars were eliminated, and the bearing structures above the supports were renovated;

Replacement of kerbs and barriers: new monolithic reinforced concrete kerbs were constructed, while new prefabricated apron elements were installed along the sides of the superstructure and retaining walls, with high-containment road barriers and fall protection fitted on top;

Renovation of the stone cladding on the abutments: the deteriorated stone cladding was refurbished and broken sections were replaced;

Aesthetic restoration: defects in the structural surfaces were repaired, graffiti was removed, and an anti-graffiti coating was applied.

The renovated bridges of Budapest have a combined structural length of 686.57 metres, in addition to the renovated sections of the connecting ramps.

The renovated Flórián Square flyover in Budapest. Photo: BKK

Flyovers completed on schedule

The project’s total gross budget is HUF 3.27 billion (EUR 9 million). Thanks to competition during the public procurement procedure, a highly favourable bid was received, meaning the works were completed for 59.45 per cent of the originally estimated value, saving Budapest residents more than HUF 2 billion (EUR 5.5 million).

The renovation is being funded by the Municipality of Budapest, with a significant part of the necessary funding coming from money recovered in litigation related to the electronic ticketing system.

The first phase of the renovation began on 1 March 2025 with the closure of the southern flyover. Once the flyover was dismantled, its technical condition was found to be worse than expected. Previously hidden damage to the deck slabs meant that additional technical works had to be added to the project, resulting in changes to the original renovation schedule.

The southern flyover reopened to traffic in November 2025, after which work began on the northern flyover. Drawing on the experience gained during the southern flyover’s renovation, specialists carried out a particularly thorough assessment of the northern structure.

Structural works continued throughout 2026, with the project exceeding 70 per cent completion in technical terms by May and passing 90 per cent by the end of July.

Once the official traffic-opening procedure has been completed, road traffic on the northern flyover is expected to resume on 30 August, in time for the start of the school year. This will mark the completion of the structural renovation of both flyovers, with the contractor maintaining steady progress despite the technical difficulties encountered during the project.

Minor repairs related to the investment and the restoration of the surface junction will continue afterwards, alongside the removal of temporary traffic-management measures, and are expected to be completed by 17 September.

The successful bus priority measures introduced on Szentendrei Road and Pacsirtamező Street will remain in place. Temporary traffic-management measures and diversions — including the U-turn facility on Pacsirtamező Street — helped traffic flow during the renovation and eased the difficulties caused by the works. BKK thanked road users for their patience and co-operation.
