World.title: Azerbaijan posts strong growth in gold export revenue
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 30. In the first seven months of this year, Azerbaijan exported gold worth $239.4 million.

This was reported in the August 2026 issue of the "Export Review" published by the Center for Analysis of Economic Reforms and Communications.

According to the information, this is $60.6 million, or 33.9%, more than the same period last year.

In July alone, Azerbaijan exported gold worth $37.2 million, which is $3.3 million, or 9.7%, more than the same period last year.

In the period from January through July 2026, Azerbaijan's non-oil sector exports (excluding non-monetary gold) increased by 18.3% compared to the corresponding period in 2025, totaling $2.5 billion.

The importance of gold to the Azerbaijani economy extends beyond export figures. The precious metal accounts for the largest share of the investment portfolio of the State Oil Fund of the Republic of Azerbaijan (SOFAZ), representing 36% of the fund’s assets.

According to the latest report by the international rating agency Fitch Ratings, as of the end of the first quarter of 2026, the assets of Azerbaijan’s State Oil Fund (SOFAZ) totaled $73.5 billion, equivalent to 93.2% of Azerbaijan’s projected GDP for 2026.

Fitch notes that from 2023 through the first quarter of 2026, gold assets directly contributed to a $19.4 billion increase in SOFAZ’s assets. Volume growth accounted for 26% of this increase.

The agency estimates that Azerbaijan’s "BBB-" sovereign rating is being upgraded by one notch due to the significant volume of SOFAZ assets. These assets provide the country with a high level of foreign exchange liquidity and the status of a net external creditor.

Fitch notes that rising gold prices have had a positive impact on the volume of SOFAZ assets; however, this effect may be offset to some extent by changes in the volume of gold reserves. According to the agency, in the period from January through April 2026, a cumulative sale of a portion of the gold reserves was carried out as part of a rebalancing of the investment portfolio.

At the same time, Fitch highlights the growing role of gold in the external financial positions of countries in the Caucasus and Central Asia.

"Gold has gained greater significance in the composition of the region’s countries’ foreign exchange reserves. Uzbekistan has the highest share of gold in its international reserves, and a significant portion of Kyrgyzstan’s reserves is also in gold. Azerbaijan’s State Oil Fund, which forms the basis of the country’s substantial foreign exchange reserves, holds significant assets in gold," the agency’s report states.

According to Fitch, rising gold prices have also supported the balance of payments of gold-exporting countries. The agency notes that Uzbekistan’s current account deficit narrowed significantly between 2023 and 2025 due to increased gold exports, and Kyrgyzstan has also benefited from gold price trends and gold exports.

However, the agency emphasizes that an increase in the share of gold in reserves and exports could make countries in the region vulnerable in the event of a sharp drop in gold prices.

"Such a decline would worsen nominal GDP, fiscal policy indicators, and the balance of payments for gold-producing countries, as well as reduce the value of reserves in countries with a high share of gold in their reserves," Fitch stated.

The agency added that a decline in gold prices, in and of itself, is expected to lead to negative rating actions against these sovereign borrowers.

Therefore, the increase in gold exports from Azerbaijan is noteworthy against the backdrop of both the expansion of non-resource exports and the growing importance of gold assets in the country’s foreign economic position.

World.title: Uzbekistan’s foreign trade turnover triples over decade to $81.2B
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 30. Uzbekistan’s foreign trade turnover more than tripled over the past decade, rising from $25.8 billion in 2016 to $81.2 billion in 2025.

This was reflected in the infographic released by Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Economy and Finance.

According to the ministry, this figure represents an increase of $55.4 billion, or approximately 215%, meaning that the volume of foreign trade for this period increased 3.15-fold. The growth reflects Uzbekistan’s deeper integration into global markets, broader trade ties, and expanding participation in international supply chains.

Exports reached $33.8 billion in 2025, up 2.5 times from 2016. This implies an increase of roughly $20.3 billion, or about 150%, over the decade. The number of export markets also expanded substantially, from 79 countries in 2016 to 132 in 2025, an increase of 53 markets, or about 67%.

Imports grew even faster, reaching $47.4 billion in 2025, nearly 3.9 times the 2016 level. Based on the reported multiple, imports increased from roughly $12.2 billion to $47.4 billion, representing an estimated gain of $35.3 billion, or about 291%. Uzbekistan imported goods from 158 countries in 2025, compared with 127 countries in 2016.

The composition of trade also changed. Exports accounted for 41.7% of foreign trade turnover in 2025, down from 52.9% in 2016, while the import share increased from 47.1% to 58.3%. The shift points to the faster expansion of imports, consistent with the country’s investment and industrial modernization drive. Uzbekistan’s machinery and transport equipment imports, for example, have been a major feature of its broader modernization process.

The figures show that Uzbekistan’s opening to international trade has produced a much larger external trade base, but they also highlight a continuing challenge: imports are growing faster than exports. In 2025, the gap between imports and exports stood at $13.6 billion, meaning export revenues covered about 71.3% of import spending. Strengthening higher-value exports and reducing the structural trade deficit will therefore remain important as Uzbekistan seeks to turn expanding global integration into sustained economic gains.

Trend's analysis indicates that Uzbekistan’s foreign trade has undergone a clear expansion and diversification trend over the past decade. Foreign trade turnover rose from $25.8 billion in 2016 to $81.2 billion in 2025, while exports increased from their 2016 level by 2.5 times to $33.8 billion and imports grew 3.9 times to $47.4 billion. The number of export markets also expanded from 79 to 132 countries, while import sources increased from 127 to 158. At the same time, the trade structure shifted toward imports: their share of total turnover climbed to 58.3% in 2025, from 47.1% in 2016, while exports fell to 41.7% from 52.9%.

Meanwhile, Trend's assessment shows that the figures indicate that Uzbekistan’s opening of the economy has significantly expanded its participation in international trade, but the faster growth of imports presents a key structural challenge. Rising imports can reflect stronger domestic demand, investment, and purchases of machinery and industrial inputs needed to expand production. However, the widening gap with exports means that stronger export capacity will be increasingly important. The expansion of export destinations is a positive sign, as it reduces dependence on a limited number of markets and provides greater opportunities for Uzbek producers to enter new markets. The next stage of trade development will therefore depend not only on increasing volumes, but also on expanding higher-value exports and improving the competitiveness of domestic industries.

Trend's calculations show that the increase in trade turnover from $25.8 billion to $81.2 billion represents a gain of $55.4 billion, or about 215%, with the total volume becoming approximately 3.15 times larger. Exports rose by roughly 150%, while imports increased by about 290%, showing that imports expanded nearly twice as fast as exports over the period. In 2025, the difference between imports and exports was $13.6 billion, with exports covering about 71.3% of imports. The number of export destinations increased by 53 countries, or 67.1%, indicating that the expansion of trade has been accompanied by a broader geographic reach.

World.title: Turkmenistan’s oil and gas service unit exceeds 2026 plan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 30. The Repair, Adjustment and Electrical Installation Department of the Nebitgazburawlaýyş trust of Turkmenistan’s Turkmennebit State Concern has provided services worth more than 24.4 million Turkmen manat ($6.9 million) to oil and gas enterprises in the Balkan region since the beginning of 2026.

This was reflected in the statement published by the press service of the Turkmen government.

According to the announcement, the figure exceeded the department’s target by 885,402 Turkmen manat ($253,437).

"The department carries out overhaul, adjustment and testing of equipment used by Turkmennebit enterprises, including power transmission lines, automatic and control and measuring instruments, drilling equipment and vehicles. It also services complex electrical systems," the statement adds.

Since the beginning of the year, the department has fulfilled a total of 1,953 orders from Turkmennebit and other organizations. The drilling specialists of the Nebitgazburawlaýyş trust reached 104.9% of their planned target.

In July alone, the department completed 264 orders for enterprises worth more than 4.24 million manat ($1.2 million), achieving 105% of its monthly plan.

Trend’s calculations show that using the official exchange rate of approximately 3.5 manat per US dollar, the year-to-date service volume equates to roughly $7.0 million, with the over-fulfilment representing about 3.8% above plan. The average order value stands at around 12,500 manat ($3,570). For broader context, Türkmennebit’s related well-repair activities in 2025 restored 437 wells and generated an additional 292,600 tons of oil (124% of target). At typical regional crude prices of $70–80 per barrel, that incremental production alone was worth an estimated $150–170 million, underscoring the economic leverage of the maintenance and electrical services that keep drilling and production equipment operational. The current department’s July run-rate (about $1.2 million in a single month) annualises to roughly $14–15 million if sustained, consistent with the pattern of steady over-performance seen across Türkmennebit’s service and drilling units in recent years.

World.title: Plibersek indicates support for ban on choking in pornography
World.content:
Australia should be "very seriously" looking at banning depictions of strangulation or suffocation in pornography, says a senior Labor minister who has indicated her support.

Advocates' calls for the ban have intensified following the death of a 16-year-old Sydney girl, understood to be treated as a suspected sexual choking act.

Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek highlighted the prevalence of the act during sexual encounters among young people after a 2024 study found that 57 per cent of 18 to 35 year olds have experienced strangulation in the bedroom.

Last year, the UK made it a criminal offence to possess or publish pornography showing strangulation or suffocation.

Ms Plibersek said Australia should "very seriously" consider following the UK's decision to outlaw depictions of choking in pornography.

"There is something wrong with a situation where 60 per cent of young people say they've experienced strangulation," she told Insiders on Sunday morning.

"This is not sex education. It's not real life," she added.

New fronts in fight against sexual violence The next five-year plan to end violence against women will have to do more than accelerate existing efforts.

Pointing to risks of long-term brain damage or aneurysms in the case of a non-fatal strangulation, Ms Plibersek said there was "no safe way to strangle someone".

NSW Liberal leader Kellie Sloane added to the calls on Sunday, writing to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to ask him to urgently introduce the ban.

"When pornography depicts an act capable of causing brain injury, unconsciousness or death, it should not be treated as just another form of adult entertainment," she wrote.

Ms Sloane said young people were being exposed to sexual violence online without understanding the danger of the behaviour.

"We cannot wait until another family is living through a tragedy before we take seriously what our children are being taught by pornography."

It is an issue found in other online content, with a 2024 study demonstrating that on average young boys are served extremely misogynistic content within 23 minutes of downloading social platforms, such as TikTok and YouTube shorts.

Ms Plibersek acknowledged the role that social media algorithms played in perpetuating harmful narratives online, following a push by advocates for the government to introduce laws that make algorithms opt-in only.

Chanel Contos has launched a campaign calling on the federal government to "fix our feeds" by making social media algorithms "opt-in" for everyone. (Supplied: Kieran Gilfeather Photography)

Among them is Teach Us Consent founder Chanel Contos, who urged the government to take the issue more seriously.

"I think it's quite obvious the harm that algorithms are doing to everyone, but particularly young people, and women are largely on the receiving end of that," Ms Contos told the ABC.

"And I think that something that has 71 per cent of Australians supporting it should be taken as a serious policy proposition."

Ms Plibersek said there were ongoing discussions about how that would look in practice, but remained open to an opt-in model as the government continued to consult on its upcoming digital duty of care bill.

The issue was also front and centre earlier in the week, when national cabinet acknowledged rates of intimate-partner homicide and sexual violence remained "unacceptably high", agreeing on priorities for the next five-year plan to tackle the issues.

Smart glasses moratorium considered

The federal government is also closely considering a moratorium on the import of smart glasses, which can be used to discreetly film people without their consent.

The devices look like ordinary glasses and yet allow the wearer to record images, video and audio, mostly surreptitiously, with the press of a button.

The Greens, with the support of some crossbenchers, have called on the government to halt the import of such glasses as well as as other wearable recording devices for at least 12 months, until tougher privacy protections are passed into law.

Ms Plibersek revealed the attorney-general was due to deliver an update on the government's position shortly, as she labelled any use of the glasses "really troubling".

"If they're going to be used, there should be safeguards around how they can be used," she said.

"I mean, it's already possible, I believe, to buy glasses where you can disable the filming light, so it's not apparent that they're filming as they're being used. That is really, really troubling".

World.title: Pacific leader heads home before PIF to face no-confidence motion
World.content:
Solomon Islands prime minister and outgoing Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) chair Matthew Wale has made a shock departure from the PIF leaders meeting, flying out of Palau just hours after arriving, in order to deal with a looming leadership challenge back home.

Mr Wale's political coalition was shaken yesterday after Solomon Islands Home Affairs Minister Manasseh Maelanga announced he had filed a no-confidence motion to topple Mr Wale, who has only been in the top job for three months.

In his motion, Mr Maelanga accused Mr Wale of "repeatedly making decisions of matters of national importance without proper consultation with, or the approval of, cabinet, thereby undermining the principles of collective cabinet responsibility, representative democracy and good governance".

Mr Maelanga was one of Mr Wale's main challengers for the top job this year, and has held a senior position in his cabinet since then.

But his arguments echo many of those made by the Solomon Islands opposition, whose leader, former prime minister Manasseh Sogavare, has accused Mr Wale of bulldozing through major changes without consulting properly with parliament or the electorate.

Mr Wale appeared to be shaken by the news on arrival in Palau on Saturday night, and declined to comment on the challenge when asked about it by reporters.

Matthew Wale has only been prime minister of Solomon Islands for three months. (Supplied: Pacific Islands Forum Secretariat)

The ABC understands Mr Wale left Palau early on Sunday morning and is due to arrive back in Solomon Islands on Monday.

Two of Mr Wale's key lieutenants in his coalition — Foreign Minister Rick Hou and Peter Kenilorea Jr — will now represent Solomon Islands at the meeting.

Mr Kenilorea Jr said in Palau late yesterday that he "had no idea as to why" the challenge was launched.

"[I'm] looking forward to finding out more," he said.

The news is a blow to the PIF, which is already facing a large number of absent leaders at this year's gathering.

Kiribati's President Taneti Maamau announced yesterday he would not attend, and that his nation would be represented instead by its ambassador to China.

China accused of influencing Pacific meeting Naoero and Kiribati stir frustration at the opening day of the Pacific Islands Forum by blocking a regional statement criticising China's ballistic missile test.

Samoa's Prime Minister Laʻauli Leuatea Schmidt and Vanuatu's Prime Minister Jotham Napat are also not set to attend, while it's unclear whether Fiji's Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka will fly to Palau for the meeting.

The challenge will also unsettle Australia, which sees Mr Wale as far more sympathetic than his predecessors Jeremiah Manale and Manasseh Sogavare.

Mr Wale fiercely criticised China's recent ballistic missile launch and has made it clear he is uneasy with China's security role in Solomon Islands — although he has not tried to tear up the 2022 agreement the Pacific nation signed with Beijing.

He also announced not long after taking power that he had agreed to kick off negotiations with Australia on a new treaty — with officials racing to complete the discussions by the end of this year.

World.title: Former White House teleprompter operator fined over insider trading
World.content:
A former White House teleprompter operator accused of using inside knowledge to make bets on the prediction market Kalshi has been ordered to turn over more than $US100,000 in profits and pay a $US65,000 fine as part of a settlement with federal authorities.

The settlement with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, announced Friday local time, also dealt Gabriel Perez a three-year trading ban.

Mr Perez was placed on unpaid leave from his job at the White House after reports emerged that he used his position to make bets on what US President Donald Trump would say in speeches.

Trump teleprompter operator suspended US President Donald Trump's longtime technician allegedly made over $142,000 by placing bets on what Donald Trump would say in speeches.

The White House did not immediately comment on the settlement.

A White House official said in July that Mr Perez was no longer in his position but did not say if he had been fired or resigned.

The commission found that Mr Perez made $US107,500 ($150,080) on prediction markets by betting on words and phrases that would appear in Mr Trump's speeches between December 2025 and February 2026.

"In his position, Perez had access to presidential speeches prior to those speeches being delivered and Perez misappropriated that information, in breach of his duty of trust and confidence," according to a release from the commission.

Mr Perez was ordered to repay his profits in full, along with the $US65,000 ($90,746) civil penalty, which the commission said was a reduction because of his "exemplary cooperation".

As details emerged on July 16, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said it was "unfortunate" and "a disgrace".

AP

World.title: Western Sydney's new observatory centuries in the making
World.content:
More than two centuries after a famed observatory was built in Parramatta, a new one has been constructed a few hundred metres away on top of a newly built museum.

The $915 million Powerhouse Parramatta in Western Sydney features research-grade telescopes powerful enough to see distant galaxies.

It will be open to students during overnight stays and to researchers who could access it remotely or during residencies at the location.

Astrophysics PhD student Nada Salama was one of the first to take advantage of Parramatta's latest window to the stars.

The telescopes are industry-grade. (ABC News) They can see distant galaxies. (ABC News)

Sitting on the museum's rooftop, the telescopes are covered by a ceiling that slides open. (ABC News)

She said the observatory represented a rare opportunity.

"I think it'll be a really good opportunity for lots of people from Western Sydney to be able to access something like this," Ms Salama said.

"These are powerful, these are research-grade, industry-grade telescopes … so you can see clusters with lots of stars, bigger nebulae, which [are] where stars are born from."

'You can collect light'

The observatory features two narrow field telescopes that can focus on smaller further away objects, and two wide field telescopes that can see the bigger picture.

The observatory features two narrow field telescopes and two wide field telescopes. (ABC News: Nabil Al-Nashar)

Ms Salama said the telescopes could not be looked through with the human eye.

"These particular telescopes have sensors on them, which collect data," she said.

"You can collect light of different colours. Some of these telescopes will have filter wheels on them, which will allow you to filter out all colours except for one or a certain band or range of colours.

"They will collect data over long periods of time or certain exposures and allow you to study those objects."

This means researchers from anywhere in the world could take advantage of the collected data without having to physically be at the observatory.

The museum is set to open on November 7. (Supplied: Powerhouse Parramatta)

Sitting on the museum's rooftop, the telescopes are covered by a ceiling that slides open and shut remotely and can automatically close if threatened by rain or other unfavourable weather conditions.

Ms Salama said the observatory was about more than just science.

"I think it allows you to put things into perspective … how insignificant we are compared to literally everything else," she said.

The new observatory holds a deep connection to Parramatta's past, as it sits 500 metres from the site of Australia's first private observatory built between 1821 and 1822 by Governor Thomas Brisbane.

It became famous for the extensive cataloguing of southern hemisphere stars.

The old Parramatta Observatory was built between 1821 and 1822. (ABC News: Monish Nand)

A sign and obelisk remain at the site. (ABC News: Monish Nand)

Students to 'interact' with astronomers

Sophie Poisel is head of the Lang Walker Family Academy at the museum, which will host up to 10,000 students a year from across New South Wales for overnight experiences.

"They [the students] will get to come up, select an object in the sky, target it and collect real scientific data that they'll be able to look at in the studios downstairs," Ms Poisel said.

The program will target year 7 to year 10 students, who will be able to stay at the museum.

Ms Poisel says students will be able to interact face-to-face with astronomers. (ABC News: Mario Conti)

Ms Poisel said she was looking forward to hosting the first cohort.

"There are two dormitories where the students will stay close by their teachers' quarters. There's a kind of lounge area for them to socialise in and there are four learning studios," she said.

"On the top floor there are residencies so the students here will get to have face-to-face interactions with leading astronauts, astronomers, researchers, artists, that are all staying here."

Ms Havilah says the rooftop area will have astronomy programs. (ABC News: Mario Conti)

Prior to the NSW government announcing she was stepping aside from the role of Powerhouse Parramatta CEO, Lisa Havilah told the ABC that Parramatta's latest attraction was more than just a museum.

"We have an incredible public domain around the rooftop now, and this rooftop will have astronomy programs … there'll be a whole range of ways that the community can engage with new ideas, new technology, and with creative practice," she said.

The building was designed by French Japanese architect Moreau Kusunoki and features a distinctive exoskeleton design, made from 18,000 tonnes of steel that wraps around the building.

The museum is set to officially open on November 7 with five exhibitions.

World.title: Police investigating suspicious death in southern Tasmania
World.content:
Police say they are treating the death of a woman inside her home in southern Tasmania early this morning as suspicious.

Police said they were called to the home in Huonville, south of Hobart, about 4.30am.

"Police, including officers from CIB, Forensics and Uniform, are at the scene conducting examinations into the circumstances surrounding the woman's death," Tasmania Police said in a statement.

"A man has been taken into custody to assist police in carrying out their investigations."

Police are expected to provide an update on the case this afternoon.

World.title: Police conclude search mission after plane crash claims life of 23yo pilot
World.content:
The search for missing 23-year-old pilot Bob Bramley in the Gulf of Carpentaria has been suspended by NT Police "following an extensive multi-day search involving air, marine and specialist dive resources".

The young Tasmanian pilot was believed to be the sole occupant aboard a small Air Frontier charter plane when it reportedly crashed in Angurugu waters, off the coast of Groote Eylandt, on Tuesday.

The company said Mr Bramley was undertaking a "non-commercial repositioning flight" from Gove to Numbulwar at the time.

Loved ones have described Mr Bramley as "a beacon of hope" who loved flying and "lived to the fullest", with his family expressing their shock and heartbreak in a moving tribute on Friday.

In 2021, Mr Bramley was nominated for Young Australian of the Year. (Supplied: Lachlan Bennett)

Mr Bramley became a passionate advocate for suicide prevention in his teenage years, raising awareness of youth suicide as he attempted to become the youngest person to circumnavigate Australia solo by plane.

Authorities are continuing to investigate, with some pieces of aircraft debris found by police divers earlier this week, but so far the cause of the crash is yet to be confirmed.

NT Police Acting Assistant Commissioner Peter Malley said the presence of "tiger sharks and crocs" had made it an especially difficult search, but authorities were supported by the local Indigenous group Anindilyakwa Land and Sea Rangers through the week.

On day four of the mission, authorities said they were scaling back aerial searches to instead focus on sonar searches and targeted dive missions.

Police divers earlier found what they believed to be parts of the plane wreckage, located on the sea floor. (Supplied: NT Police)

In a statement to the ABC on Saturday, NT Police said its search and recovery operation had been called off after "careful consideration of all available information".

"The search mission coordinator said the decision was made following an extensive multi-day search involving air, marine and specialist dive resources," NT Police said.

The coordinator said "every reasonable search option" had been "considered and undertaken" by authorities.

NT Police said it would continue to assist lead investigators, the Australian Transport Safety Bureau, where possible.

World.title: Scott turns back clock in Tour Championship title tilt
World.content:
A much-craved second major continues to elude him but Adam Scott may be one great round from capping his decorated career with a second season-ending Tour Championship title.

As golf's biggest names jostle for the $US10 million ($A14 million) winner's cheque in Atlanta, Scott quietly but steadily climbed into a tie for third place entering the final round.

The 2006 champion compiled a classy third-round five-under-par 65 at Atlanta's East Lake Golf Club to position himself three shots behind Norwegian leader Viktor Hovland.

With his own 65, Hovland turned a halfway share of the lead into a one-shot buffer over American Ryan Gerard (66) as he reached 15 under.

So often cruelling his winning chances on the greens, putting was for once Scott's saving grace on Saturday (Sunday AEST).

The former world No.1 drained 132 yards worth of putts, including near 25-footers for three of his six birdies on the eighth, 13th and 17th holes.

It was Scott's second-best putting round of the year and presented the 2013 Masters champion with an enticing opportunity to land first PGA Tour victory since February 2020.

"It's a good spot," Scott said.

"Within striking distance. It's so congested, though. It's going to need a really great round, I think. There's someone lurking who's going to have that."

Min Woo Lee, Australia's only other player in the elite 30-man field for the $US40 million showpiece, remains an outside hope of becoming the first Tour Championship debutant to win since Xander Schauffele in 2017.

Lee is equal ninth after carding a third-round 66, but will need to reel in a raft of superstars.

At 12 under, world No.1 Scottie Scheffler (66) shares third spot with fellow American Chris Gotterup (67), Scott and Swede Ludvig Aberg (65).

Rory McIlroy was the biggest mover of the day, a round of 63 vaulting the world No.2 from 23rd to joint seventh with Cameron Young (68) at 10 under.

Then it's Lee and American trio Russell Henley (66), Jacob Bridgeman (66) and Sam Burns (67) all at nine under.

The 46-year-old Scott is relishing his crack at another big title.

"I can kind of stick with my game plan of being fairly conservative at least for the front nine," Scott said.

"And if I can execute that, then maybe I've got to start flag hunting a little bit and being a bit more aggressive than I have been.

"But I'll try to play that by ear when I'm out there. It's fun to be in the mix for the Tour Championship and the FedExCup."

World.title: Socceroo Volpato scores long-range goal in Serie A win
World.content:
A long-range strike from Socceroo Cristian Volpato has helped his Italian side Sassuolo claim a 2-1 win over Torino in its Serie A clash.

With the match scoreless through the opening half hour, Sassuolo counterattacked from its own half in the 32nd minute.

The ball came to Socceroo Volpato, who ripped a shot from well outside the penalty box.

The low strike curled and beat Torino goalkeeper Diego Mascardi to break the deadlock.

Torino levelled the score at the end of the first half, but Domenico Berardi's 78th-minute winner secured Sassuolo its first win of this league campaign.

Elsewhere, fellow Socceroo Mohamed Toure scored a double in Norwich City's 4-1 win over Burnley in the English Championship.

He has now scored 11 goals from 14 Championship matches since making his first appearance in the league in February.

Twenty-year-old Socceroo Paul Okon-Engstler made his debut in Germany's top flight for club Köln.

Okon-Engstler played 65 minutes as Köln defeated Hoffenheim 3-2 in the opening round of the Bundesliga season.

World.title: In Nepal, once-busy towns are turned to wastelands of mud
World.content:
The flood arrived in Dhunge with a roar of a jet engine. There must have been some warnings, but no one imagined it would be like this.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It wasn’t a mere flood that dumped these metres of mud and carved new riverbanks through homes and shops; that swept away a pair of bridges on a sunny morning, and the people standing on them. It was a beast, arriving with the roar of a jet engine on a runway, says KP Bharaisain, a 68-year-old resident of Dhunge, a small town in Nepal’s devastated Nuwakot district. He ran up the nearest hill, watching helplessly. “It was a giant wave of water, bouncing up and down like a football,” he says. A crowd gathers as heavy machinery begins to clear debris from the ruins of Dhunge. Kate Geraghty The river kept rising for about 15 minutes after the initial surge, before quickly receding. Within half an hour, he says, the new wasteland of Dhunge was revealed. “I never expected something this big to happen,” he says, gesticulating to the main street and the rushing Trishuli River, which, at about 9.30am on Wednesday morning, were one and same. Nepalese soldiers give directions to local residents, thousands of whom have been left homeless. Kate Geraghty



A glacial lake, about 50 kilometres north, had collapsed not an hour earlier, unleashing a rapid surge of water that has left thousands dead or missing along the river system, 41 Australians among them. It has been days since the disaster, and while it may be cool at altitudes, the valleys bake. Rescue teams pick through the wreckage of a building in Dhunge. KATE GERAGHTY Residents of Dhunge wait to be evacuated by helicopter. KATE GERAGHTY Dhunge, busy with passing Hindu pilgrims this time of year, is now the last town before the roads become impassable. Every aid agency is here, even the Scientologists. Police blow piercing whistles at people moving too close or seeking scant shade in areas that may be unstable. Nepalese soldiers assist an elderly woman. Kate Geraghty



Everywhere is mud, and though it has the appearance of being compact, it is quicksand capable of swallowing a person two times over in some parts. Straying and sinking onlookers need help back to solid ground. What must be greeting the choppered-in crews upstream, where people had no warning or time to react? Australian tourists like Sreedharan Iyer and his family, who had just checked out of their hotel near the source of the floods at 8.45am and were making their way to sacred Mount Kalaish – what must they have seen? No one has been found alive in Dhunge since the first emergency crews arrived. KATE GERAGHTY No human in Dhunge has been pulled from the debris alive since rescue workers have been on the scene. Some joy on Saturday morning, though, when they helped retrieve a dog from the ruins in which it had been hiding. “Last night we were close to getting it, but it was trying to bite us,” says one. A displaced family waits for evacuation. KATE GERAGHTY And neither have they recovered bodies. Any remains have been washed downstream, buried in mud or wedged under broken concrete walls. Police say they can see body parts on the sparsely populated opposite bank, but it’s impossible to cross the river now because the bridges are gone.



Residents say people were standing on them when the surge arrived, trying to get a neat photo. Though there had been some warnings from upstream, no one imagined it was going to be like this. The once-busy town has been reduced to a muddy wasteland by the flood. KATE GERAGHTY A nearby army camp has been set up as a staging ground for helicopters delivering survivors and the dead from upstream, attracting dozens of families desperate to see disembarking loved ones. People are trying to go the other way too. They want to look for their relatives and friends, or they have been cut off from their unaffected villages and need to get home. With roads destroyed, helicopter is the only way in and out. KATE GERAGHTY Even in the short breaks between coming and leaving helicopters, the scene at the camp’s gates is chaos, a clamour of whistles, pleas and megaphones. At Dhunge, there is talk that rescuers have located human remains in the ruins of the Agricultural Development Bank, which has blown-out doors and windows inclusive of the second floor. The building is only about 30 metres from stable ground.

World.title: Sydney Marathon results 2026: Gobena and Jepchirchir crowned champions as thousands race across Sydney
World.content:
Australia’s most decorated Olympian, Emma McKeon, has crossed the finish line.

McKeon, a six-time Olympic gold medallist and one of the best freestyle swimmers in Australian history, finished in a time of 4:41:30.

She knows what it takes to be the best, but today’s race was a little different to what she is accustomed to.

“Oh my god, it’s so different. I didn’t really know what to expect to be honest,” McKeon said after the race.

“Once we passed the 28km it was just unchartered territory for me. I’ve done 28km in my training, and it was just curiosity... Around the whole course, everyone is just cheering you on so much, and I feel like every time you run past a big group of loud cheerers, you just get goosebumps, and I think that’s what got me through.”

World.title: ‘Didn’t panic’: Kiss hails Wallabies’ character after nervy win over Argentina
World.content:
Updated SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby ‘Didn’t panic’: Kiss hails Wallabies’ character after nervy win over Argentina Iain Payten Updated August 30, 2026 — 11:28am ,first published August 30, 2026 — 7:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Les Kiss hailed his side’s calmness under pressure after the Wallabies continued their unbeaten run under the new coach with a 27-21 win over Argentina in San Salvador de Jujuy on Sunday morning (AEST). The downside was that most of that pressure was self-inflicted, with the Wallabies’ mistakes giving the Pumas plenty of opportunity to snatch victory in a tense final 20 minutes. Loading But based on gutsy defence and another dominant performance from the Australian forwards - who scored three of the Wallabies’ four tries and dominated Argentina in the set-pieces - Kiss’ men got home for another victory. It was a third straight win under Kiss since he took over at the start of August, and the fourth consecutive win by the Wallabies; a feat not achieved since Dave Rennie’s side won five in a row in 2021.



The Wallabies led 19-7 early in the game, but Argentina fought back to trail by just one point with 30 minutes remaining. But a 54th-minute try from back-rower Tom Hooper pushed the Wallabies back out to a six-point lead, one they held on to in a see-sawing final 25 minutes. It was again far from perfect, and the Wallabies were fortunate Argentina’s inexperience and ill-discipline scuttled many chances they had to steal a win in the second half. The Pumas, ranked No.7 in the world, were without many of their top stars. Tom Hooper of the Wallabies scores a try while being tackled by Ignacio Ruiz. Getty Images But it was still a victory in Argentina, which is regarded as one of the toughest places to win in the world, and at altitude as well. And just as they did in Osaka, the win came down to plenty of character shown in defence in the dying stages. “Certainly happy with the win, for sure,” Kiss said.



“To get the wins in a row that we’ve had lately, four now, it’s a real plus for us. That’s a positive. So happy with that. Happy with certain elements of our game. However, we did put ourselves under pressure and offered too many opportunities with some options that just gave them field position and gave them the ball freely. Brandon Paenga-Amosa of the Wallabies celebrates after scoring a try. Getty Images “We’re not going to lose the run of ourselves, but we’ll also accept that it’s Test rugby, and to get a win is very important.” There was concern the win may have come at a high cost, with in-form halfback Ryan Lonergan leaving the field after taking a head knock during a try-saving cover tackle in the second half. But he passed an HIA and is expected to be fit for the second Test in Mendoza next weekend. Kiss said the character shown by the Wallabies’ players - in several different combinations - during his first month with the side has been noteworthy.



“Really buying into what it takes when we haven’t got the ball to dig in and find a way to make sure we can repel the opposition,” he said. “We weren’t perfect for sure, but we really fight hard for each other and fight hard for staying in the game under the best terms that we can. They (Argentina) are a dangerous side. Carter Gordon of the Wallabies is challenged by Ignacio Mendy and Santiago Carreras. Getty Images “Talking to Al (Alaalatoa) and Fraser afterwards, who took over captaincy after Al left, there was a certain strong calmness on the pitch. We didn’t let the pressure get on top of us and weigh us down. “Fraser talked about how the team didn’t panic at all. They stayed calm and connected to the things that we believe can contribute to staying together and connected.”



The Wallabies led 22-14 at halftime after an opening 40 minutes where they had the majority of possession and territory. Superb handling by Wallabies locks Josh Canham and Jeremy Williams laid on a first try for hooker Brandon Paenga-Amosa in the sixth minute, and a second try followed for Carter Gordon in the 10th minute from close range. Isaac Henry of the Wallabies is challenged by Simon Benitez Cruz. Getty Images The Wallabies defence was wobblier, however, and Argentina sliced through the middle near the ruck for their first try to Gerónimo Priscinatell. But a McReight pick-and-drive gave Australia a third try inside the opening 19th minutes. The Wallabies survived a yellow card to Harry Potter without conceding, but then gave up a try to Joaquin Moro a minute after he returned. A Lonergan penalty after the halftime siren pushed the lead back out, but the Pumas scored in the 51st minute, bringing it back to a one-point ballgame.



Up against a strong Pumas defence, the Wallabies sought to use passing skill to find gaps, with mixed results. But some slick passes helped put Hunter Paisami through a gap, and it ended with Hooper scoring with 26 minutes left on the clock. That proved to be the match-winner. Related Article Opinion

Wallabies Strong forwards and liberated backs. The Wallabies have received a ‘Kiss of Life’ Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author Kiss said there was a balance to be found in over-playing in the last quarter and not going into shells. “It was just the execution that let us down at times as well. The boys have their hands up for that,” he said. “A few things to work on for sure. “This won’t be an easy game than the next one. History tells any team that comes to Argentina.”



The Wallabies have won the first game of their last three trips to Argentina, in 2022 and 2024. But on those two tours, the Wallabies then got flogged in the second game. Kiss has kept calvalry in reserve, however, with captain Harry Wilson, Taniela Tupou, Len Ikitau, Carlo Tizzano and Lukhan Salakaia-Loto all unused in the Jujuy win. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii also turned in a strong performance from the bench in the last 15 minutes.

World.title: Tom Cruise announces sequel to once-mocked, now-loved Days of Thunder
World.content:
CultureMoviesCinema Tom Cruise announces sequel to once-mocked, now-loved Days of Thunder Mark Long August 30, 2026 — 11:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Tom Cruise has revealed that he will star in a sequel to Days of Thunder 38 years after the debut of his motor-racing movie in 1990. The sequel, due to hit cinemas in 2028, will also star Anne Hathaway as a team owner and engineer in the world of NASCAR (the National Association for Stock Car Auto Racing). Tom Cruise attends the drivers meeting before a race at Daytona last week. Chris Graythen/Getty Images The 64-year-old Cruise announced the project at Daytona International Speedway in Florida on Saturday, making a characteristically flamboyant entry in front of 40 race-car drivers, jumping over a row of potted plants and directly onto a stage. Cruise will reprise the role of NASCAR driver Cole Trickle, loosely based on the late NASCAR driver Tim Richmond, in the new film, which will be written by Will Staples and directed by Jonathan Levine, with Cruise producing alongside Jerry Bruckheimer and Tommy Harper.



“It’s not just about racing,” Cruise told a packed room that included NASCAR executives, fans, corporate sponsors and military personnel. “It’s about the community and the people here. There’s something very special about racers and the whole community. It’s a culture, and I was very proud to be able to reflect that in the first Days of Thunder, and I am honoured to share it with the world. “That’s basically what we’re going to really go for with this one. Give the audience that opportunity to understand what it is as a team, as a community, what it is for NASCAR, and the speed, the excitement and all that danger and stuff.” Cruise as driver Cole Trickle in the 1990 film. Stephen Vaughan The Hollywood Reporter reported in November 2024 that Cruise had talked to Paramount about a follow-up to his racing film, which was critically panned on its release and largely lampooned throughout the NASCAR industry for its exaggeration and overindulgence.



But it has since become a cult favourite in NASCAR circles, and is still quoted by race fans to this day. Related Article Cinema Nicole Kidman was warned marrying Tom Cruise would hurt her career but ‘didn’t care’ “Rubbin’, son, is racin’” – the immortal line from crew chief Harry Hogge, played by Robert Duvall – still lives on. Riding high from his Top Gun fame and having grown up racing cars on the “back streets of Kentucky”, Cruise had an idea for a movie based on fast cars and the characters who raced them. And so began the making of Days of Thunder. The movie introduced NASCAR to a wider audience that had very limited exposure to stock-car racing before that summer. There had been racing movies before – Thunder Road, Grand Prix, Stroker Ace or even Smokey and the Bandit – but none that had depicted NASCAR in such a mainstream style.



It’s likely that Cruise will handle many of his own stunts, as he did in the original. “Last time I was at this track, actually, I was on the back straight, and I was shooting with two very heavy cameras travelling – I don’t know, 180 miles an hour – and suddenly the hood was off of the car,” Cruise recalled on Saturday. “The sun is setting and I’m trying to get all my lines out before we lost the light. And, suddenly, the whole car was in flames. It turned from a barbecue to a bonfire on the back straight. Couldn’t even get the crew to come in and help me just because radio (communications) didn’t work in the back straight. “I hear that’s still possible, correct,” he asked the rapt audience. “You guys didn’t fix that. Well, that’s good.” AP

World.title: WA’s Planning Commission boss talks housing, density – and pushback
World.content:
NationalWAPlanning and development WA’s Planning Commission boss talks housing, density – and pushback Indigo Lemay-Conway August 30, 2026 — 11:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It was never Emma Cole’s plan to become the head of WA’s Planning Commission, but she wouldn’t have it any other way. “I really liked geography, and perhaps that should have been a bit of a clue,” Cole tells this masthead as part of a series of sit-downs with the decision-makers guiding WA’s future. WA Planning Commission chairperson Emma Cole. WA Planning Commission Cole credits her time in local government for her success over the past 2½ years at the helm of the government board that has statewide responsibility for integrated urban and regional land use planning and development. “What really got me interested in planning was joining local government because I’d been a public servant, I just had young children, I was working part-time, I was feeling like I needed something new,” she said.



“There was a development on my laneway, and it was really interesting that all of my neighbours hadn’t been consulted, even though we were really close to it. “It was an apartment building, and it was quite a new departure for our suburb. I didn’t have a problem with that, but I thought, ‘This is really odd that we haven’t been consulted’. “So, that got me quite interested in local government, and somehow, I found myself in that space, and I thought, ‘Oh, maybe I’ll have a go’ and ended up running for council and being elected to the City of Vincent.” Cole remained on the council for a decade, and for 6½ years stood at the forefront of the local government as mayor before stepping down in 2023. “I had the opportunity to apply to the WAPC while I was the mayor of the City of Vincent, and the passion for planning just grew and grew,” she said.



“I ended up finding myself back at uni as a mature-age student, I did a Masters of Urban and Regional Planning, which I absolutely loved.” From local mayor to state authority Cole joined the WAPC in 2020 as the metropolitan representative for local government before being reappointed as former chairperson David Caddy’s deputy. “Then six months later he announced pretty quickly he was retiring, which was a bit of a shock, and then I was appointed to the role in January 2024 as chairperson.” While many people think of the WA Planning Commission as the people who approve development applications, Cole says it goes far deeper than that.



Related Article Waste Trash to power: Councils to send rubbish to Kwinana as leachate takes over Tamala Park “I think some of the things that people think about when they think ‘What does a planning commission do?’ They think of us approving development applications. But that’s at the pointy end and almost like the last stage of planning,” she said. “A lot of people don’t quite understand that there’s the WA Planning Commission and then there’s the Department of Planning, Lands and Heritage.” Cole describes the Planning Commission as a board of nine members and a number of committees who make the strategic decisions and provide the guidance and advice on land use. “We provide advice to the minister, we review local government planning instruments, and we have statutory decision-making, and that’s often through our statutory planning committee where we’re making decisions on structure plans and subdivision and development applications,” she said.



“Then the department is like the arms and legs of the operation because we don’t actually employ staff. We’re a statutory authority, and the department undertakes the work on behalf of the commission.” “We are very conscious that planning is all about people. It’s all about communities.” Emma Cole Building for the future The WAPC often faces criticism for approving developments local residents aren’t often in favor of, but Cole says public opinion does have a sway in the final decision. “We run transparent meetings where people can come in and provide deputations. We read all of the submissions, and we’re very much about opening up the meetings and including the community so that they can have their view,” she said.



“That is one informing factor, but we also have to take into consideration all of these other competing elements that we’re forming a balanced view on.” Related Article Property development WA is set for 100,000 new homes in the next three years. Where will they be built? “We have to think about that person and their sense of their local community and its character, and we’re really mindful of things like character and heritage and not wanting to have homogenous development everywhere. “But we’re also thinking about the kids and the grandkids of the future? Where are they going to live? Where are they going to work and how do we cater for this growing population?” One thing Cole says WA does well, as far as planning goes, is being responsive to changes in context.



“If I think about some of the reforms that have been underway, like even since COVID, and we introduced a significant development pathway, we’ve been very flexible in terms of the way we’ve approached the way the planning system works,” she said. “I think that our responsiveness to change, our ability to look to the future and not just plan for today, but actually forecast where we’re heading into the future [is what we do well].” She says WA is also doing a lot of work to create more transit-oriented developments, but would like to see more developers seize the opportunity to build in the near future. “It’s been written into our Perth and Peel framework since 2018 and even before that in previous iterations of our metropolitan blueprint,” she said. “Of course, we have some complexities facing us in terms of construction. We understand that getting apartments built at the moment is tricky in terms of who’s available in terms of tier-one builders.”



Ultimately, her message to people is that the WAPC is focused on the quality of life and the next iteration of where the state is headed. “We are very conscious that planning is all about people. It’s all about communities,” she said. “We are not a dispassionate entity. “We really care about that, and we actually want to deliver really good outcomes for our community.”

World.title: The little coastal corner of Perth sending shivers through Australian politics
World.content:
One Nation is no longer just a headache for the conservative side of Australian politics – it poses a clear and present danger to Labor too. That is the message sent loud and clear at the Secret Harbour byelection on Saturday night from the sleepy little coastal electorate in the mortgage belt about 50 kilometres south of Perth’s CBD. One Nation candidate Luke Herdegen with Premier Roger Cook and Labor’s Georgia Tree. Colin Murty By 10.30pm, the populist right-wing party candidate, gym owner Luke Herdegen, had sealed his victory as the first-ever lower house One Nation MP in WA parliament with a primary vote swing of 30 per cent, carved from both Labor and the Liberals. It was a stunning loss for Labor, which has firmly held various iterations of the seat since the 1980s, and confirms suspicions that One Nation has made inroads into outer suburban Australia and can draw votes away from Labor heartlands.



With a caveat that byelections often draw votes away from incumbent governments when the stakes around who will actually govern the state aren’t as high, this result has serious lessons for the state and federal MPs whose electorates straddle Perth’s urban fringes. Related Article WA election One Nation claims victory in Secret Harbour as last-minute votes seal Labor’s fate One Nation had a primary vote of 8 per cent in Secret Harbour at the 2025 state election. Any other state MP who saw the same kind of result should be sweating – Armadale, Darling Range and Thornlie are some notable examples. Federally, the results are an even more pressing lesson. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and federal political issues loomed during the campaign, despite Albanese’s absence from the battleground.



Most fuel stations yesterday in Secret Harbour were selling ULP 91 for more than $2 per litre. Coupled with big mortgages and high grocery prices, it bubbled to the surface during the campaign as discontent with the Albanese government. This was not a byelection fought on a policy battlefield. One Nation didn’t have any, which Herdegen and party leader Rod Caddies often reminded journalists. West Australian One Nation Leader Rod Caddies and Secret Harbour candidate Luke Herdegen claim victory. Michael Philipps Their argument boiled down to, “We don’t need policies yet, it’s not a state election”. The pitch was: “If you’re fed up, vote for me.” “Have you ever tried to sleep with a mosquito in your room?” Caddies told this masthead, noting that Herdegen’s main job was to be a thorn in Labor’s side.



On the booths, former state Liberal candidates were now donning the orange, as well as candidates from other fringe parties like Legalise Cannabis who saw One Nation as their great hope of upending the current political status quo. Related Article Exclusive

Political leadership ‘Treading water’: Albanese pivots to positivity to counter Hanson gloom One Nation volunteer and Secret Harbour voter Trevor Hale said he’d voted mostly Liberal, but in the past few elections he had switched to Hanson’s party because of federal Labor’s performance. “We only joined the party formally just recently, but we’ve been following Pauline for some time, and we voted One Nation at the last two or three elections, federal and state,” he told this masthead. “I’ve had enough of Labor. I’ve only voted twice for Labor in my whole life. Normally Liberal, but Liberals no longer are a threat to anybody, and Labor is just destroying the country, both state and federal.



“To me, this is more a vote against Albanese than it is against Roger [Cook].” WA Premier Roger Cook and Labor’s candidate for Secret Harbour Georgia Tree. Hamish Hastie Migration remained a constant bugbear of voters who saw the current rates as contributing to the housing crisis in the state. Federally, urban fringe MPs, particularly Liberal Canning MP Andrew Hastie, and Labor’s Madeleine King and Matt Keogh, will be looking at the results closely. It may even move Labor’s migration changes up the priority list a few spots.



Labor’s dissection of its campaign will reveal plenty of missteps. Related Article WA election Prime minister dodges WA byelection dominated by One Nation It got off to a shocker by selecting candidate Georgia Tree, who may have grown up in the area but now lived in a $1.4 million house 61 kilometres away in inner-city Perth. Byelections are hyper-local by nature, and that fact was hammered home during the campaign. Some awkward moments during press conferences, where Tree was hurried away before answering questions, made for great social media fodder by the Liberals and One Nation.



The Liberals unearthed a potential future star of its party in Ryan Robertson, but the results show the party’s existential crisis is still raging, and they have no idea how to grapple with One Nation. With a federal election potentially 18 months away and the next state election in 2029, both major parties have some homework to do. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It wasn’t a mere flood that dumped these metres of mud and carved new riverbanks through homes and shops; that swept away a pair of bridges on a sunny morning, and the people standing on them. It was a beast, arriving with the roar of a jet engine on a runway, says KP Bharaisain, a 68-year-old resident of Dhunge, a small town in Nepal’s devastated Nuwakot district. He ran up the nearest hill, watching helplessly. “It was a giant wave of water, bouncing up and down like a football,” he says. A crowd gathers as heavy machinery begins to clear debris from the ruins of Dhunge. Kate Geraghty The river kept rising for about 15 minutes after the initial surge, before quickly receding. Within half an hour, he says, the new wasteland of Dhunge was revealed. “I never expected something this big to happen,” he says, gesticulating to the main street and the rushing Trishuli River, which, at about 9.30am on Wednesday morning, were one and same. Nepalese soldiers give directions to local residents, thousands of whom have been left homeless. Kate Geraghty



A glacial lake, about 50 kilometres north, had collapsed not an hour earlier, unleashing a rapid surge of water that has left thousands dead or missing along the river system, 41 Australians among them. It has been days since the disaster, and while it may be cool at altitudes, the valleys bake. Rescue teams pick through the wreckage of a building in Dhunge. KATE GERAGHTY Residents of Dhunge wait to be evacuated by helicopter. KATE GERAGHTY Dhunge, busy with passing Hindu pilgrims this time of year, is now the last town before the roads become impassable. Every aid agency is here, even the Scientologists. Police blow piercing whistles at people moving too close or seeking scant shade in areas that may be unstable. Nepalese soldiers assist an elderly woman. Kate Geraghty



Everywhere is mud, and though it has the appearance of being compact, it is quicksand capable of swallowing a person two times over in some parts. Straying and sinking onlookers need help back to solid ground. What must be greeting the choppered-in crews upstream, where people had no warning or time to react? Australian tourists like Sreedharan Iyer and his family, who had just checked out of their hotel near the source of the floods at 8.45am and were making their way to sacred Mount Kalaish – what must they have seen? No one has been found alive in Dhunge since the first emergency crews arrived. KATE GERAGHTY No human in Dhunge has been pulled from the debris alive since rescue workers have been on the scene. Some joy on Saturday morning, though, when they helped retrieve a dog from the ruins in which it had been hiding. “Last night we were close to getting it, but it was trying to bite us,” says one. A displaced family waits for evacuation. KATE GERAGHTY And neither have they recovered bodies. Any remains have been washed downstream, buried in mud or wedged under broken concrete walls. Police say they can see body parts on the sparsely populated opposite bank, but it’s impossible to cross the river now because the bridges are gone.



Residents say people were standing on them when the surge arrived, trying to get a neat photo. Though there had been some warnings from upstream, no one imagined it was going to be like this. The once-busy town has been reduced to a muddy wasteland by the flood. KATE GERAGHTY A nearby army camp has been set up as a staging ground for helicopters delivering survivors and the dead from upstream, attracting dozens of families desperate to see disembarking loved ones. People are trying to go the other way too. They want to look for their relatives and friends, or they have been cut off from their unaffected villages and need to get home. With roads destroyed, helicopter is the only way in and out. KATE GERAGHTY Even in the short breaks between coming and leaving helicopters, the scene at the camp’s gates is chaos, a clamour of whistles, pleas and megaphones. At Dhunge, there is talk that rescuers have located human remains in the ruins of the Agricultural Development Bank, which has blown-out doors and windows inclusive of the second floor. The building is only about 30 metres from stable ground.

World.title: ‘Didn’t panic’: Kiss hails Wallabies’ character after nervy win over Argentina
World.content:
Updated SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby ‘Didn’t panic’: Kiss hails Wallabies’ character after nervy win over Argentina Iain Payten Updated August 30, 2026 — 11:28am ,first published August 30, 2026 — 7:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Les Kiss hailed his side’s calmness under pressure after the Wallabies continued their unbeaten run under the new coach with a 27-21 win over Argentina in San Salvador de Jujuy on Sunday morning (AEST). The downside was that most of that pressure was self-inflicted, with the Wallabies’ mistakes giving the Pumas plenty of opportunity to snatch victory in a tense final 20 minutes. Loading But based on gutsy defence and another dominant performance from the Australian forwards - who scored three of the Wallabies’ four tries and dominated Argentina in the set-pieces - Kiss’ men got home for another victory. It was a third straight win under Kiss since he took over at the start of August, and the fourth consecutive win by the Wallabies; a feat not achieved since Dave Rennie’s side won five in a row in 2021.



The Wallabies led 19-7 early in the game, but Argentina fought back to trail by just one point with 30 minutes remaining. But a 54th-minute try from back-rower Tom Hooper pushed the Wallabies back out to a six-point lead, one they held on to in a see-sawing final 25 minutes. It was again far from perfect, and the Wallabies were fortunate Argentina’s inexperience and ill-discipline scuttled many chances they had to steal a win in the second half. The Pumas, ranked No.7 in the world, were without many of their top stars. Tom Hooper of the Wallabies scores a try while being tackled by Ignacio Ruiz. Getty Images But it was still a victory in Argentina, which is regarded as one of the toughest places to win in the world, and at altitude as well. And just as they did in Osaka, the win came down to plenty of character shown in defence in the dying stages. “Certainly happy with the win, for sure,” Kiss said.



“To get the wins in a row that we’ve had lately, four now, it’s a real plus for us. That’s a positive. So happy with that. Happy with certain elements of our game. However, we did put ourselves under pressure and offered too many opportunities with some options that just gave them field position and gave them the ball freely. Brandon Paenga-Amosa of the Wallabies celebrates after scoring a try. Getty Images “We’re not going to lose the run of ourselves, but we’ll also accept that it’s Test rugby, and to get a win is very important.” There was concern the win may have come at a high cost, with in-form halfback Ryan Lonergan leaving the field after taking a head knock during a try-saving cover tackle in the second half. But he passed an HIA and is expected to be fit for the second Test in Mendoza next weekend. Kiss said the character shown by the Wallabies’ players - in several different combinations - during his first month with the side has been noteworthy.



“Really buying into what it takes when we haven’t got the ball to dig in and find a way to make sure we can repel the opposition,” he said. “We weren’t perfect for sure, but we really fight hard for each other and fight hard for staying in the game under the best terms that we can. They (Argentina) are a dangerous side. Carter Gordon of the Wallabies is challenged by Ignacio Mendy and Santiago Carreras. Getty Images “Talking to Al (Alaalatoa) and Fraser afterwards, who took over captaincy after Al left, there was a certain strong calmness on the pitch. We didn’t let the pressure get on top of us and weigh us down. “Fraser talked about how the team didn’t panic at all. They stayed calm and connected to the things that we believe can contribute to staying together and connected.”



The Wallabies led 22-14 at halftime after an opening 40 minutes where they had the majority of possession and territory. Superb handling by Wallabies locks Josh Canham and Jeremy Williams laid on a first try for hooker Brandon Paenga-Amosa in the sixth minute, and a second try followed for Carter Gordon in the 10th minute from close range. Isaac Henry of the Wallabies is challenged by Simon Benitez Cruz. Getty Images The Wallabies defence was wobblier, however, and Argentina sliced through the middle near the ruck for their first try to Gerónimo Priscinatell. But a McReight pick-and-drive gave Australia a third try inside the opening 19th minutes. The Wallabies survived a yellow card to Harry Potter without conceding, but then gave up a try to Joaquin Moro a minute after he returned. A Lonergan penalty after the halftime siren pushed the lead back out, but the Pumas scored in the 51st minute, bringing it back to a one-point ballgame.



Up against a strong Pumas defence, the Wallabies sought to use passing skill to find gaps, with mixed results. But some slick passes helped put Hunter Paisami through a gap, and it ended with Hooper scoring with 26 minutes left on the clock. That proved to be the match-winner. Related Article Opinion

Wallabies Strong forwards and liberated backs. The Wallabies have received a ‘Kiss of Life’ Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author Kiss said there was a balance to be found in over-playing in the last quarter and not going into shells. “It was just the execution that let us down at times as well. The boys have their hands up for that,” he said. “A few things to work on for sure. “This won’t be an easy game than the next one. History tells any team that comes to Argentina.”



The Wallabies have won the first game of their last three trips to Argentina, in 2022 and 2024. But on those two tours, the Wallabies then got flogged in the second game. Kiss has kept calvalry in reserve, however, with captain Harry Wilson, Taniela Tupou, Len Ikitau, Carlo Tizzano and Lukhan Salakaia-Loto all unused in the Jujuy win. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii also turned in a strong performance from the bench in the last 15 minutes.

World.title: Tom Cruise announces sequel to once-mocked, now-loved Days of Thunder
World.content:
CultureMoviesCinema Tom Cruise announces sequel to once-mocked, now-loved Days of Thunder Mark Long August 30, 2026 — 11:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Tom Cruise has revealed that he will star in a sequel to Days of Thunder 38 years after the debut of his motor-racing movie in 1990. The sequel, due to hit cinemas in 2028, will also star Anne Hathaway as a team owner and engineer in the world of NASCAR (the National Association for Stock Car Auto Racing). Tom Cruise attends the drivers meeting before a race at Daytona last week. Chris Graythen/Getty Images The 64-year-old Cruise announced the project at Daytona International Speedway in Florida on Saturday, making a characteristically flamboyant entry in front of 40 race-car drivers, jumping over a row of potted plants and directly onto a stage. Cruise will reprise the role of NASCAR driver Cole Trickle, loosely based on the late NASCAR driver Tim Richmond, in the new film, which will be written by Will Staples and directed by Jonathan Levine, with Cruise producing alongside Jerry Bruckheimer and Tommy Harper.



“It’s not just about racing,” Cruise told a packed room that included NASCAR executives, fans, corporate sponsors and military personnel. “It’s about the community and the people here. There’s something very special about racers and the whole community. It’s a culture, and I was very proud to be able to reflect that in the first Days of Thunder, and I am honoured to share it with the world. “That’s basically what we’re going to really go for with this one. Give the audience that opportunity to understand what it is as a team, as a community, what it is for NASCAR, and the speed, the excitement and all that danger and stuff.” Cruise as driver Cole Trickle in the 1990 film. Stephen Vaughan The Hollywood Reporter reported in November 2024 that Cruise had talked to Paramount about a follow-up to his racing film, which was critically panned on its release and largely lampooned throughout the NASCAR industry for its exaggeration and overindulgence.



But it has since become a cult favourite in NASCAR circles, and is still quoted by race fans to this day. Related Article Cinema Nicole Kidman was warned marrying Tom Cruise would hurt her career but ‘didn’t care’ “Rubbin’, son, is racin’” – the immortal line from crew chief Harry Hogge, played by Robert Duvall – still lives on. Riding high from his Top Gun fame and having grown up racing cars on the “back streets of Kentucky”, Cruise had an idea for a movie based on fast cars and the characters who raced them. And so began the making of Days of Thunder. The movie introduced NASCAR to a wider audience that had very limited exposure to stock-car racing before that summer. There had been racing movies before – Thunder Road, Grand Prix, Stroker Ace or even Smokey and the Bandit – but none that had depicted NASCAR in such a mainstream style.



It’s likely that Cruise will handle many of his own stunts, as he did in the original. “Last time I was at this track, actually, I was on the back straight, and I was shooting with two very heavy cameras travelling – I don’t know, 180 miles an hour – and suddenly the hood was off of the car,” Cruise recalled on Saturday. “The sun is setting and I’m trying to get all my lines out before we lost the light. And, suddenly, the whole car was in flames. It turned from a barbecue to a bonfire on the back straight. Couldn’t even get the crew to come in and help me just because radio (communications) didn’t work in the back straight. “I hear that’s still possible, correct,” he asked the rapt audience. “You guys didn’t fix that. Well, that’s good.” AP

World.title: WA’s Planning Commission boss talks housing, density – and pushback
World.content:
NationalWAPlanning and development WA’s Planning Commission boss talks housing, density – and pushback Indigo Lemay-Conway August 30, 2026 — 11:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It was never Emma Cole’s plan to become the head of WA’s Planning Commission, but she wouldn’t have it any other way. “I really liked geography, and perhaps that should have been a bit of a clue,” Cole tells this masthead as part of a series of sit-downs with the decision-makers guiding WA’s future. WA Planning Commission chairperson Emma Cole. WA Planning Commission Cole credits her time in local government for her success over the past 2½ years at the helm of the government board that has statewide responsibility for integrated urban and regional land use planning and development. “What really got me interested in planning was joining local government because I’d been a public servant, I just had young children, I was working part-time, I was feeling like I needed something new,” she said.



“There was a development on my laneway, and it was really interesting that all of my neighbours hadn’t been consulted, even though we were really close to it. “It was an apartment building, and it was quite a new departure for our suburb. I didn’t have a problem with that, but I thought, ‘This is really odd that we haven’t been consulted’. “So, that got me quite interested in local government, and somehow, I found myself in that space, and I thought, ‘Oh, maybe I’ll have a go’ and ended up running for council and being elected to the City of Vincent.” Cole remained on the council for a decade, and for 6½ years stood at the forefront of the local government as mayor before stepping down in 2023. “I had the opportunity to apply to the WAPC while I was the mayor of the City of Vincent, and the passion for planning just grew and grew,” she said.



“I ended up finding myself back at uni as a mature-age student, I did a Masters of Urban and Regional Planning, which I absolutely loved.” From local mayor to state authority Cole joined the WAPC in 2020 as the metropolitan representative for local government before being reappointed as former chairperson David Caddy’s deputy. “Then six months later he announced pretty quickly he was retiring, which was a bit of a shock, and then I was appointed to the role in January 2024 as chairperson.” While many people think of the WA Planning Commission as the people who approve development applications, Cole says it goes far deeper than that.



Related Article Waste Trash to power: Councils to send rubbish to Kwinana as leachate takes over Tamala Park “I think some of the things that people think about when they think ‘What does a planning commission do?’ They think of us approving development applications. But that’s at the pointy end and almost like the last stage of planning,” she said. “A lot of people don’t quite understand that there’s the WA Planning Commission and then there’s the Department of Planning, Lands and Heritage.” Cole describes the Planning Commission as a board of nine members and a number of committees who make the strategic decisions and provide the guidance and advice on land use. “We provide advice to the minister, we review local government planning instruments, and we have statutory decision-making, and that’s often through our statutory planning committee where we’re making decisions on structure plans and subdivision and development applications,” she said.



“Then the department is like the arms and legs of the operation because we don’t actually employ staff. We’re a statutory authority, and the department undertakes the work on behalf of the commission.” “We are very conscious that planning is all about people. It’s all about communities.” Emma Cole Building for the future The WAPC often faces criticism for approving developments local residents aren’t often in favor of, but Cole says public opinion does have a sway in the final decision. “We run transparent meetings where people can come in and provide deputations. We read all of the submissions, and we’re very much about opening up the meetings and including the community so that they can have their view,” she said.



“That is one informing factor, but we also have to take into consideration all of these other competing elements that we’re forming a balanced view on.” Related Article Property development WA is set for 100,000 new homes in the next three years. Where will they be built? “We have to think about that person and their sense of their local community and its character, and we’re really mindful of things like character and heritage and not wanting to have homogenous development everywhere. “But we’re also thinking about the kids and the grandkids of the future? Where are they going to live? Where are they going to work and how do we cater for this growing population?” One thing Cole says WA does well, as far as planning goes, is being responsive to changes in context.



“If I think about some of the reforms that have been underway, like even since COVID, and we introduced a significant development pathway, we’ve been very flexible in terms of the way we’ve approached the way the planning system works,” she said. “I think that our responsiveness to change, our ability to look to the future and not just plan for today, but actually forecast where we’re heading into the future [is what we do well].” She says WA is also doing a lot of work to create more transit-oriented developments, but would like to see more developers seize the opportunity to build in the near future. “It’s been written into our Perth and Peel framework since 2018 and even before that in previous iterations of our metropolitan blueprint,” she said. “Of course, we have some complexities facing us in terms of construction. We understand that getting apartments built at the moment is tricky in terms of who’s available in terms of tier-one builders.”



Ultimately, her message to people is that the WAPC is focused on the quality of life and the next iteration of where the state is headed. “We are very conscious that planning is all about people. It’s all about communities,” she said. “We are not a dispassionate entity. “We really care about that, and we actually want to deliver really good outcomes for our community.”
