World.title: The little coastal corner of Perth sending shivers through Australian politics
World.content:
One Nation is no longer just a headache for the conservative side of Australian politics – it poses a clear and present danger to Labor too. That is the message sent loud and clear at the Secret Harbour byelection on Saturday night from the sleepy little coastal electorate in the mortgage belt about 50 kilometres south of Perth’s CBD. One Nation candidate Luke Herdegen with Premier Roger Cook and Labor’s Georgia Tree. Colin Murty By 10.30pm, the populist right-wing party candidate, gym owner Luke Herdegen, had sealed his victory as the first-ever lower house One Nation MP in WA parliament with a primary vote swing of 30 per cent, carved from both Labor and the Liberals. It was a stunning loss for Labor, which has firmly held various iterations of the seat since the 1980s, and confirms suspicions that One Nation has made inroads into outer suburban Australia and can draw votes away from Labor heartlands.



With a caveat that byelections often draw votes away from incumbent governments when the stakes around who will actually govern the state aren’t as high, this result has serious lessons for the state and federal MPs whose electorates straddle Perth’s urban fringes. Related Article Updated

WA election One Nation claims victory in Secret Harbour as last-minute votes seal Labor’s fate One Nation had a primary vote of 8 per cent in Secret Harbour at the 2025 state election. Any other state MP who saw the same kind of result should be sweating – Armadale, Darling Range and Thornlie are some notable examples. Federally, the results are an even more pressing lesson. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and federal political issues loomed during the campaign, despite Albanese’s absence from the battleground.



Most fuel stations yesterday in Secret Harbour were selling ULP 91 for more than $2 per litre. Coupled with big mortgages and high grocery prices, it bubbled to the surface during the campaign as discontent with the Albanese government. This was not a byelection fought on a policy battlefield. One Nation didn’t have any, which Herdegen and party leader Rod Caddies often reminded journalists. West Australian One Nation Leader Rod Caddies and Secret Harbour candidate Luke Herdegen claim victory. Michael Philipps Their argument boiled down to, “We don’t need policies yet, it’s not a state election”. The pitch was: “If you’re fed up, vote for me.” “Have you ever tried to sleep with a mosquito in your room?” Caddies told this masthead, noting that Herdegen’s main job was to be a thorn in Labor’s side.



On the booths, former state Liberal candidates were now donning the orange, as well as candidates from other fringe parties like Legalise Cannabis who saw One Nation as their great hope of upending the current political status quo. Related Article Exclusive

Political leadership ‘Treading water’: Albanese pivots to positivity to counter Hanson gloom One Nation volunteer and Secret Harbour voter Trevor Hale said he’d voted mostly Liberal, but in the past few elections he had switched to Hanson’s party because of federal Labor’s performance. “We only joined the party formally just recently, but we’ve been following Pauline for some time, and we voted One Nation at the last two or three elections, federal and state,” he told this masthead. “I’ve had enough of Labor. I’ve only voted twice for Labor in my whole life. Normally Liberal, but Liberals no longer are a threat to anybody, and Labor is just destroying the country, both state and federal.



“To me, this is more a vote against Albanese than it is against Roger [Cook].” WA Premier Roger Cook and Labor’s candidate for Secret Harbour Georgia Tree. Hamish Hastie Migration remained a constant bugbear of voters who saw the current rates as contributing to the housing crisis in the state. Federally, urban fringe MPs, particularly Liberal Canning MP Andrew Hastie, and Labor’s Madeleine King and Matt Keogh, will be looking at the results closely. It may even move Labor’s migration changes up the priority list a few spots.



Labor’s dissection of its campaign will reveal plenty of missteps. Related Article WA election Prime minister dodges WA byelection dominated by One Nation It got off to a shocker by selecting candidate Georgia Tree, who may have grown up in the area but now lived in a $1.4 million house 61 kilometres away in inner-city Perth. Byelections are hyper-local by nature, and that fact was hammered home during the campaign. Some awkward moments during press conferences, where Tree was hurried away before answering questions, made for great social media fodder by the Liberals and One Nation.



The Liberals unearthed a potential future star of its party in Ryan Robertson, but the results show the party’s existential crisis is still raging, and they have no idea how to grapple with One Nation. With a federal election potentially 18 months away and the next state election in 2029, both major parties have some homework to do. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: National vows to reduce student loan repayment rate if re-elected
World.content:
The National Party is promising to reduce the compulsory student loan repayment rate if re-elected, while cracking down on overseas-based borrowers.

It said it would reduce the repayment rate from 12 percent to 10 percent from April 2027.

The party's finance spokesperson Nicola Willis said compulsory student loan repayments were paid at 12 cents on every dollar earned above $24,128.

"It is often one of the biggest weekly expenses for a young graduate," she said.

''Reducing this to 10 cents means an accountant starting out in their career and earning $75,000 per year would keep an extra $39 a fortnight, or around $1000 a year.''

National would also introduce new financial penalties for borrowers who left the country before paying back their student loan.

That included adding to student loan interest, restricting KiwiSaver withdrawals and making it easier for police to issue arrest warrants for "serious, sustained loan defaults".

Willis said it was not fair for graduates to take their skills offshore after receiving a heavily subsidised tertiary education, and not try to repay their loan.

"Overseas-based borrowers currently account for 93 percent of overdue student loan debt. Only around three in 10 meet their repayment obligations in a given year, compared to 95 percent of New Zealand-based borrowers," she said.

Speaking to media, party leader Christopher Luxon said the policy would give Kiwis "real money in their back pockets" and encourage them to stay and work in New Zealand.

"Those New Zealand graduates that are here, you're the beneficiary of an interest-free loan, that means it can get paid back slower, [and] that is giving you more cash in your back pocket, and the accumulated effect of that gives you a really good core part to a deposit for a house and other things," he said.

"We're talking about teachers, we're talking about young engineers, we're talking about young doctors, people who are contributing to our community who will repay their loan over time, but we're easing up on it, giving them a bit more breathing space in those early years."

Labour's tertiary education spokesperson Shanan Halbert said National increased the repayment rate from 10 to 12 percent in 2012 and were now reversing that decision.

"Any relief for graduates will be welcome. But young people will judge National on its whole record.

"National has allowed back-to-back fee hikes of up to 6 percent and is proposing another next year. That would allow fees to rise by up to 19 percent over three years. They've also frozen the student loan repayment threshold so around 370,000 borrowers have to repay their loans faster."

Halbert said students were facing higher living costs and a tougher job market.

"Of course people should repay what they owe. But the bigger question is why so many young New Zealanders are struggling to get ahead and choosing to build their futures overseas." he said.

Nicola Willis said it was not fair for graduates to take their skills offshore after receiving a heavily subsidised tertiary education, and not try to repay their loan. Tu Natanahira/RNZ

The Victoria University Students Association's president, Aidan Donoghue, said the announcement didn't go far enough.

"Our initial response is a solid 'meh'. For students this is a step in the right direction, however it isn't much of a tangible change. The savings are zero, in the long run you are still paying that money back, and it means you're just kicking the can down the road in terms of repayment," he said.

"For us, it's a bit of a struggle to hear that you can pay it back slower, but we've also increased your loan by $12,000 by the removal of Fees Free. The entire system needs a proper review and reformation to actually reflect longevity and sustainability, not only for the universities, but for the students getting it."

Donoghue was doubtful that imposing tougher measures on overseas loan defaulters would work.

"We agree with the fact that if students do take a loan, they need to be aware that they will pay it back. However, we don't see that the one percent increase [to loan interest] would be effective in mitigating immigration outside of the country," he said.

World.title: Pacific leaders gather in Palau ahead of key PIF meeting
World.content:
RNZ's Teuila Fuatai in Koror, Palau

PIF flags at the Palau Cultural Center where the meetings will be held. Stefan Armbruster

The 55th Pacific Islands Forum leaders meeting officially kicks off Monday night in Koror, Palau. The runway leading in is already proving eventful, with at least one partner withdrawing its leader last-minute.

For those who aren't acclimatised, the mugginess of Koror's 30 degree heat is stifling. After five minutes in the sun, you're sweating and whatever you're carrying feels a few kilos heavier. Finding relief, even if it's momentary, quickly becomes a priority.

The fury at which geopolitics is wrapped into this year's Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) leaders' meeting is a lot like Koror's heat - even though you can't see it, it's all-encompassing and impossible to avoid.

Already, questions have been raised over the last-minute withdrawal of Kiribati president Taaneti Maamau. Now, it is also uncertain whether Naoero (formerly Nauru) president David Adeang will be attending as planned.

Maamau's late withdrawal, and the current lack of certainty around Naeoro's president Adeang, goes to the heart of problems around unity and outside interference in the PIF.

At the end of the PIF foreign ministers' meeting in Suva earlier this month, the lack of agreement from members over a statement condemning China's missile test dominated headlines. The dummy warhead landed in Pacific waters near Tuvalu last month.

Naoero and Kiribati, which have strong ties to Beijing, were understood to be the members which did not support a statement on it. Both those countries were also understood to be isolated from the wider collective for their stance in Suva.

The lack of agreement means the issue of a statement on the missile testing was deferred to Koror. In the last few weeks, officials across the region have been working on a statement that is due to be submitted and considered this week by leaders.

Despite that, four PIF states - Australia, New Zealand, Palau and Marshall Islands - decided to go their own way after the Suva meeting and sign a joint statement released by the US government criticising China for the missile testing. Palau and Marshall Islands, alongside Tuvalu, are the three PIF states which have formal diplomatic ties with Taiwan.

New Zealand foreign minister Winston Peters, who is representing his government in Koror before Prime Minister Christopher Luxon arrives, made his displeasure over the lack of a result in Suva clear at the time.

"They didn't actually lay out any reasons, apart from their disagreement, and not wishing for us to make the clear statement such as 'we are opposed to missiles being fired into the Pacific.

"That's what the statement should have said, and we're still waiting for that to get laid out."

It seems that disharmony has rolled straight from Suva into the beautiful islands of Palau.

Maamau's decision not to attend this week, and instead send David Teaabo, his Director of Foreign Service and the former ambassador to China, means any potential statement on missile testing won't have sign-off from Kiribati's top representative or an elected official. It also sends a clear message over Maamau's current discontent with the PIF. And if Naeoro's Adeang also withdraws, there will be concerns over unity and stability of the PIF - particularly as that will leave the week short two leaders from the Micronesia bloc.

Furthermore, alongside a potential missile statement, there are high hopes for leaders to agree on the specifics of the partnerships policy which was endorsed by leaders in Solomon Islands' last year.

The policy means the PIF partners, currently 21 dialogue partners and a group of development partners, would be divided into tier one and tier two, with the top tier having greater access to member states.

Unsurprisingly, the behemoths-in-the room on this agenda issue is where China and the US would sit. Both are dialogue partners under the current set-up and have high-level representation in Koror. China has its Special Envoy for Pacific Island Countries Affairs, Qian Bo, on the ground, while deputy secretary of state Christopher Landau is leading the US delegation. Taiwan, which is currently a PIF development partner, will also be jostling for a place in the tier system. It has sent its foreign minister Lin Chia-lung to Koror, along with a large delegation to Palau.

Notably, Fiji Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka has also withdrawn from his planned schedule in Koror last-minute due to urgent domestic issues, however he may still arrive later in the week for the leaders' retreat.

Early this morning, Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale also left Palau after less than 24 hours after a motion of no confidence was tabled back home against him. Mr Wale is the current Chair of the Pacific Islands Forum, who was suppose to hand over the chairmanship to Palau President Surangel Whipps Jr in Palau.

Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale ABC News / Adam Kennedy

Sāmoa, New Caledonia, and Vanuatu have also decided not to send leaders, however this was signalled in advance, and the states' delegations are headed by deputy prime ministers or senior ministers.

World.title: Man charged after fire engulfs two Rotorua residential units
World.content:
A man is due in court next month following a fire at a residential unit in Rotorua.

Emergency services were called to the blaze on Fenton Street just before midnight on Friday.

Police say all residents and neighbours were safely evacuated and no injuries were reported.

At least two units were engulfed by fire.

A 29-year-old man was arrested at the scene and charged with wilfully setting fire to property.

He is due to appear at Rotorua District Court on 11 September.

World.title: One dead, SH85 closed after serious South Island crash
World.content:
One person has died following a serious crash in the lower South Island.

The closure of State Highway 85, also known as Dunback-Morrisons Road, has been extended to the town of Kyeburn and Waynes.

Police were called to the single-vehicle crash on Happy Valley Creek Bridge, in the Waitaki District, around 8:10am on Sunday morning.

The person was found dead at the scene.

World.title: ACT announces plans for fisheries reform, would impose shellfish bag limits and increase fines
World.content:
ACT has announced plans to impose a nationwide daily bag limit of 10 shellfish if elected, as part of their wider plan to rebuild fish stocks and protect vulnerable marine environments.

The policy would also apply to other covered species that do not already have their own individual daily limit.

The party also wants to end scallop dredging in fisheries that are currently closed, as well as increase infringement fees for people who break the rules to provide a "genuine deterrent".

The full plan sets out a number of priorities.

It would set up a "distinct fisheries management area" matching the boundaries of the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park, so depleted stocks can be rebuilt while preserving existing quota holders' proportional property rights.

It would also require Fisheries New Zealand to measure the economic and environmental cost of high-impact fishing methods and adjust existing fisheries levies so they are proportionate to damage caused.

ACT also intends to change the way fisheries are managed to ensure higher fish stocks and "greater abundance" rather than treating maximum sustainable yield as the target.

Conservation spokesperson Cameron Luxton said a healthy marine environment was the foundation of a successful fishing industry.

"ACT's six-part plan will unlock New Zealand's fishing potential by rebuilding fish stocks, protecting vulnerable marine environments, and creating the conditions for better recreational and commercial fishing.

"ACT's approach is to protect the resource while preserving the freedom to use it.

"That means rebuilding fisheries where they are depleted, protecting vulnerable habitats from genuine damage, and replacing blunt restrictions with rules focused on actual risks," he said.

World.title: Some patients face 24-hour wait at Wellington Hospital emergency department
World.content:
Patients presenting at Wellington Hospital's emergency department have faced wait times of more than 24 hours to be seen this month.

An ED nurse said, on a recent Monday night shift, one man fell asleep and hit his head, while waiting 12 hours to be seen.

Health Minister Simeon Brown said the current situation in Wellington ED was unacceptable, as it continued to be one of lowest-performing in the country, while Health NZ said the hospital was under extreme winter pressure, and very long waits occurred for complex circumstances and weren't the experience of most patients.

The New Zealand Nurses Organisation (NZNO) delegate said she feared speaking out would result in repercussions - RNZ agreed not to name her for this reason.

She said, on the overnight shift on Monday 17 August, the hospital escalated to Code Red several times.

Health NZ has said code red in ED referred to the amount of pressure the department was under. It's based on waitingroom congestion, staffing skill mix, changes in care hours and the seriousness of the patient cases.

One man had come to the emergency department in the evening, she said, and wasn't admitted until about 6am.

"The only reason he was brought through then was because of him falling asleep and face-planting, and they were checking him for any injuries."

The nurse said ED wait-times recently were extremely long - at times reaching 24 hours - although the peak was 18 hours more recently.

The six-hour ED treatment and discharge target was only achieved 57.6 percent of the time at Wellington Hospital in January-March. RNZ / REECE BAKER

In internal Health NZ documents RNZ has seen, the agency said in early August that some patients exceeded 24-hour waits in ED, with high numbers of patients waiting more than six hours, due to medical bed shortages.

Hospitals throughout the country have a target that 95 percent of patients are admitted, discharged or transferred from an emergency department within six hours.

Latest results from Health NZ, between January and March 2026, show Capital & Coast hospitals only met that target 57.6 percent of the time.

An ED summary shift report from a staff member from Monday, 17 August said the department that night was operating under "extreme pressure", experiencing "significant and sustained over-crowding".

A mental health patient locked themselves in the bathroom and self-harmed, the nurse said, while a member of the public walked in and threatened to "kill staff", assaulting a security orderly.

Police confirmed to RNZ they attended the hospital at 11.30pm to a report of disorderly behaviour - a person was arrested for breach of conditions, a spokesperson said.

Health NZ said it wouldn't comment or confirm details about the specific patient incidents, without a privacy waiver.

File photo 123RF

'Lots of pressure'

The nurse said the hospital was full and bed-blocked that night, with at least 11 patients needing to be treated in corridors, although this was normal.

"It's just a sh**show to work in at the moment. Lots of pressure.

"We're getting high presentations, but the pressure's coming from where we can't get patients off to wards to free up our ED space, so that we can continue to see the new ones coming in."

She said there could be up to 24 patients in corridors on other days.

"It's awful, you know, and every day you're seeing your corridors full and we're all walking past these corridors.

"There's no privacy for any of these patients."

Twenty-seven nurse vacancies at Wellington ED

A Health NZ spokesperson said there were 27.1 full-time nurse vacancies at in the ED.

In the coming months, 18 new nurses would come on board, leaving 8.8 full-time nurse vacancies, which were being recruited.

Michelle Sutherland, interim group director of operations for the region, said the hospital had 212 ED patients on 17 August, following several days of high demand.

Winter was an extremely busy time for health services, so more patients were expected.

She said 66 percent percent of patients on 17 August were discharged from the ED within six hours.

"We acknowledge that a number of patients experienced very long waits. The longest waits tend to reflect particularly complex circumstances, rather than the experience of most people in the department."

Health Minister Simeon Brown RNZ / Mark Papalii

Wellington ED wait-times 'not acceptable' - minister

Brown said the current situation at Wellington Regional Hospital's emergency department was not acceptable.

"It continues to be one of the lowest-performing in the country, and that is not good enough for patients or for staff.

"Our doctors, nurses and healthcare workers work incredibly hard every day, but they are operating in a facility that does not support safe patient flow or timely treatment."

Brown said the government had prioritised a redevelopment of ED in the Health Infrastructure Plan and work was underway across the hospital campus.

His office said additional beds had been provided, among other planning measures made for the winter season.

Space in the hospital has been a long-standing issue, with the redevelopment likely to be complete by 2029.

He said wait times at Wellington Hospital had come down under the current government, compared to the previous Labour government, and the ED now met the wait-time target 57.6 percent of the time, increasing from 43.8 percent in 2023.

Code Red instances had also fallen, he said, with his office providing a table that showed 729 Code Reds in 2023, compared to 567 in 2025.

"However, there is still a long way to go before Wellingtonians can access emergency care as quickly as they deserve."

World.title: Aussie qualifer completes rare grand slam feat
World.content:
There is a very good reason why facing big-hitting French Open and Wimbledon semifinalist Marta Kostyuk in the US Open first round holds no fears for late-blooming Australian trailblazer Storm Hunter.

The 32-year-old has just sent tennis officials scrambling through the record books after qualifying for the Open's main draw for the first time.

Historians could only confirm Hunter is the first active Australian player to successfully qualify for all four grand slams, a rare feat few others from anywhere have accomplished.

De Minaur gets qualifier in US Open first round Alex de Minaur appears to have a kind draw for the year's final grand slam, but Australia's perennial hope will face a precociously formidable obstacle if he wants to make it to the quarterfinals for the third straight year.

Hunter did not do it easily, taking out compatriot and great mate Maddison Inglis in her first match, fending off two match points in her second and waiting through a 24-hour weather delay to advance with a third straight sudden-death victory.

"This is the last slam on my list to tick off to get through qualies and coming in I hadn't played many singles matches in the last few months so, yeah, it feels amazing," Hunter said.

Having missed more than a year after rupturing an Achilles tendon, Hunter is back in the Flushing Meadows main draw for a first time since 2023.

Her "reward" is a first-round tussle on day one with the 11th-seeded Kostyuk, who is coming off charges to the last four at both Roland Garros and the All England Club.

"Yeah, it's tough," said the one-time world number one doubles ace.

"She's obviously having a really good year. She's a great player, very physical with the way she plays and a really good competitor.

"So it's going to be tough. Obviously a very quick turnaround from playing qualifiers to my first round tomorrow, but I'm feeling good and she's the one who's under all the pressure to play against me and I have practised with her before.

"I know what her level is and I know it's going to be a challenge, but I'm up for a challenge. It's going to be fun. I'm going to enjoy it.

"There's been lots of times in my career I didn't think I'd be back playing at this level, so to be back in the main draw of a slam is awesome, and I'm just going to go out and enjoy it and give it a good crack."

Hunter is among six Australians playing on Monday.

Kim Birrell faces Petra Marcinko, Talia Gibson also plays a Croatian in veteran Donna Vekic and fellow rising star Taylah Preston takes on American Alycia Parks.

Adam Walton, up against China's Yibing Wu, and Aleksandar Vukic playing Japan's Rei Sakamoto are the only Aussie men in first-round action.

Sixth seed Alex de Minaur opens his campaign on Tuesday (Wednesday AEST).

AAP

World.title: 'Once in a lifetime': Schoolteacher wins AFL Fantasy competition
World.content:
Tyler Wagner could hardly watch as the outcome of this year's AFL Fantasy competition came down to the wire.

In the 13 years the Fremantle Dockers diehard had been playing the online game, he never envisioned he would make it here.

With less than a minute to go, Wagner's fantasy team, named Wagmantle, was in the lead by just three fantasy points.

If the opposing team, The Powerhouse, recorded a single stat, the 2026 title was theirs.

As the ball approached Powerhouse's Jarman Impey, the seconds were ticking down, and Wagner could not bear to watch.

Tyler Wagner's Wagmantle managed to beat a number of other fantasy players. (Supplied: Tyler Wagner)

But when he did finally look back up, Impey had dropped the mark.

"It was still nerve-racking because the siren had gone, but sometimes the AFL do late stat corrections," Wagner said.

"My mates went absolutely mental and it was a very, very cool moment.

"But I was still sitting there pacing the hallway just hoping there was no stat correction."

Thirteen years in the making

AFL Fantasy allows users to coach a virtual team of players, who score points based on their real-life performances, using an allocated budget.

Each year approximately 140,000 Australians compete to crown one winner.

This year, the prize on offer was $20,000, two tickets to the AFL Grand Final and a car.

Tyler Wagner is footy obsessed and spends most of his free time either watching or playing. (ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne)

Wagner, a 28-year-old PE teacher from South Australia's Riverland, described his win as "overwhelming".

The A-grade footballer had been playing AFL Fantasy since 2014 when he was a teenager.

"I've had a lot of messages from friends and family, which has been really awesome," he said.

"There's a group of year four, fives and sixes that I teach that follow it pretty closely.

"They were ripping me some weeks where I dropped a few in ranks and then they'd give me a kudos when it went up, but those last couple of weeks, they were pretty excited."

Long-suffering Fremantle fans dare to dream

What started as a bit of fun has now given Wagner the opportunity to live out his childhood dream alongside his father.

Fremantle has never won a premiership in its 32-year history and has only once made it to the big dance in 2013.

"My old man has been a Docker supporter since 1995," he said.

Tyler Wagner (right) never had any choice in which team he supported, following in the footsteps of his dad (centre). (Supplied: Tyler Wagner)

"I reckon he might have been the bloody first Fremantle fan in SA.

" It's a no-brainer — if Freo manage to make it, I'm definitely taking dad. "

Wagner is hoping the Dockers, who finished 2026 as minor premiers, can go one better than 2013 and make history.

"I'm definitely a self-confessed Dockers nuffy," he said.

Luke Jackson is Tyler Wagner's favourite player and was a key piece for his fantasy team. (AAP: Richard Wainwright)

" To see that would be absolutely everything, especially alongside my dad. "

Luck or strategy?

AFL Fantasy expert Ryan "Heff" Gerlach has been playing fantasy football since 2004, back when it was called Dream Team.

He has since made a career out of the hobby, running a successful podcast known as The Keeper League.

"Winning the competition against 140,000 people is lucky in itself," Gerlach said.

"To do it in a year where there's a good chance of your team playing in the Grand Final, I don't think it could have worked out any better for Tyler."

Ryan "Heff" Gerlach is well known within the growing fantasy football community. (Supplied: Ryan Gerlach)

The statistical side of fantasy sports, mixed with a sense of gaming is what Gerlach said made it such an appealing pastime.

He said while anyone in a position to beat out more than 140,000 people had to be knowledgeable, luck was bound to play some role.

"If I was going to give it a number, I'd say [it's] probably 60 per cent strategy, 40 per cent luck," Gerlach said.

"But you talk to different people and that answer will differ."

Despite the temptation to attribute his once-in-a-lifetime season to skill, Wagner remained humble in his assessment.

"I didn't think that I would even be in the top ten this year, let alone winning the thing," he said.

"In other years I've probably felt like I've put the same amount of effort in, but it just hasn't fallen my way.

"There's definitely a lot of luck involved, but you still need to know your stuff."

World.title: Marshall fires up over 'outrageous' refereeing in loss to Cowboys
World.content:
A fired-up Benji Marshall says he will issue a "please explain" to the NRL after a series of "outrageous" calls went against Wests Tigers in their loss to North Queensland.

The Cowboys punched their ticket to the finals for a second time in three years with a 24-10 win at Townsville Stadium on Saturday night, but the victory wasn't without controversy.

NRL live Roosters halfback Sam Walker will go for scans after sustaining a concerning ankle injury in his side's 26-12 loss to the Dolphins, while North Queensland lock in a finals spot with a 24-10 victory over Wests.

Tigers five-eighth Jarome Luai had his length-of-the-field try chalked off in the first half because of a rake in the lead-up, and prop Terrell May's was also denied by the bunker after Cowboys fullback Scott Drinkwater was impeded, despite standing metres away from the ball.

"The level of some of the refereeing decisions today was honestly outrageous, and I thought we copped the raw end of the stick all night," Tigers coach Marshall said.

"We'll be sending in a few questions and asking for a please explain.

"We get penalised for contesting. They go down, take Jock Madden out [the] same thing. We get no penalty. They score.

"I feel like I need to stand up for my players because the way they're fighting, it's just not right."

To make matters worse, the joint venture (8-15) will sweat on Luai, who hobbled off the field in the second half and was also placed on report in his penultimate game for the club.

North Queensland (13-10) will not worry about the contentious calls after becoming the last team to seal their top-eight spot, after South Sydney secured their finals place with a 42-22 victory over Gold Coast earlier on Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Tadej Pogačar crashes out of La Vuelta a España
World.content:
Five-time Tour de France champion and overwhelming favourite Tadej Pogačar has pulled out of the Vuelta a España after crashing during the eighth stage of the race.

The Slovenian held a big lead in the race but got caught in a crash about 33 kilometres from the finish on Saturday, local time.

He tried to get back on his bike but could not carry on and walked to an ambulance. Race organisers confirmed he pulled out of the race.

The UAE Team Emirates leader was trying to become the ninth male rider to win all three grand tour races.

Pogacar won the Tour de France for a third straight time and a record-tying fifth overall in July, and he claimed the Giro d'Italia win in 2024. He had not raced in the Vuelta since making his grand tour debut at the event in 2019.

Footage showed Pogačar with cuts on his head as well as his left arm and shoulder. Pogačar veered to his right, into other cyclists, as he appeared to try to either hit or avoid something in the road.

He lost control and flew over his handlebars, hitting his head and shoulder.

UAE Team Emirates sports manager Matxin Joxean Fernandez said after the stage that Pogačar had needed stitches in his eyebrow and elsewhere.

"It's no-one's responsibility … It's simply one of those things that happens in cycling, unfortunately," Fernandez said.

"He initially wanted to keep going, but we saw he was in a lot of pain in his shoulder and decided he couldn't continue. There isn't much else to say.

"After seven days Tadej was happy and it's a very big shame for him, cycling is about good and bad and [we hope] Tadej recovers as soon as possible because hopefully it's not something too bad, we're not going to think about that right now but we'll see what the doctor says."

Pogačar — who had led since winning the opening stage — had an advantage of 3 minutes, 50 seconds over Enric Mas of Movistar before Saturday's stage, which did not feature any major difficulty and offered sprinters a chance to shine along a flat 171-kilometre route from Puçol to Xeraco. Bryan Coquard, from the Cofidis team, claimed the stage win ahead of Mads Pedersen and Jordi Meeus.

Pogačar wins Vuelta stage four Tadej Pogačar has taken a dominant lead in the Vuelta a España, winning his second stage with a phenomenal 50km solo attack in Andorra.

Mas took the race leader's jersey from Pogačar, becoming the first Spanish rider to lead the race since Jesus Herrada in 2018. Felix Gall stood second overall, 1:11 off the pace, with Primoz Roglic in third.

The 31-year-old Mas did not put on the leader's red jersey when he was presented with it in the post-race ceremony, instead just holding it up. He was also not wearing it in television interviews after the stage.

"To get the red jersey thanks to a crash, it's not a good feeling," he told Eurosport in translated comments.

"We'll try to defend it tomorrow but tonight we need to assimilate what happened and give Tadej all our support and hopefully he will recover soon. We decided with the team that I was not going to wear the red jersey [today] and then if I deserve it tomorrow, I will wear it."

Pogačar's main rival, Jonas Vingegaard, is not competing in the Vuelta after crashing during this year's Tour de France.

This was Pogačar's 10th Grand Tour and the first he has ever abandoned. He had never finished lower than third place.

The three-week race concludes in Granada.

AP

World.title: A 16-year-old sprint prodigy, Ellie Beer was consumed by pressure to perform
World.content:
At age 16, 400 metre runner Ellie Beer was exceeding expectations.

She was the new kid on the block in Australian sprinting, smashing her personal best (PB) time and making history.

But maintaining that level of performance was all-consuming.

"It was just spotlight moment after spotlight moment," Beer tells ABC Sport.

"I remember feeling the pressure of what others were thinking.

"I felt like I had to rise to the occasion, like every race I had to run a PB and that it would be good enough."

It took another five agonising years for Beer to beat her 2019 PB of 52.53 seconds.

"There were moments where I was like, 'Will I ever get better?' I [felt] like maybe I peaked at 16," Beer says.

"I had thoughts of wanting to give up and not pursue it anymore."

Ellie Beer competed for five years without running a personal best. (Getty Images: Andy Cheung)

The transition from a junior to a senior athlete, from about 17 to 19 years of age, was particularly hard.

"I had set my standards so high that I had to run consecutive 52 second runs, but I wasn't getting close to that time due to the pressure," Beer says.

She started overthinking her races, predicting what would happen before they had even begun.

"I would be worrying about the lactic [acid] hitting the last hundred. 'How am I going to run down that back straight?'

"I went out and pretty much just ran stressed and nervous."

Ellie Beer started to overthink races and then tied her identity to her results. (ABC Sport: Glenn Mullane)

Beer credits her coach and support team with getting her on the start line during that time.

"The back of my head [was saying] 'I don't want to give up the sport,' but the front of my head was telling me, 'No, [I] want to be done.'"

"I knew in my heart that I didn't want to give up," she says.

But moving forward wasn't easy.

When passion turns to pain

Beer stands out. She's more than 1.8m tall, with long, bouncy blonde locks and an infectious smile.

You can't miss her on the track thanks to her trademark arm sleeves, which help her to get in the zone.

Ellie Beer says wearing arm sleeves helps her to get in the zone. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"My coach always says, 'Wear your arm sleeves, Ellie, because you feel fierce,'" she says.

"[They] make me feel like I'm ready to go out there and perform."

Now 23, Beer is a different person to the 16-year-old who stormed onto the world stage. But it's only because of where she's been.

Beer's big break came at the Queensland Track Classic in 2019 when she won the 400m in a PB of 52.53.

It earned her a spot in the Australian 4 x 400m relay team for the 2019 IAAF World Athletics Championships, and the title of the youngest-ever Australian selected.

A young Ellie Beer competes at the IAAF World Athletics Championships in 2019. (Getty Images: Christian Petersen)

She then ran a flying time, which helped Australia qualify for the Tokyo Olympics.

Beer was selected for that 4x400m relay team for Tokyo, and at 18 her Olympic dream was realised.

Ellie Beer (right) realised her dream to compete at an Olympics in Tokyo. (Getty Images: Matthias Hangst)

After Tokyo, Beer won the 2022 national senior 400m title and placed seventh in the 400m final at the World Under 20 Championships. But still no breakthrough runs, no personal bests. That pressure to rise to every occasion was weighing heavily.

"I was just really worrying about trying to perform a perfect race, sometimes for others," Beer says.

Ellie Beer was constantly worrying about the race, before it even began. (Getty Images: Pedro Vilela)

"I used to be, after bad races, quite down on myself.

"And then [I] would kind of dwell into the rest of my season."

The power of pushing through

At 21 years old, already having graced the international stage for five years, Beer knew something had to change.

It was 2024, leading into the Paris Olympics, when her mindset switched thanks to a supportive team.

A mindset change in the year leading up to the Paris Olympics helped Ellie Beer make a breakthrough. (Getty Images: Christian Petersen)

She now has a wellbeing coach, a psychologist, and Brett Robinson, who has been her running coach since she was 11.

"He [Robinson] has helped me so much along the way," Beer says.

"Particularly during times when I didn't believe in myself, he would always believe in me more.

"I don't even want to call him a coach; I want to call him family."

What they did together seems so simple, but it worked.

"Nerves, they never go away, [but] I've changed my mindset around them," Beer says.

"I channel them and [have learned to] embrace them.

Ellie Beer now embraces the nerves and leans into them, rather than letting them consume her. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"It's a word that Robbo and I have used quite often.

"Embrace the hurt, [because] the 400 [is] a very tactical event, but learning to embrace that lactic acid, embrace where you are and being grateful to go out there and perform."

With that, Beer stopped worrying about the uncontrollable and she wasn't so driven by the outcome.

She also stopped tying her identity to her race results.

"I'm learning, yes, I'm Ellie Beer the athlete, but I'm also Ellie Beer the daughter, coffee enthusiast, social girl, the friend," she says.

Loading Instagram content

"I've just learned that you [might have] one bad race, [and] yes, it sucks at the time, but it's just one race. We move forward and we focus on the next."

Mind over matter

That change has seen results.

2024 was a good year for Beer. She broke the personal best drought at the Adelaide Invitational, took the national 400m title, the Oceania 400m title, and then produced another PB at the Paris Olympics.

In 2025, she won her third national title and got her PB down to its current form of 51.3 seconds. She also won a bronze relay medal at the World Indoor Championships.

Loading Instagram content

This year, she secured her fourth national title, was crowned Oceania Champion again, and recently helped the mixed and women's relay teams qualify for the 2027 World Athletics Championships.

Her biggest goal now is running the 400m in under 51 seconds.

"I've had that goal for the last couple of years and we just haven't quite got it yet," Beer says.

"We've got PBs which I'm happy with, but our standard for Australia to get into most major teams is to run a 50.7.

"To run a sub-50, oh my gosh, I'm going to be ecstatic.

"But I've learned [that with] running, even just a PB is amazing [and] I'll be happy with that."

Ellie Beer's goal now is to run the 400 metres in under 51 seconds. (Getty Images: Andy Cheung)

Beer stresses the nerves are still there and probably always will be.

When asked what her greatest challenge is in getting that sub-51 mark, her answer is not a surprise.

"Probably my own self," Beer says.

"I'm a different athlete compared to when I was a junior, [but I] still struggle with the self-doubt and the what if."

The Gold Coast local is now an ambassador for the Australian Institute of Sport's mental fitness program, and says she is happy to share her experiences of vulnerability to help other athletes.

"Having that experience of not running a PB for five years, that's the reason as to why at this age now I want to share better ways to deal with it," she says.

"As part of my training, I speak with my sports psychologist, I speak to my wellbeing officer, I speak with my coaches to help rewire my mindset leading into races.

"There's a major percentage physically, [but] mental plays a massive part as well."

It is possibly a contradiction, but mentally, Beer likes to switch off with coffee.

Loading Instagram content

She just can't survive without her two iced long blacks a day, on top of an espresso shot with eggs on toast in the morning.

"I love coffee," Beer says.

"My favourite thing to do outside of training is search for the best cafes and try all of them."

The focus is just one part of rebuilding her identity outside of running.

In the long term, Beer has her sights set on being selected for the Brisbane 2032 Olympics.

"I would love to perform in front of a home crowd," she says.

But for now, there's always coffee.

World.title: Wallabies win tense Test in Argentina as coach Kiss remains unbeaten
World.content:
The Wallabies have won a gritty and tense Test match described by two separate players as "bloody hard", securing a 27-21 win over Argentina.

Australia scored four tries to three in Sunday morning's clash in the mountain town of San Salvador de Jujuy, where the stadium sits more than 1,200 metres above sea level.

The Wallabies made a hot start with three tries in the opening 20 minutes, but had to show plenty of determination to hold off an Argentine fightback to secure the team's fourth Test win in a row.

The Australian forwards were excellent for much of the match, especially disrupting the Los Pumas' line-out in the second half.

Australia's forwards were very good in the set piece against Argentina. (AP: Gustavo Garello)

Wallabies flanker Fraser McReight was named player of the match after an effort where he was a constant feature around the ball, including a crucial penalty won late in the contest with Argentina attacking inside the 22m.

"It was a back-and-forth sort of match," McReight told the host broadcaster.

"Argentina were very good. I felt like we were pretty poor in some areas, but [I'm] just really proud of the group and I'm happy we got the win over here."

The Wallabies were by no means perfect in Jujuy, with winger Max Jorgensen and flanker Tom Hooper each describing the match and conditions as "bloody hard" in separate interviews.

The Wallabies made a hot start with the opening two tries of the match. Hooker Brandon Paenga-Amosa finished off a lovely passage of passing between forwards to score in the seventh minute, then fly half Carter Gordon touched down four minutes later from close range after the Wallabies forwards pounded their way to the goal line.

Argentina struck back through fullback Geronimo Prisciantelli after a lovely backline move, but when McReight scored in the 20th minute, the Wallabies were in control at 19-7.

But Los Pumas wrestled back the momentum, and a sin bin with Wallabies winger Harry Potter for deliberately knocking the ball down in the 25th minute put the home side in the ascendancy.

Argentina number eight Joaquin Moro took a quick tap from close range and powered over the line to reduce the deficit to five points, but a penalty goal from Wallabies scrumhalf Ryan Lonergan gave Australia a 22-14 lead at the break.

Lonergan came off after just five minutes in the second half after making a desperate cover tackle to deny Prisciantelli a second try.

Los Pumas were denied a try due to a forward pass picked up by the TMO in the 48th minute, but loosehead prop Boris Wenger dove over three minutes later to reduce Australia's lead to one point.

But the Wallabies responded quickly, with a line break from centre Hunter Paisami putting Australia into the attacking 22m, and leading to Hooper reaching out a few plays later to give the Wallabies a 27-21 lead.

The Wallabies were on top as the second half wore on, but could not get the try to seal the game. Jeremy Williams knocked on while trying to score, then reserve scrumhalf Tate McDermott was held up over the line.

It kept Los Pumas in the contest, but the Wallabies' defence held firm in the final five minutes to secure the win.

"It was a very tough game. Everyone knows that coming over to Argentina is a bloody hard place to win. It's you against them, plus the whole stadium," Jorgensen told Stan Sport.

"It wasn't near perfect, we've still got a lot of work to do, but to come away with a win in Argentina is very good."

The win is Australia's fourth in a row, and maintains coach Les Kiss's perfect record after three Tests in charge.

Australia has leapfrogged Argentina into seventh on the World Rugby rankings, with both sides to meet next week in the second Test at Mendoza.

Follow all the live action from the first Test between the Wallabies and Argentina in the blog below.

World.title: Blues' resurgence continues with stirring wildcard win over Demons
World.content:
Carlton will play an elimination final against Geelong after winning a wildcard clash against Melbourne at the MCG.

Despite conceding the first four goals of the game, the Blues improved steadily throughout the game to grind the Demons down, before finally emerging 19-point winners.

Ben Ainsworth kicked three goals for Carlton, while Sam Walsh and rising star Jagga Smith were sensational in the midfield.

The Blues had multiple opportunities to put the game to bed in the last quarter, but it wasn't until Smith converted a set shot for his second of the evening when the result was put to bed.

World.title: Jai Arrow makes emotional return for South Sydney
World.content:
Jai Arrow has made an emotional return for South Sydney, leading the side out and officially playing his 99th match for the club against Gold Coast.

Arrow, who was diagnosed with MND earlier this year, has received special dispensation from the NRL to play the opening seconds of the Rabbitohs' final two matches for the year.

He was substituted before kick-off for Cameron Murray and left the field at Skilled Park to a standing ovation.

Rabbitohs coach Wayne Bennett and former stalwart Jason Clark helped Arrow put his boots on before the match.

The Titans wore a commemorative jersey with Arrow's face on the front.

He played 56 matches for the club from 2018 to 2020.

Arrow will lead South Sydney out again next week in their final game of the regular season against the Sydney Roosters.

Arrow was in tears as he left the field. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde )

It will mark his 100th game for the club and the 180th and final match of his career.

Arrow was in the room when elated Souths players were told about the plan during their team review session on Monday morning.

"We all play a tough sport and we all mean so much to so many people, but it's so special to see what players mean to other players when things are going tough," said Rabbitohs fullback Matt Dufty.

"[Jai] brings a smile to everyone's face. Whatever we can do to give back to him, even if it's a little bit, it's just what we need to do. We're all behind him."

The NRL world has rallied around Arrow since his shock diagnosis and immediate retirement in May.

Murray replaced Arrow before kick off. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde )

The league threw Arrow "the world's biggest birthday party" on the day Souths beat Newcastle in July, rolling out a birthday cake in the shape of his jersey and presenting him with a commemorative jersey.

Fundraising efforts have already passed $1 million in support of Arrow, who is the father of a young daughter.

Players from all clubs showed their support by marking tries with 'arrow' celebrations during July.

AAP/ABC

Tech.title: Vicariously hike the Appalachian in the gorgeous A Trail Tale
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

I used to be an avid hiker and would try to go backpacking a few times a year. I always dreamed of thru-hiking the Appalachian Trail, but life kind of got in the way. (Turns out jobs, wives, and children aren’t thrilled with the idea of you disappearing for three months.) But I’ve been longing to reconnect with my love of the outdoors and just recently took my kids on their first camping trip. So I discovered A Trail Tale at a really opportune time. It’s an interactive trail journal created by Andy Moliski with help from his brothers Adam and Alex.

The various segments of the trail are rendered in beautiful pixel art reminiscent of a ‘90s Sierra point-and-click adventure. Alex recorded an equally gorgeous original score that combines nature sounds, acoustic guitar, strings, and even what sounds like clarinet.

As you click through each day, you’re greeted with information about landmarks and a game-like UI that is partially inspired by titles like Oregon Trail. (Spoiler: nobody dies of dysentery in this one.) Clicking on Andy unfurls a menu of icons that offer details about the journey, his mental state, and even bits of poetry. There are even little icons for things that impact his fortitude and morale meters, like inclement weather or picturesque scenery.

It’s insanely easy to just get lost in Andy’s journey for hours. And it’s making me wonder if I should get back out there and start tackling some more of the AT myself.

Tech.title: Alt-right troll Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Alt-right troll Milo Yiannopoulos was arrested by ICE on Thursday, and today the Department of Homeland Security confirmed to Reuters and the Washington Post that he had been deported to the UK. Yiannopoulos came to the US legally in 2019, but overstayed his visa. After he failed to appear in court for an immigration hearing, a final order of removal was issued ​on July 22.

The British national made a name for himself as an editor at Steve Bannon’s Breitbart and an early supporter of Donald Trump’s. He has had a long history of controversial statements and associations, including reportedly helping arrange Trump’s dinner with Kanye West and white nationalist Nick Fuentes, and he was a key figure in the online harassment campaign Gamergate.

In recent years, however, his antics have led to a falling out with most significant figures on the right, including MAGA influencer Laura Loomer. He has denied condoning statutory rape or pedophilia, but he has suggested it’s acceptable for an adult to have a sexual relationship with a 13-year-old.

There’s no word if the 44 interns in a trenchcoat who also constitute the entity known as Milo Yiannopoulos have also been deported.

Tech.title: Sony Music and Warner Chappell are suing Anthropic
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Sony Music and Warner Chappell have filed suit against Anthropic in the US District Court for the Northern District of California seeking damages for “tens of thousands” copyrighted works. The companies are asking for up to $150,000 per work, plus up to $25,000 for each instance when identifiable copyright data was stripped. In total, the damages could amount to several billion dollars if a court finds in Sony and Warner’s favor and awards the maximum amount.

In addition to suing Anthropic as an entity, the complaint names Co-Founders Dario Amodei and Benjamin Mann as individual defendants. The suit alleges that Mann used BitTorrent to download over five million pirated books, and that employees downloaded at least two million more from Pirate Library Mirror. It also claims that Anthropic scraped lyrics from sites like MusixMatch and LyricFind, which paid to license content from the labels.

According to the filing:

Plaintiff Music Publishers, a group of the world’s leading music publishers, bring this action to hold accountable the culprits behind one of the largest and most blatant ongoing thefts of intellectual property in history. Defendants Anthropic and its founders Dario Amodei and Benjamin Mann have conducted a brazen campaign of illegally torrenting, scraping, and downloading copyrighted works on a massive scale in order to develop, operate, and reap enormous profits from Anthropic’s “Claude” series of artificial intelligence (“AI”) models.

Specific songs named as being found in Anthropic’s training data include Marvin Gaye and Tammi Terrell’s “Ain’t No Mountain High Enough,” Bon Jovi’s “Livin’ On a Prayer,” Earth, Wind & Fire’s “September,” Leonard Cohen’s “Hallelujah,” and TaylorSwift’s “Paper Rings.” Antrhopic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Tech.title: Distraction-free writing gadget BYOK is adding custom extensions
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

BYOK is a no-frills, single-purpose gadget that 90 percent of people will find absolutely frivolous. But for those who spend a significant chunk of their lives putting words to virtual paper, there is an obvious allure. Personally, I think it’s at its best when you just stick to the bare minimum, focusing on pure text drafting. Certain users, though, need more. They want BYOK to take notes, they want to use it for writing screenplays, or maybe they want to organize a sprawling novel.

Balancing the wants and needs of these more demanding users has been a challenge that BYOK founder Nick Sjolinder has been trying to figure out how to tackle. The answer he seems to have landed on, is scripts. Rather than clutter BYOK with a ton of features that 80 percent of its users wont touch, or crowd the Studio app with even more formats, the company is planning to implement optional scripts that expand the capabilities of BYOK.

A few examples of the kinds of thing people will be able to create are a screenplay assistant, a character note tool, and a writing analyzer. This could let users highlight text in a document and pull it out as a note or tell them when they’re using the passive voice. It’s still early in development and the scripting features haven’t rolled out publicly, but BYOK is asking for feedback from its users.

Tech.title: Welcome to Night Vale cocreator Joseph Fink learned storytelling from Grim Fandango
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Joseph Fink is the cocreator and cowriter of Welcome to Night Vale, arguably the most important fiction podcast ever. He’s also the creator of the noir podcast Unlicensed and Alice Isn’t Dead, which takes some of the conspiratorial cosmic horror of Night Vale and turns it into fodder for a more serious series about relationships, trauma, and the open road. There’s also a sequel series out now called Don’t Tell Alice that takes the story down an even darker path in which protagonist Keisha is the one with a secret.

Joseph is also an accomplished author. In addition to co-writing the three Welcome to Night Vale novels, he’s also penned the Alice Isn’t Dead novel and The Halloween Moon. His latest work is The Nudge, which features some gorgeous illustrations from Jessica Hayworth, who also provides the art for Night Vale, hits shelves on September 1st. It’s a brief and unsettling novella about a man trying to outrun some mysterious evil.

What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer?

Podcast Addict. It’s an Android-only podcast app made by one guy named Xavier, and it is so much better than any other podcast app that it’s the main reason I can never switch to an iPhone. I’m maybe the one guy in the entire country who chooses phones based on how they play podcasts.

Which social media platform do you use the most?

I use Bluesky, which I used to like because no one was there and so no one read my posts, which is really the ideal social media for me. Now there are more people there, and sometimes people read and respond to my posts, which is a drag.

What game do you have the fondest memories of?

My entire understanding of storytelling is probably shaped by Grim Fandango, a 1999 adventure game about a sad sack grim reaper navigating a film noir afterlife. There are lines and images from that game that will live in my head forever, even if a lot of them were parodies or references to classic films I wasn’t even aware existed when I first played that game.

What creation are you most proud of?

Our Audible show Unlicensed was one of those few projects that turned out exactly how I wanted it to in my head. A mystery series set in the least cool parts of Los Angeles, the parts where the actual people live. I didn’t want it to be “good for two writers who usually don’t write mysteries.” I just wanted us to write a damn good mystery, and I think we did. We got three seasons out of Audible, but then they mostly shut down their original shows department, and that was it. If I had my choice though, I’d happily spend the rest of my life writing Unlicensed.

What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?

I recently watched a talk with Meshell Ndegeocello, and she described having to shush a fellow student in a guitar workshop who was noodling on his guitar while the teacher was trying to demonstrate something. Meshell said: “As a musician, it doesn’t matter how well you play if you can’t listen.” I don’t know if it’s the best advice I’ve ever received, but I think it’s damn good advice and applies to a lot of things outside of music.

What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?

I buy too many books, constantly. I like to hang out in bookstores, and I’ve never left one without buying at least a couple of books. I’m mostly not a physical media guy, I have no interest in owning records or DVDs, but I’ll build an addition to my house before I get rid of any books.

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

“It turns out watching a guy write audio fiction on his computer is boring, this movie was a mistake sorry, we’re sorry.”

What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

I don’t really use GIFs or memes. I’m very much a text guy, which is why I stick to text social media mostly, even though that doesn’t really help you sell books or stuff like that.

Tech.title: The Galaxy Z Flip 8 is at its best when there’s friction
Tech.content:
is a news editor with over a decade’s experience in journalism. He previously worked at Android Police and Tech Advisor.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

What do you want from a flip phone when it’s closed? A simple interface, perhaps notifications and a widget or two, for handling the basics? Or a fully fledged Android experience shrunk down for the Flip form factor? For years, Samsung has insisted on the former, even as some fans — and Razr rival Motorola — have pushed for the latter. With the Galaxy Z Flip 8, Samsung has given in.

Although the Z Flip 8’s hardware is almost unchanged year-on-year, Samsung has fundamentally rethought how this phone is meant to be used when shut. The cover screen feels more like a regular Android phone, with easier access to the full versions of every single app, letting you browse social media, watch movies, and play games without ever opening the phone. Not every app works well on a tiny square screen with two cameras in the middle of it, but even when they don’t, that friction between me and the distractions of my phone still feels as much a feature as a bug.

Everything exciting about the Z Flip 8 lies in its 4-inch cover screen, which is now more versatile than ever thanks to a homescreen redesign. Swiping down from the top left now brings up your notifications, while swiping from the top right instead shows a cover-screen-optimized version of the Quick Settings panel. Immediately, this feels more like a phone.

More exciting is what happens when you swipe up from the bottom: you get an app drawer. By default, this is populated with a selection of Samsung’s own apps that are optimized for the square screen, plus a “Labs” section with third-party options including Netflix and WhatsApp. But right below that, Samsung has included an easy prompt to install MultiStar, the Good Lock module that lets you run any app you’d like on the outer screen.

Samsung used to bury the option deep in the phone’s settings, only to be found by those who knew to look for it. The bottom of the app drawer isn’t quite front and center, but it’s much more prominent than it used to be.

You can run any app you’d like on the cover screen. The Withings app scales badly: The graph takes up too much space to even show both axes, and it becomes impossible to scroll past it. Google Maps works, but it’s busy and awkward, especially when you try to zoom in. HBO Max works flawlessly, but it wouldn’t be my first choice to watch Lanterns.

You can still run apps in three forms: full-screen, with the cameras blocking part of the software; a square display that stops just above the level of the cameras; or a thin portrait-aspect ratio that letterboxes the sides. A small virtual button at the bottom of the screen lets you cycle through them.

Good performance isn’t guaranteed. Some apps, like Withings’ health tracker companion app, are almost impossible to use on the cover screen, with no configuration that leaves enough space for its graphs to fit. Google Maps is only a bit better — I love the idea of quickly checking my walking route without opening the phone, but there are so many floating interface elements that it’s unwieldy at best. Others work smoothly, but feel pointless: I can stream HBO Max on the tiny outer display, but I’d never want to.

But for other apps, the new cover screen options feel genuinely freeing. I can open Todoist and tick off a task, dip into WhatsApp to send a message, or open MyFitnessPal to log the snack I just ate. They’re quick actions that work well enough on the small screen, and because other apps — *cough* Instagram *cough* — don’t, I can dive into them without the risk of getting dragged into doomscrolling. That little bit of friction is just enough to save me from wasting 20 minutes I’ll never get back.

Like last year’s phone, the cover screen wraps around the cameras.

As for the hardware, little has changed. The Z Flip 8 is 0.6mm thinner and 8g lighter than its predecessor. This is the thickest of Samsung’s three current foldables, but it’s more compact than Motorola’s Razrs, its only real rivals.

Samsung didn’t upgrade the Z Flip 8 with the thinner, tougher titanium display stack found in the two new Z Fold 8 phones, which also means this has just as visible a crease as ever. It rarely bothers me, and is hard to see head-on, but you may feel differently. The IP48 rating is a more objective issue, and means that while this phone is mostly safe from water, it’s still vulnerable to dust.

On the inside, you’ll find the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 if you’re in the US, though my UK model runs Samsung’s Exynos 2600. Exynos chips get a bad rep, but performance has been smooth so far, and I have no real complaints.

This is the online-exclusive mint, but the phone’s also available in pink, cream, and gray. It’s a little thinner and lighter than before, but not by much. And the crease is still pretty noticeable compared to the two new Fold 8 phones.

As with the Z Fold 8 phones, Samsung switched to more energy-dense silicon-carbon batteries for the Z Flip 8. Unlike those phones, it didn’t actually increase the battery capacity, but instead used smaller cells with the same 4,300mAh capacity — the key to shrinking the phone itself. Still, battery life is solid, reliably lasting the full day with battery to spare. The charging — 25W wired, 15W wireless — is relatively unimpressive, and the only way to get Qi2 charging is still by using a compatible magnetic case.

Storage and RAM remain the same as on the Z Flip 7; the screens do too apart from small bumps to peak brightness, and the cameras are also identical to last year’s. The 50-megapixel main camera is impressive, and especially helpful since the form factor means you can use it for selfies too. The 12-megapixel ultrawide and 10-megapixel inner camera aren’t remarkable, but they get the job done. A slab phone at this price would have better cameras, and most likely a telephoto lens, but the lenses here are good enough.

Previous Next























1 / 13 The main camera mostly gets good results.

The question is whether it’s all good enough for the price, given Samsung has bumped the Z Flip 8 up to $1,199.99, a $100 increase. Z Flip 7 owners certainly shouldn’t upgrade, and anyone else should consider buying that phone instead, since the difference between the two is slight.

After all, the big upgrades are software, and unlikely to remain exclusive. Last year’s Z Flip 7 hasn’t yet been updated to One UI 9, but since its outer screen is almost identical, it seems likely to get the upgraded software, giving one less reason to opt for the new model. The Z Flip 6 and earlier, with their smaller cover screens, seem more likely to miss out. I’ve asked Samsung about its upgrade plans, but haven’t yet heard back.

Customizable Now Brief cards were added in One UI 9. The camcorder-inspired video recording is still one of the phone’s best features. If you find the full apps frustrating, various cover screen widgets are still available.

Most of the other software upgrades aren’t even Flip-specific. Customizable, AI-powered cards have been added to the daily Now Brief; My FanCam lets you crop video to focus on a specific subject; and Audio Eraser can now dim background noise and highlight dialogue in apps like YouTube and Netflix. You’ll find those features across all of Samsung’s new foldables, plus the new Galaxy S26 FE.

Modest as the Z Flip 8’s hardware upgrades are, it feels like a turning point for Samsung, which is mostly done trying to limit the ways people use the cover screen. Given the speculation that the short, wide Z Fold 8 could replace the Flip form factor as Samsung’s “small phone that unfolds to a big phone,” it makes sense to close the gap between them.

The Z Fold 8 is definitely bigger than the Z Flip 8. But the Flip’s small, obstructed screen is less functional — for better or worse. Open, the Z Fold 8 feels like a compact tablet. While the Flip opens up to a pretty regular phone.

The Z Fold 8 is a more capable phone than the Z Flip 8 when closed, its squat screen more usable than the Flip’s tiny one, despite Samsung’s software upgrades. But I have a real soft spot for the Flip form factor, which is tiny and pocketable when closed and a normal, almost compromise-free flagship phone when open — and endlessly satisfying to flip shut.

More than that, I enjoy its frictions. I welcome Samsung’s move to make it easier to use full apps on the cover screen, but I also welcome that it will never be entirely successful. Some apps simply don’t work on a screen this size, and the Z Flip 8 is all the better for it.

Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge

Agree to Continue: Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8 Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate. To use the Galaxy Z Flip 8, you must agree to: Google Terms of Service

Google Play Terms of Service

Google Privacy Policy (included in ToS

Install apps and updates: “You agree this device may also automatically download and install updates and apps from Google, your carrier, and your device’s manufacturer, possibly using cellular data.”

Samsung End User Licence Agreement

Samsung Privacy Notice

Samsung Terms and Conditions There’s also a variety of optional agreements, including: Provide anonymous location data for Google’s services

“Allow apps and services to scan for Wi-Fi networks and nearby devices at any time, even when Wi-Fi or Bluetooth is off.”

Send usage and diagnostic data to Google

Google Gemini Apps Privacy Notice if you opt in to using Gemini Assistant

Turn on Samsung offline finding

Samsung news and special offers

Samsung personalized advertising

Bixby personal data intelligence

Samsung customization service Other features, like Google Wallet, may require additional agreements. Final tally: seven mandatory agreements and more than nine optional agreements.

Tech.title: Musicians-turned-detectives are hunting for AI grifters
Tech.content:
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.

For musicians — especially those creating art in technologically-focused spaces like electronic dance music — the increasingly complicated question of what is “real” and what isn’t feels particularly urgent and personal. Professional courtesy can make this only more complex; listeners can call out performers they suspect of using gen AI, but it’s something else for artists to raise concerns about their professional peers. There are some though, like 26-year-old EDM producer Max “H4RRIS” Harris, who are taking a stand against generative technology with videos calling out anyone they believe is trying to pass off AI slop as human-made art.

When I recently spoke with Harris, he told me that he sees AI-generated music as “a kind of decoy art form,” and he thinks that the people making it don’t really have anything meaningful to say with their creations. He feels that true art in any medium is “created by people that are trying to express feelings and messages,” and he believes that the only thing AI boosters are really interested in is making a quick profit.

“I don’t consider AI-generated material to be art, and I don’t think this technology is really advancing art in any meaningful way,” Harris said. “It’s a technological advancement that’s giving people a way to steal real art and pass it off as their own.”

Harris, originally from Maine, described his approach to making music as being fairly similar to working in other creative mediums. He always begins with a core concept before he starts “throwing more ideas down until I find something that sticks.” And as complicated as his workflow might look to someone unfamiliar with all of the tools and programs that he uses — his production setup includes Ableton Live, Novation Launchkey 49 MIDI controller, Ableton Push 3, Launchpad X, a couple of analog synthesizers, Serum, Diva, and the software sampler Kontakt — he said that the entire process is “really just me making creative decisions” that culminates in a sound that feels right.

“Each of those decisions — and there’s hundreds of them to go into each song — brings me closer to evoking a specific kind of idea or emotion,” Harris explained. “And then once I have a song mapped out, I have to start making even more choices about how to mix it in a way that makes it sound good and presentable.”

In Harris’ view, being a real artist means being able to make those kinds of experimental but informed creative decisions using your own studied understanding of a given medium. One of Harris’ biggest issues with gen AI is the way the technology often eliminates a user’s need to think about how songs (or books, films, podcasts, etc.) come together. But he has also been dismayed at the way that AI posers are muddying listeners’ understanding of what human-made EDM actually sounds like.

“Aside from the similar vocals, you can usually hear a sharp hissing throughout the track,” Harris said of AI-generated songs. “I think that comes from the way that these models often work by starting with a big white noise block and then making guesses about waveforms by referencing data taken from real songs.”

Harris pointed to MANSA’s “Midnight on My Mind” and Danny and Ian Asher’s “Take Me (To The Moon)” as what he thinks are examples of AI-produced songs that embody what he jokingly refers to as “the AI revolution” that’s responsible for polluting the EDM space. MANSA, Danny, and Asher have not publicly commented on whether they use generative tools in their music. But Harris and other EDM fans have noticed the similarities between “Take Me (To The Moon)” and another person’s AI-generated track. There’s no definitive evidence that MANSA produced “Midnight on My Mind” with AI. Harris could very well be wrong about these songs being generated with AI. But his insistence that they are reflects the larger culture of mistrust that has developed in response to the growing presence of AI content online.

“People are just straight up uploading original, copyrighted tracks of artists like Madonna and asking [AI] to remix them.”

Harris holds AI production company Suno responsible for the recent spike in this kind of music being uploaded to the internet, but he also credits specific quirks of the platform for helping him learn how to spot songs worth calling out.

“Something I’ve noticed with a lot of Suno-generated tracks is that a lot of the time, you’ll hear the vocals and other melodic elements will start stuttering at the same exact time,” Harris explained. “These models still have a hard time fully separating different parts of the songs they’re trained on, and they treat these elements like one big instrument. As a music producer, all of these things come across like choices that a human just wouldn’t make with their compositions because it just doesn’t make sense.”

In some instances, the visuals accompanying AI tracks are part of what prompts Harris to accuse people of slinging AI. You might not be able to hear the generative models behind evangelical Christian AI persona Lionsaddle’s music, but you can clearly see the character’s fingers vanishing in and out of existence in videos. There is also an overly glossy visual quality to most of the videos posted by Christian house musician Midnite Manna that makes their content look a lot like what we typically refer to as AI slop.

Suno also came up multiple times during my conversation with 39-year-old Italian turntabilist-turned-producer Nihil Young. Young’s posts on Threads about people using Suno are what initially inspired Harris to make his videos. Like Harris, Young has spent the past few months watching multiple EDM newcomers’ stars rise after they post music he thinks was generated with AI tools like Suno’s. And while Young isn’t usually one to get involved with online discourse, he felt it was important to speak out about how many people are flooding the scene with AI tracks.

“These songs are the sound of Suno, which to me means that the people behind the songs are just straight up uploading original, copyrighted tracks of artists like Madonna and asking the platform to remix them,” Young told me, referring to Josh Fawaz’s “Like a Prayer” cover, which now includes AI credits following a wave of online backlash. “If they can do it with major artists like her, they can do it with you, me, and everyone else, which just isn’t cool. They can take your entire catalog, feed it to Suno, and generate ‘new’ songs from that stolen work.”

Young claimed that in response to his Threads posts, he received multiple hacking attempts and a wave of online harassment from AI defenders. He also told me that he thinks people bought fake followers to boost his Spotify numbers as a way of casting doubt on his authenticity. That spooked Young — who is raising a young daughter and just put out a new album of his own — to rethink whether he should continue. He’s taken a break from callouts, but he still thinks it’s important to know about the way AI music is harming human artists.
